title: A stable procedure can live in the weights instead of the prompt
takeaway: The prompt is only one place to store a workflow; the weights can be a cheaper one.

blocks.text: Most agent systems treat the system prompt as the only place a procedure can live, so every turn carries the full instructions. The experiment treats the adapter as the storage layer: the procedure is compiled into the weights and the prompt keeps only a stable trigger. That changes both the per-turn token cost and how the procedure is edited.

title: A 3B model matched Gemini on incident triage at 8.4× lower cost
takeaway: A stable, repeated procedure can be compiled into model weights instead of resent on every turn.

blocks.text: The experiment compiled a 3,500-token incident-triage SOP into a QLoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-3B. It reached 93.0% end-to-end accuracy against Gemini 2.5 Pro's 92.0%, while shrinking the prompt from 5,200 to 450 input tokens per incident.

items: 93.0% accuracy vs 92.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro
5,200 → 450 input tokens per incident, a 91.3% cut
$1.85 → $0.22 per 1,000 incidents, an 8.4× cost reduction
115 MB adapter, trained in under four hours on one RTX 3060

title: A procedural prompt is a tax you pay on every turn
takeaway: The cost of a long SOP is not writing it once; it is resending it forever.

blocks.text: Most agent setups paste the whole workflow into the system prompt and send it back on every turn. A 3,500-token SOP across five or six turns becomes roughly 5,200 input tokens per incident. The model rereads the same instructions instead of learning them.

title: Replace the SOP with a trigger token
takeaway: If the procedure is stable, the prompt can shrink to a name the weights already understand.

blocks.text: The compiled setup keeps zero instructions, schemas and runbooks in the prompt. The entire system prompt is `incident_triage_v1`. The state machine lives in the adapter, and the model still executes the diagnostic turns in the right order.

title: Mask the loss on tool outputs
takeaway: Train the model on its decisions, not on the simulated environment it reads.
section: The Training Setup: Loss Masking On Assistant Turns

blocks.text: In a multi-turn tool-calling trace, most tokens are user alerts and tool responses. Computing loss over all of them teaches the model to memorize random telemetry and commit hashes. Label those tokens `-100` so gradients flow only through the assistant's actions.

title: Build a simulator and an oracle before you fine-tune
takeaway: Synthetic multi-turn data only works when every trace is verifiably correct.
section: Building A Simulator And Generating Training Data

blocks.text: The experiment used a deterministic simulator with 12 microservices and 9 root causes, plus an oracle that knows the optimal path through the state machine. The oracle generated 5,116 conversations across five alert styles.

items: Model the workflow as a finite state machine.
Build a deterministic environment with known root causes.
Write an oracle that produces the optimal sequence.
Vary the alert format: PagerDuty, Slack, email, SMS, freeform.
Reject any trace that fails step order, schema, entity, root-cause, runbook or evidence checks.

title: Compiled weights are fast and cheap, but frozen
takeaway: Compile stable procedures; keep prompts for rules that change every week.
section: What I Learned From The Experiment

blocks.text: Prompts are easy to edit when the process changes; compiled weights are not. The compiled model wins on speed, prompt overhead and predictable local execution, but a rule change means retraining or versioning the adapter.

title: Slop debt is incoherence, not technical debt at volume
takeaway: The danger of LLM-generated code is not how much there is; it is that nobody chose its shape.

blocks.text: Slop debt is what accumulates when most of a codebase is generated by an LLM, reviewed by nobody who understands it, and merged because the tests pass. It compiles and works for now, but it was predicted one plausible token at a time rather than designed.

title: Tech debt comes from a decision; slop debt comes from the absence of one
takeaway: A decision leaves a reason you can recover. Slop leaves no author to ask.
section: Why It Is Not The Same Thing

blocks.text: Classic tech debt is a tradeoff: skip the abstraction, hardcode a value, ship now. The reason survives in the person or the git history. Slop debt has no architect; the model chose the variable names and error handling independently for every file, with no memory of the last one.

title: Slop debt compounds because the model reads its own slop
takeaway: Every generation pass turns existing incoherence into context for the next pass.

blocks.text: Once a codebase has hundreds of files of locally correct but globally inconsistent code, the next generation pass uses that code as context. It copies the bad abstraction because that is what it sees, and adds a third error-handling style because it cannot tell which of the first two is intended.

title: Code review cannot catch slop because slop is plausible
takeaway: Reviewers pattern-match on plausibility; slop is wrong in how it fits, not in how it reads.
section: The Point Where Debugging Stops Working

blocks.text: A slop diff reads correctly. It is only wrong in the way it fails to fit with everything around it, and that kind of wrong does not show up in a line-by-line diff. The person who "wrote" it clicked accept.

title: Incremental refactoring does not fix smeared incoherence
takeaway: Tech debt is local; slop debt is everywhere at low intensity.
section: Why Refactoring Does Not Save You

blocks.text: The normal move for tech debt is to isolate a module, test it, clean it up and move on. Slop debt has no single module to point at. Cleaning one file does not reduce the system's confusion while the file next to it generates new confusion at the same rate.

title: Past a certain size, rewrite with a human-owned architecture
takeaway: At scale, the honest fix is not "clean it up" but "start over with a shape a human chose".

blocks.text: Once slop debt has metastasized, refactoring cannot restore coherence. The workable reset is a rewrite where a human makes the architectural calls and the model is used as a tool inside a shape someone designed, not as the designer.

items: Stop treating it as high-volume tech debt.
Accept that incremental cleanup will not reduce system-wide confusion.
Budget for a rewrite once incoherence is smeared across the codebase.
Keep a human in charge of architecture and use the model as an implementation tool.

title: AI moves the bottleneck from writing code to verifying it
takeaway: If your process still optimizes for typing speed, it is optimizing for a constraint that no longer exists.

blocks.text: Every process was built to manage scarce engineering time. Agentic coding removes typing as the bottleneck, but verification, review and security take its place. The constraint moves; it does not disappear.

title: Plan just in time, not six months ahead
takeaway: If a decision can be undone with one more prototype, skip the design doc.

blocks.text: A six-month roadmap is out of date by month three because the tools keep changing what is possible. AI-first teams do the minimum planning right before they need it and reserve a full design doc for decisions that are expensive to reverse.

items: Prototype before writing a design doc.
Put it in front of 5–10 internal users within a day or two.
Move product decisions into the pull-request thread.
Write a design doc only for data-model or public-API changes.

title: Ask the model before the person
takeaway: The model watched the change; the author may no longer be the fastest path to context.
section: Ask The Model Before The Person

blocks.text: Before agentic coding, "who wrote this" was the fastest way to get context. Now the model can walk the git history, summarize ownership from CODEOWNERS and recent commits, and pull the PR discussion. Ask what you actually need to know, then go to a human for judgment calls the model cannot make.

items: Regression: correlate git history with the failing test.
Ownership: summarize CODEOWNERS and recent commit activity.
Decision context: read the PR description and linked discussion.
Repeated question: turn it into a standing job.

title: Let AI own style, bugs and tests; humans keep security, legal and product judgment
takeaway: The test for a human gate: is a wrong call expensive to reverse, or does it require risk-tolerance judgment?

blocks.text: The model handles style, linting, PR feedback, bug fixes and tests. Humans stay where domain judgment cannot be automated: legal and compliance, security and trust boundaries, product taste and whether the feature solves the user's problem. If the answer to both questions is no, the PR does not need a human gate.

title: Hire for product sense and systems depth, not raw throughput
takeaway: When the model absorbs the typing, the scarce skill is knowing where a human must decide.
section: Team Makeup - Roles Blur On Purpose

blocks.text: Roles blur: PMs ship prototypes, engineers pick up content and design. The two profiles that matter are creative builders with product sense and engineers with deep systems expertise—distributed state, latency budgets, security boundaries—that a model cannot yet reason about reliably.

title: AI-assisted commit percentage is a trap metric
takeaway: Throughput measures activity, not outcomes; pair it with retention, incidents or adoption.
section: Metrics That Tell You The New Norms Are Sticking

blocks.text: A team can drive AI-assisted commits to 100% and still ship the wrong thing faster. Track onboarding ramp time, PR cycle time and the share of AI-assisted commits, but always pair throughput with a metric tied to the actual problem being solved.

title: Audit your noisiest workflow
takeaway: A ritual built for a bottleneck that no longer exists should be deleted or automated.

blocks.text: Pick the workflow your team dreads most: the status meeting, the manual release checklist, the weekly report nobody reads twice. Ask whether it still serves its original purpose, and if it does, whether it can be automated instead of run by hand.

items: Name the gap the ritual was created to close.
Check whether that gap still exists with AI tools in the loop.
Kill the ritual if the gap is gone.
Automate it if the purpose remains.

title: Docs rot silently; tools fail loudly
takeaway: Encode operational knowledge as executable tools, not prose nobody notices is stale.
section: Why Build Tools Instead of Writing Docs

blocks.text: A stale wiki can mislead people for months. A broken tool fails in front of the next person who uses it, which means it actually gets fixed. That difference matters more now that AI agents act on the same instructions.

title: The three skills are create-service, deploy and debug
takeaway: These are the three places where missing knowledge turns into waiting, guessing and 2 AM incidents.
section: Why Build Tools Instead of Writing Docs

blocks.text: The three skills are: provision a new service end to end, deploy and roll back with tests and smoke checks, and diagnose an incident from symptoms to evidence. Each turns a manual, stale process into an executable one.

title: Build the debugging skill first
takeaway: Incidents happen on their own schedule, so every one can add a verified failure pattern.

blocks.text: The debugging skill should match live symptoms to known failure patterns for that service, link directly to the relevant logs, traces and dashboards, and run diagnostics instead of pointing at raw data. Start with the service that pages most and takes longest to fix.

items: Keep a running incident history per service.
Link dependencies and their health dashboards.
Extract verified failure patterns from retros.
Return a likely cause, evidence and links—not "check the logs".

title: Build deployment second, with rollback and smoke tests
takeaway: Rollback is the path used under pressure and the one most teams exercise least.

blocks.text: The deployment skill should run tests against the real target environment, roll out gradually, execute smoke tests automatically, and roll back without a human remembering a separate procedure. It needs deployment history, migration state, environment config and a defined set of smoke-test endpoints.

items: Test against the real target environment.
Roll out gradually.
Run smoke tests automatically.
Roll back on failure without a separate manual runbook.

title: Build create-service last
takeaway: It touches the most infrastructure; a half-built version is worse than none.

blocks.text: The create-service skill provisions the database, wires logging, registers identity and deploys to production before anyone writes business logic. It is the most valuable day-one fix, but also the riskiest to half-build because it relocates confusion instead of removing it.

title: Track one metric per tool
takeaway: Pick a number that is cheap to measure and hard to argue with.

blocks.text: Measure time from a fresh repo to a live deployment, deployment frequency alongside rollback rate, and mean time to diagnose an incident. Feed incidents and rough onboarding experiences back into the tools as requirements.

items: Create-service: time from a fresh repo to a live deployment.
Deploy: deployment frequency alongside rollback rate.
Debug: mean time to diagnose an incident.

title: G-Eval turns an LLM into a rubric-driven judge
takeaway: Use it when output quality is real but there is no single gold answer to compare against.

blocks.text: G-Eval is a prompting framework for reference-free evaluation. It gives a model a precise rubric, lets it generate its own evaluation steps, and converts its token probabilities into a fine-grained score instead of trusting a printed digit.

title: Reference-free evaluation is the point
takeaway: Most real outputs—support replies, summaries, chatbot turns—have no one correct answer in a dataset.

blocks.text: A reference-based metric needs a gold-standard example. G-Eval does not. It defines the dimension precisely and asks the judge to evaluate the candidate against that definition, which is why it can cover custom criteria like brand voice or refund-policy compliance.

title: Make the rubric precise, not a 1–5 vibe check
takeaway: A vague rubric collapses to "does this look fine"; a precise one gives the judge specific things to check.

blocks.text: Instead of "rate this 1 to 5", define what coherence means in concrete terms. A vague rubric gives the model nothing to anchor against, so it cannot discriminate a mediocre output from a strong one. A precise rubric is also what makes human raters consistent.

title: Generate the evaluation chain-of-thought once per rubric
takeaway: Commit to a procedure before seeing outputs, then cache it.

blocks.text: G-Eval asks the model to write its own evaluation steps from the task and criterion before it sees a candidate. That forces a concrete procedure instead of pattern-matching, and leaves an audit trail: when a score looks wrong, read the chain-of-thought to see where the judge diverged.

title: Never judge with the same model family
takeaway: LLM judges show a measurable self-preference bias toward their own family.
section: The Bias You Need to Know About

blocks.text: Even when human reviewers prefer the alternative, judges favor text generated by models from their own family. Use a different family for the judge than for the system under test, pin the judge version, and recalibrate the rubric against human-labeled examples.

title: Use a classifier or parser when the answer is closed-form
takeaway: G-Eval is the wrong tool for toxicity, PII or valid JSON.
section: When This Is the Wrong Tool

blocks.text: Anything with a sharp, closed-form answer does not need a reasoning model reading a rubric. A fast classifier or parser is cheaper, faster and more reliable. Reach for G-Eval only when the judgment is open-ended.

items: If the check has one correct answer, start with a parser or classifier.
Reserve a rubric-driven judge for open-ended quality.
Measure latency and cost before adding a judge.

title: An AI workflow is a dependency graph, not a list
takeaway: If you cannot draw the edges, you cannot know what can run in parallel or what a failure affects.
section: The Dependency Problem in AI Workflows

blocks.text: Every workflow has producers and consumers, and consumers cannot run before their inputs exist. A DAG models tasks as nodes and dependencies as directed edges; topological sort turns that graph into a valid execution order.

title: Dependencies are correctness constraints, not scheduling preferences
takeaway: Running a step early does not save time; it reads stale data or calls a tool with missing context.
section: The Dependency Problem in AI Workflows

blocks.text: Embedding before chunking embeds dirty text. Retrieving before the index is complete queries an incomplete index. The edges are not optional; they are the difference between a correct pipeline and a plausible-looking one.

title: Let the graph find parallelism
takeaway: Nodes in the same topological level have no dependency between them and can run concurrently.

blocks.text: In a branching RAG pipeline, keyword filtering and retrieval can run in parallel once the index is built; the merge node waits for both. Topological sort produces the order automatically, so the orchestrator does not hardcode sequencing.

title: Recompute only the affected subgraph
takeaway: On failure or input change, traverse forward from the affected node and reuse every cached output outside it.

blocks.text: This is how Bazel and Buck avoid rebuilding the world. The DAG makes it tractable: without explicit dependency edges, you cannot know which downstream nodes are affected.

title: Topological sort does not balance work
takeaway: It tells you the order, not where the critical path is.

blocks.text: If ten parallel tasks feed one merge node, the merge waits for the slowest. Profile the longest chain of dependent tasks to see where parallelism actually helps; fan-in bottlenecks remain.

title: Validate cycles at definition time, not at 2 AM
takeaway: A cycle means deadlock: A waits for B, B waits for A, nothing progresses.

blocks.text: If the topological order is shorter than the graph, there is a cycle. Catch it when the workflow is defined, surface the offending cycle, and reject the workflow before a single task runs.

items: Compare the topological order length with the node count.
Identify the nodes that remain in the cycle.
Reject the workflow at definition time.
Show a clear error instead of hanging at runtime.

title: A DAG is a contract
takeaway: The graph is the spec; the topological order is the scheduler's input.

blocks.text: Drawing the dependency graph first forces you to separate truly sequential tasks from independent ones. Parallelism, cycle safety and incremental recomputation all fall out of the structure you declared.

title: The embedding model sets the floor; chunking and evaluation decide the ceiling
takeaway: Most retrieval failures are bought before the model is chosen, in how documents are split and measured.
section: Picking a Model Is Not The Hard Part

blocks.text: Teams spend weeks comparing embedding benchmarks, then split every document at a fixed character count and wonder why recall is poor. The model supplies the semantic space, but the chunks decide what can be found inside it. A boundary through the middle of a fact makes that fact unretrievable no matter how good the encoder is.

title: A chunk must be precise enough to retrieve and complete enough to answer
takeaway: Chunk size is a direct trade between findability and usable context, not a formatting detail.

blocks.text: Small chunks isolate one idea, so their vectors match narrow queries, but they strip away the surrounding context an answer needs. Large chunks preserve context while averaging several ideas into a single vector, which makes any one idea harder to retrieve. Most prose works best around 256–512 tokens with 10–20% overlap, so a fact at a boundary still appears whole in a neighbouring chunk.

title: A flattened table embeds as noise unless every row carries its headers
takeaway: Tables need a serialization that preserves row-column meaning, or retrieval will never surface the values inside them.

blocks.text: A table is two-dimensional meaning forced into a one-dimensional string. Serialized naively, a row of values loses the labels that explain what each number represents, so the encoder produces a vector with nothing useful to match against. Repeating the header on every row, or writing cells as `column: value` pairs, restores the relationship; large tables can also embed at parent level with individual rows as children.

title: Every vector is stamped by the model that produced it
takeaway: Embedding model choice is a migration commitment, not a swappable implementation detail.

blocks.text: Vectors from different encoders occupy different geometric spaces, so a query embedded by one model cannot be meaningfully compared with documents embedded by another. Changing models therefore invalidates the entire index, and a zero-downtime move requires two indices running side by side. The decision deserves the same care as a database schema change, because undoing it is a full offline batch job.

title: Hybrid retrieval buys recall; the reranker buys precision
takeaway: Dense search and BM25 fail on different queries, and a reranker can only improve a candidate set that already contains the answer.

blocks.text: Dense search misses exact product codes and rare jargon that never became a stable direction in embedding space, while lexical search catches them. Merging both candidate lists, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, widens the pool that a cross-encoder can then score jointly. The reranker fixes ordering, not coverage, so low recall has to be repaired upstream before reranking is worth its latency.

title: Diagnose the retrieval stage before replacing the model
takeaway: Separating missing context from irrelevant context turns a vague quality complaint into a specific fix.

blocks.text: A weak answer can come from missing context, irrelevant context, or a model that ignored good context, and a new encoder only helps some of those cases. RAGAS separates recall from precision so each pipeline change can be judged against the previous one. Absolute scores do not transfer between evaluation sets; the before-and-after delta is the usable signal.

items: Build 100–200 query and answer pairs from real domain traffic.
Measure context recall and precision before changing anything.
If recall is below 0.7, fix chunking or widen retrieval.
If precision is low, add a reranker before swapping models.
Change one stage at a time and keep the golden set fixed.

title: A stale embedding answers yesterday's question with today's confidence
takeaway: Outdated vectors are worse than missing ones because the model presents old text as current fact.

blocks.text: When a document is updated, its old vectors can keep retrieving the outdated version, and the model then explains that version fluently. The user sees a confident answer with no signal that the source moved, which is harder to catch than an empty result. Incremental re-indexing plus a `last_embedded_at` timestamp keeps the index from drifting away from the documents.

title: Durable execution makes crash recovery a property of the runtime, not your code
takeaway: If a process must survive crashes mid-flight, encode it once and let the platform own recovery.

blocks.text: A process that charges a card, provisions a resource, and sends an email cannot simply restart after a timeout without risking duplicate effects. Teams rebuild status tables, retry loops, and sagas to approximate what a durable execution platform records automatically. The workflow stays linear in code while the platform persists each completed step and resumes from the last one.

title: One determinism line separates orchestration from side effects
takeaway: The workflow-versus-activity split is the rule that makes replay possible and failure recovery safe.

blocks.text: Workflow code decides order and branching and must produce the same decisions from the same history. Activity code touches the outside world, may fail, and may return a different result on every attempt. Workers are stateless processes polling a queue, so any worker can take over after a crash, but only if the workflow itself is replay-safe.

title: Recovery replays the event history instead of restoring a snapshot
takeaway: Persisted events, not in-memory state, are what let a new worker continue exactly where the old one stopped.

blocks.text: Every scheduling decision, activity completion, timer, and signal is appended to an immutable history. On recovery, a worker re-executes the workflow function from the start, but completed activity calls return their recorded results instead of running again. The workflow fast-forwards to the end of that history and continues, which is why taking a different path breaks it.

title: Renaming an activity can break workflows that are already running
takeaway: Deploying workflow code is a compatibility problem, and in-flight executions are the clients you must not break.

blocks.text: Old executions replay old history against the newly deployed code. Reordering activity calls, renaming one, or inserting a step changes the commands the workflow emits, so they no longer match the recorded events and Temporal raises a non-determinism error. A version gate records which branch an execution took, letting old runs replay the old path while new runs take the new one.

title: A signal lets a workflow wait days for a human without polling
takeaway: Durable suspension removes the polling table and background job that approval workflows usually grow.

blocks.text: Signals are asynchronous messages delivered to a running workflow, and `wait_condition` suspends that workflow until the expected state arrives. Nothing sits in a loop and no resources are consumed during the wait; if the worker dies, another one resumes the same wait. This makes approval gates and human-in-the-loop steps ordinary workflow state instead of a polling service.

title: A durable timer replaces the cron job and its state table
takeaway: Sleeping inside a workflow is persistent, so delayed work survives restarts without a scheduler re-reading state.

blocks.text: A timer is not a thread sleep: the execution is suspended and its wake-up time is stored by the server. A thirty-day delay still fires after redeployments or a server restart, because the schedule lives in persistent storage rather than in a process. Any process that must do something, wait, then continue is simpler as a timer than as repeated cron runs.

title: Long-lived workflows must periodically restart their own history
takeaway: An execution that runs forever will eventually hit a replay ceiling, so long-running designs need a planned reset.

blocks.text: Temporal caps an execution at 50,000 events or 50 MB because replay cost grows with history length. A perpetual monitor or subscription manager will hit that ceiling unless it calls continue-as-new, which closes the current run and starts a fresh one with the same workflow ID and the current state as input. Trigger it well before the limit, around 10,000 events, to keep replay latency predictable.

title: Production RAG fails through the index, not the prompt
takeaway: If you cannot explain which chunks produced an answer, you cannot tell a retrieval bug from a model bug.

blocks.text: A demo retrieves something plausible from a handful of PDFs, so the model appears to work. In production, documents are updated and deleted, chunks are cut badly, and an answer can be confidently wrong because the model reasoned faithfully over the wrong context. Index freshness, retrieval quality, and chunk-level tracing are the actual engineering work.

title: An index is married to the embedding model that built it
takeaway: A model upgrade is a corpus migration, so the encoder deserves more up-front thought than a config value.

blocks.text: Query vectors are only comparable with document vectors produced by the same encoder, because each model defines its own geometry. Upgrading the model therefore invalidates every stored vector at once, and the migration is a batch re-embed rather than a setting change. The workable path is a shadow index, a sample of shadow traffic, then a gradual alias shift.

title: A document registry is what makes deletes and updates possible
takeaway: Vector stores have no parent-document concept, so deletion needs an external map from documents to chunks.

blocks.text: A document split into fifteen chunks has fifteen independent vector IDs, and the vector store does not know they came from one source. Without a mapping from document ID to current chunk IDs, an update leaves orphans and a delete leaves retrievable ghosts. A small relational table closes the gap: look up the old chunks, remove them, then insert the new set.

title: Hash content so unchanged documents never reach the embedding API
takeaway: Most update events do not change the text, and hashing turns a full rebuild into a small diff.

blocks.text: Most updates change a title or a timestamp rather than the body that was embedded. A content hash compared against the registry skips those documents entirely, and per-chunk hashes narrow re-embedding to the sections that actually changed. For long, mostly stable files this is the difference between re-embedding a corpus and re-embedding a few paragraphs.

title: A crashed re-index leaves a seam that retrieval cannot see
takeaway: Partial index updates mix document versions invisibly, so index deployment needs the same atomicity as a database migration.

blocks.text: If a rebuild dies halfway, some documents are on the old version and some on the new, and every query silently mixes them. The alias pattern avoids the seam: build a complete new index, validate it, then atomically point the read alias at it and keep the old one for rollback. No query ever sees a partial build.

title: A useful RAG trace names the chunks, their scores, and the index version
takeaway: Chunk-level attribution is what turns a vague bad answer into an actionable retrieval finding.

blocks.text: A span that records only the final prompt cannot explain why an answer went wrong. Emit an event per retrieved chunk with its source, score, rank, and index version, then nest embedding, search, rerank, and generation under one root span. When quality drops after a deploy, the index version is what lets you correlate the two.

title: Wrong document, wrong section, and ignored context need different fixes
takeaway: Three retrieval failures look identical from the answer alone, and only chunk attribution separates them.

blocks.text: All three produce a confident wrong answer, so tuning the model treats symptoms at random. Chunk-level evidence separates them: a wrong document points to index corruption or model drift, a right document with the wrong section points to chunk boundaries, and correct context that the model ignored is a generation problem. Each has a different repair.

title: A chat is a role-tagged message list, and the roles are trained behaviour
takeaway: Once you see the message list as structure the model was trained on, prompt bugs become architecture bugs.

blocks.text: A base model only continues text, so a bare question may be answered with more questions. Instruction tuning teaches the model that system text is persistent guidance, user text is a request, and assistant text is the continuation it should produce. The message list is therefore a control surface, not a display format.

title: The system prompt is a strong lever, not a security boundary
takeaway: System instructions shape behaviour reliably, but they cannot enforce a permission the model can be talked past.

blocks.text: System content gets heavy attention because instruction tuning taught the model to treat it as persistent, which makes it the right place for persona, scope, format, and fallback rules. It is still token prediction, so a hostile user message can sometimes override the instruction. High-stakes applications must validate outputs and enforce permissions outside the prompt.

title: The model remembers nothing; you resend the conversation on every call
takeaway: Conversation memory is an application-level illusion built by paying for the whole history on each request.

blocks.text: Each API call is stateless, so a second turn must include the system prompt, the first user message, and the first assistant reply. Token cost therefore grows with conversation length, and a long chat plus retrieved documents can exhaust a large context window. History is also editable: you can summarize, prune, or replace prior turns before sending them.

title: Prefill the assistant turn to constrain the model's output shape
takeaway: A partial assistant message is a cheap structural constraint that works alongside instructions.

blocks.text: If the assistant message already begins with `{`, the model continues from that token instead of deciding how to start. Prefilling is useful when a parser needs a predictable opening and instruction-following alone has been unreliable. It constrains the beginning, not the whole output, so the result still needs validation.

title: A wrong chat template degrades a local model without raising an error
takeaway: Self-hosted models fail through quietly worse output when the wrapper ignores the format they were trained on.
section: How Format Maps to Raw Text

blocks.text: Hosted APIs serialize roles into special tokens invisibly; runtimes such as llama.cpp and Ollama leave that step to you. The model was fine-tuned against one exact marker format, so using another produces subtly worse output rather than a failure. The symptom looks like a weak model when the real problem is the wrapper.

title: Treat system prompts as versioned dependencies, not editable text
takeaway: A prompt shared by every conversation is production infrastructure, so changes need review and evaluation.

blocks.text: Every conversation in an application depends on the same system prompt, so one edit can alter behaviour everywhere. Versioning it and evaluating changes against representative prompts turns an invisible regression into a reviewable diff. The same discipline applies to separating persona from hard constraints.

items: Keep persona, scope, format, and fallback rules in separate labelled sections.
Store prompts in version control and review changes like code.
Run a fixed evaluation set before deploying any prompt change.
Never interpolate raw user input into the system prompt.
Decide the context-window policy before conversations grow long.

title: An LLM is a next-token probability machine; reasoning is an emergent effect
takeaway: One sampling operation, repeated at scale, explains both the fluency and the failure modes.

blocks.text: At each step the model outputs a distribution over its vocabulary, samples one token, and feeds that token back in. Apparent reasoning, code generation, and conversation all come from repeating that operation over a large training corpus. The loop is a better mental model than a lookup table or a store of facts.

title: Temperature changes where you sample, not what the model knows
takeaway: Temperature is a distribution-shaping parameter, so it cannot add knowledge or improve reasoning by itself.

blocks.text: Temperature divides the logits before softmax. Below 1 it sharpens the distribution toward the most likely token; above 1 it flattens the distribution and gives unlikely continuations more mass. The underlying knowledge and reasoning are unchanged; only the region you draw from changes.

title: Chain-of-thought works because generated tokens become context
takeaway: Intermediate reasoning is functional scratch space, not a ritual the model performs for the reader.

blocks.text: The model has no separate planning step; it commits to each token left to right. Asking it to write intermediate reasoning places those tokens into the context that conditions the final answer, which genuinely changes the distribution. The scratch space is real, and that is why removing it can make a multi-step answer worse.

title: Hallucination is a plausible continuation, not a failed lookup
takeaway: A model cannot distinguish a fact it learned from a pattern that merely fits, so precise claims need external verification.

blocks.text: The model stores co-occurrence statistics, not rows of facts, so familiarity in training data is not the same as correctness. When a prompt expects a name, number, or citation, sampling can produce something that sounds right without being true. Confidence tracks how often similar text appeared, not whether the claim was verified.

title: One successful run does not prove a prompt works
takeaway: Plausible alternatives mean outputs vary, so reliability has to be measured across runs rather than judged from one sample.

blocks.text: When several continuations are plausible, repeated runs produce different outputs, and the model can even contradict itself across calls. A single good result hides the variance that will appear in production. Consistency requires either near-zero temperature or validation logic that tolerates variation.

title: Choose temperature by task, then test at that setting
takeaway: Matching the sampling regime to the task is more reliable than turning one global creativity dial.

blocks.text: Low temperatures exploit the model's most confident predictions, which suits code, extraction, and factual answers. Middle settings preserve some variation for chat and summaries, while high settings explore unusual phrasing at the cost of reliability. The ranges are starting points, not guarantees.

items: Use 0–0.3 for code, structured extraction, and factual Q&A.
Use 0.7–1.0 for chat, summarisation, and general writing.
Use 1.2–2.0 only for brainstorming or deliberately varied prose.
Run each candidate prompt multiple times at the chosen setting.
Validate parsed output rather than trusting format stability.

title: A shared-database monolith already pays the coordination cost of distribution
takeaway: Judge the architecture by its real coupling, not by the number of deployable artifacts.
section: What Your Monolith Has Actually Become

blocks.text: Distribution is expensive because of coupling, contracts, and failure propagation, not because packets cross a network. A monolith with many feature areas on one schema has all three while looking simple. The danger is that nobody treats it as a distributed system, so none of the usual boundaries get designed.

title: A shared database is a global variable with an unversioned contract
takeaway: When every module can query every table, a schema change becomes an invisible broadcast to unknown consumers.

blocks.text: Any module can read any table, so a column rename reaches code the team has forgotten about. The repository and service references get updated; the analytics job querying the table directly breaks later. In a service architecture that contract would be an API schema, but here it is implicit and invisible.

title: Module boundaries that nothing enforces are only aspirational
takeaway: A clean box-and-arrow diagram is not an architecture until dependencies are enforced by something stronger than intent.

blocks.text: A diagram of boxes and arrows does not create a compilation boundary, an ownership model, or a contract. Under deadline pressure one module calls another directly, or reads its tables, and the diagram stops matching the code. The coupling only becomes visible when someone tries to extract a module and finds dependencies everywhere.

title: A synchronous call chain inherits every failure domain it touches
takeaway: Function calls feel free because they are fast, which lets risk accumulate until one dependency can stop the whole operation.

blocks.text: Function calls cost nanoseconds, so chains grow across payments, inventory, notifications, and analytics without visible cost. Every step must complete for the operation to finish, which means the operation fails if any dependency fails. Replacing network calls with function calls hides that risk rather than removing it.

title: Audit the monolith you have, not the one in the diagram
takeaway: Measuring real coupling is the only way to know whether the architecture deserves its reputation.
section: What Your Monolith Has Actually Become

blocks.text: The useful questions are about actual coupling: how many feature areas share tables, what the real call graph looks like, and how many people must coordinate a deploy. If those answers are large, the system is already distributed. The point is to make the invisible structure visible before it causes another outage.

items: Count the feature areas reading each core table.
Draw the real call graph from imports and queries, not the intended one.
List synchronous chains that cross more than four concerns.
Count the engineers who must coordinate one deployment.
Find the last shared utility change that broke unrelated tests.

title: Keep the monolith, but give each module its own data and interface
takeaway: The alternative to microservices is not an unowned pile of tables; it is a monolith with real internal contracts.

blocks.text: One module should write a set of tables, and other modules should read through its interface rather than querying underneath it. Shared utilities need the same versioning discipline as a library owned by several services, since that is effectively what they are. This keeps the deployment simplicity of a monolith without leaving the coupling invisible.

title: The curse of dimensionality is a distance problem before it is a modelling problem
takeaway: Separate distance-based components from linear-algebraic ones before choosing a mitigation.
section: Distance concentration: when nearest means nothing

blocks.text: High-dimensional data is not harder merely because it has more columns; it is harder because proximity stops meaning what it did in two or three dimensions. Algorithms that depend on nearness, density, or spherical neighbourhoods degrade together. Knowing which parts of a system are distance-based tells you where the curse will bite.

title: Covering a high-dimensional space needs exponentially more samples
takeaway: Sample requirements grow with dimension, so the data gets thinner exactly when more features demand more evidence.
section: The volume explosion that breaks everything

blocks.text: Keeping points 0.01 apart in a unit interval needs 100 samples; the same density in ten dimensions needs 10^20. The rule of thumb of five examples per dimension sounds manageable until the data is images, genomes, or embeddings. Sparse coverage makes every neighbourhood unrepresentative, so local estimates are built on almost no evidence.

title: In high dimensions the nearest neighbour is barely closer than the farthest
takeaway: When distances concentrate, nearest-neighbour guarantees evaporate and tree indexes degrade toward scanning everything.
section: Distance concentration: when nearest means nothing

blocks.text: Each added dimension contributes an independent term to squared distance, so distances crowd around a common value as dimension grows. The relative gap between nearest and farthest shrinks roughly as 1/√d, which strips k-NN of its guarantees and leaves DBSCAN without a meaningful epsilon. Tree indexes such as kd-trees often collapse to linear scans somewhere between 10 and 30 dimensions.

title: Adding features without adding samples eventually makes classifiers worse
takeaway: Feature selection and regularization are responses to geometry, not stylistic preferences.
section: The Hughes phenomenon: more features, worse classifiers

blocks.text: With a fixed training set, accuracy rises as useful features arrive, peaks, then falls as extra dimensions give the model more ways to fit noise. When dimensions outnumber samples, every test point sits far from the training data and the model extrapolates. The optimal feature count depends on sample size, so more columns are not automatically more information.

title: Hubness makes a few embeddings answer almost every query
takeaway: A retrieval index dominated by a handful of vectors is a symptom of geometry, not evidence that search is working.
section: The hubness problem: a less-discussed failure mode

blocks.text: When distances concentrate, the k-nearest-neighbour graph becomes heavy-tailed: a small set of points appears in many neighbour lists while most points appear in none. In retrieval this looks like the same few documents surfacing for unrelated queries, and in clustering the hubs act as false centroids. A healthy index should not have 500 embeddings serving most results.

title: Random projection can shrink dimensions without breaking distances
takeaway: Dimensionality reduction can preserve distances rather than only discarding signal.
section: The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma: a structural escape hatch

blocks.text: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma says a set of n points can be mapped to O(log n / ε²) dimensions while keeping pairwise distances within 1 ± ε. The target depends on point count and allowed distortion, not on the original dimension, so a million points at 10% distortion need roughly a few thousand dimensions regardless of whether the source has 10,000 or millions. A random Gaussian matrix is enough to build the projection.

title: Instrument for concentration before choosing a dimensionality fix
takeaway: The right mitigation depends on whether the failing component actually relies on distance.

blocks.text: Plot the distance distribution, check retrieval diversity, and estimate intrinsic dimensionality before reducing anything. PCA is the cheap production default, but it preserves variance rather than the target signal, while UMAP is better for visualization than for invertible transforms. The measurement should decide the intervention.

items: Plot pairwise distances at the dimensionality you serve.
Measure how many embeddings cover most retrievals.
Reduce with PCA to 90–95% explained variance and re-measure recall.
Try Lp norms with p < 2 for genuinely sparse data.
Tune embedding size empirically instead of copying a default.

title: Agents invalidate the database contract that assumed a careful human caller
takeaway: Design the data layer for a caller that can be wrong, can retry, and is not watching.

blocks.text: For decades the caller was deterministic code, reviewed before deploy, issuing a bounded set of queries and noticing when something broke. Agents reason their way to new queries, retry on their own, hold connections while thinking, and may never notice a wrong result. Practices once treated as optional become load-bearing once that caller disappears.

title: An empty result with HTTP 200 is the most dangerous answer an agent can receive
takeaway: Silent semantic failure is harder to catch than an exception because the agent keeps working on bad data.

blocks.text: A downstream connection pool exhausted, a legacy API returned success with no rows, and the agent read 'no data' as 'no problem'. It then processed 500 transactions on incomplete information with no exception and no alert. A semantically wrong query that returns rows is invisible in a way an error is not.

title: A stable idempotency key collapses agent retries into one write
takeaway: At-least-once orchestration only becomes safe when the database can recognise a repeated logical operation.

blocks.text: Orchestrators deliver at least once, so a timeout can cause the same logical step to run twice. A key derived from the task ID and the operation, enforced by a unique constraint, makes the second attempt a no-op that the database absorbs. The agent still gets a success response and does not need to know which attempt actually landed.

title: Give agents soft deletes and append-only logs, not destructive writes
takeaway: If the caller may misunderstand the task, reversible writes turn a catastrophic action into an inspectable event.

blocks.text: An agent that misreads the task can remove thousands of rows before anyone reacts. Soft deletes preserve the row and record `deleted_by`, which makes 'what did this agent remove?' a query instead of an investigation. High-stakes state changes are safer as append-only events, where undo becomes a projection rather than a restore.

title: LLM think time turns connection pooling into a queueing problem
takeaway: Agent sessions hold connections across model latency, so pooling must be sized for thinking time rather than query time.

blocks.text: An agent holds a connection across query, inference, and another query, so hold time becomes execution plus model latency times reasoning steps. Sub-agents multiply one task into several sessions, and agent headcount can grow tenfold from development to production. A dedicated pool with a short timeout plus PgBouncer transaction pooling lets 20 Postgres connections serve hundreds of agent sessions.

title: When an agent reads your schema, column names are prompt text
takeaway: Schema legibility becomes a correctness feature once a language model is writing the queries.
section: Assumption - Schema is a Contract With Engg

blocks.text: A text-to-SQL agent or MCP server sees table names, column names, nullability, and comments, and those details shape whether it writes a correct query. Names designed for developer convenience produce confident nonsense; descriptive names and comments produce correct joins with less prompting. Legacy schemas can be translated through an agent-facing view layer.

title: Least privilege is the guardrail an agent cannot reason its way around
takeaway: Application code constrains a deterministic program, but only the database constrains a general-purpose reasoner.

blocks.text: Application code constrains a deterministic program, but an agent can invent a query path nobody anticipated. A database role with broad rights turns one bad reasoning step into a system-wide incident. The design question is not what the agent needs, but what the worst case looks like if its reasoning or credentials fail.

title: BM25 wins because every part of its score has a job you can inspect
takeaway: The formula is not magic; it is a set of explicit relevance assumptions you can trace and tune.
section: What BM25 Was Built To Solve

blocks.text: TF-IDF rewards repetition linearly and ignores document length, so a long document can outrank a focused one just by accumulating terms. BM25 replaces the linear count with a saturating curve and scales it by relative document length. Each component maps to a relevance assumption, which makes unexpected rankings explainable rather than mysterious.

title: Term frequency should saturate, not scale linearly
takeaway: The first occurrences of a term carry most of the evidence, so repetition should have diminishing returns.

blocks.text: The first few occurrences of a query term are strong evidence that a document is about it; later occurrences add progressively less. BM25 models this with a curve that rises steeply and approaches an asymptote of k1 + 1. A low k1 saturates quickly, while a higher k1 lets repetition keep contributing.

title: Length normalization stops long documents from winning by accumulation
takeaway: A term appearing in a short focused document is stronger evidence than the same term buried in a long one.

blocks.text: Three mentions in a 300-word note are a stronger signal than three mentions in a 10,000-word chapter. BM25 divides the effective term frequency by the document's length relative to the corpus average, controlled by b. At b = 0 length is ignored; at b = 1 the adjustment is full; the default 0.75 applies partial normalization.

title: Tune k1 and b to the corpus, not to the default
takeaway: The defaults are a starting point; repetition and length behave differently in every corpus.

blocks.text: The right values depend on whether repetition is informative and whether length correlates with relevance. Short documents and exact identifiers favour faster saturation; long, jargon-heavy documents favour slower saturation. Changing the analyzer also changes token counts and therefore the effective b.

items: Increase k1 when long documents repeat domain terms meaningfully.
Decrease k1 for short items, SKUs, or keyword-stuffed pages.
Raise b when document lengths vary widely.
Lower b when long documents are long because they are comprehensive.
Fix the analyzer before tuning b, because it changes token counts.

title: BM25 cannot see synonyms, word order, or intent
takeaway: BM25 is strongest when exact terms carry meaning and weakest when the user's vocabulary differs from the document's.

blocks.text: The bag-of-words assumption means 'New York' and 'York New' score identically, and 'heart attack' shares nothing with 'myocardial infarction'. A query for 'python' cannot be routed to programming, zoology, or comedy by term statistics alone. Those blind spots are predictable, which makes them a boundary for when lexical retrieval is the right tool.

title: Use BM25 as the lexical leg of a hybrid retriever
takeaway: Lexical and dense retrieval fail on different queries, so combining them covers exact matches and paraphrases at once.
section: When To Use BM25 vs Alternatives

blocks.text: BM25 is fast, interpretable, and hard to beat for codes, names, and legal phrases that embeddings blur. Dense retrieval covers the paraphrases and natural-language queries BM25 misses. Running both and fusing the candidate lists gives recall that neither style achieves alone.

title: Elasticsearch computes IDF per shard, so the same document can score differently
takeaway: Distributed term statistics make scores shard-dependent unless you explicitly request a global pass.

blocks.text: Each shard calculates document frequency from only the documents it holds, so a term's rarity depends on where the document landed. Scores are therefore not directly comparable across shards, and adding shards changes the statistics. A global statistics pass is available when consistency matters more than the extra round trip.

title: Every join algorithm is a way to dodge the full cross product
takeaway: Knowing which structure a join exploits tells you why the planner picked it and when it will betray you.

blocks.text: A join asks for all row pairs whose keys match; compared naively that is |R| × |S| comparisons, which becomes trillions on two million-row tables. Real algorithms buy their speed by exploiting one of four structures: sorted order, a hash table, an index, or a partition. The choice is therefore a statement about what the data already has, not a matter of taste.

title: Nested loop join is an I/O problem disguised as a comparison problem
takeaway: The outer side matters because every restart of the inner scan can cost disk reads, not because the comparison count changes.

blocks.text: The naive loop does |R| × |S| comparisons, but swapping which table is outer leaves that product unchanged. What changes is how many times the inner table is rescanned, and whether it still sits in the buffer pool. A small outer table means the inner table is read once and then largely served from cache; a large outer table evicts those pages before the next row can reuse them.

title: Hash join turns a quadratic join into two linear passes
takeaway: For large equality joins with no useful order, hashing is usually the cheapest way to avoid scanning the inner table.

blocks.text: The build phase streams the smaller relation into an in-memory hash table keyed on the join column. The probe phase walks the larger relation once, hashing each key and emitting matches from the table. That gives O(|R| + |S|) instead of a product, but only while the predicate is equality and the build side fits in memory.

title: One dominant key can collapse a hash join into a serial scan
takeaway: Average row counts hide the skew that actually decides join performance.

blocks.text: Hashing assumes keys spread evenly, but a status column where most rows are `active`, or a flood of NULLs, puts most rows in one bucket. That bucket is probed and emitted row by row while the rest of the table sits idle, and the work starts to resemble the nested loop the hash was meant to replace. A single hot key cannot be rebalanced across workers.

title: Merge join only wins when the sort is already paid for
takeaway: Sorted input makes a linear merge; unsorted input makes the sort the dominant cost.

blocks.text: A merge join walks two sorted inputs with one pointer each, comparing keys and advancing the smaller one, which costs a single linear pass. If neither side is sorted, the planner must add O(n log n) sorts first, and that becomes the real price. The compensation is memory behavior: sorting can spill and merge in chunks, so it degrades gracefully where a hash build would fail outright.

title: An index join replaces a scan with a seek, one outer row at a time
takeaway: Index joins are excellent for small outer inputs and selective matches, and terrible for the reverse.

blocks.text: Instead of reading every page of the inner table, the executor looks up matching rows through a B-tree or hash index, turning O(|R| × |S|) into roughly O(|R| log |S|). That works when the outer side is small and each lookup returns few rows. If the outer side is large and the index is not selective, the plan becomes a storm of random I/O that a sequential scan would beat.

title: When the hash table won't fit, partition both sides first
takeaway: Grace hash join makes an out-of-memory hash join possible at the cost of writing everything to disk once.

blocks.text: Both relations are hashed into k partitions on disk with the same function, so matching keys always land in the same partition pair. Each pair is then loaded and joined in memory using a second hash function. The cost is about three passes over the data, and the partition count must be large enough that a single partition fits the buffer pool.

title: Broadcast the small table only while copying it everywhere beats a shuffle
takeaway: In a distributed join, the decision is a network-cost comparison, not an algorithmic one.

blocks.text: Broadcast sends a full copy of the small relation to every node, then lets each node join its local slice of the large table without moving that slice. The network cost is the small table times the node count, against a shuffle that moves both tables. Broadcast is the right call only when N × |small| is far below |large|; a 10 GB table sent to 1,000 nodes is 10 TB.

title: Half of a software engineer's knowledge expires in a handful of years
takeaway: Treat the currency of your knowledge as a maintenance cost, not a one-time acquisition.

blocks.text: The half-life of professional knowledge is the time in which half of what you know is replaced. For an engineering degree earned in 1930 it was roughly 35 years; by 1960 it had fallen to about a decade. Estimates for software now sit between two and a half and seven years, clustered at the low end.

title: A five-year half-life turns learning into a permanent second job
takeaway: The weekly hours needed to stay current are large enough to plan for, not squeeze in.

blocks.text: Thomas Jones estimated an engineering degree at about 4,800 hours, so a ten-year half-life writes off roughly 2,400 of them within a decade. His remedy was about five hours of study per week, which over a career totals 9,600 hours, roughly two more degrees. At a five-year half-life the modern estimate rises to seven to ten hours per week.

title: Most daily engineering work sits in the layer that decays fastest
takeaway: Fluency in frameworks is necessary but is the least durable asset you can hold.

blocks.text: Software knowledge splits into fundamentals — data structures, algorithms, distributed systems, complexity — and tooling: frameworks, APIs, configuration conventions. The first layer transfers across stacks, while the second is tied to a version and a vendor. The awkward part is that the ephemeral layer is where most day-to-day work happens, so it feels like the important one.

title: Twenty years of experience is not twenty years of current knowledge
takeaway: Knowledge decay explains why seniority does not compound linearly in software hiring.

blocks.text: A senior engineer holds more total knowledge, but if half of it turns over every five years, much of that store no longer matches current stacks. Hiring screens that reward current keywords and the salary premium on seniority push in the same direction. The result is a market response to decay, not simply age bias.

title: Buy durability with fundamentals, real problems, and T-shaped depth
takeaway: The way to survive a short half-life is to learn things that transfer and apply them where they stick.

blocks.text: A few strategies make permanent learning affordable: invest in fundamentals such as system design and algorithmic thinking, learn how to learn so you can find the core of a new tool quickly, and adopt tools through real production problems. Breadth across ecosystems plus depth in a couple of areas adapts better than a single-stack specialty.

items: Spend a fixed share of study time on fundamentals that outlive tools.
Practice extracting a framework's core concept before its API details.
Introduce a new tool through a live business problem, not a toy project.
Build breadth across ecosystems and depth in two or three areas.

title: AI removes the tasks that used to create senior engineers
takeaway: Tools that amplify experienced judgment also make the path to that judgment harder to walk.

blocks.text: Coding assistants now handle boilerplate, suggest implementations, find bugs and write tests — much of the work that once trained juniors. Senior engineers gain leverage because generated output still needs review and architectural judgment. The paradox is that the same automation shrinks the entry-level reps from which that judgment was built.

title: Multi-Paxos is basic Paxos with the prepare phase amortized across a leader
takeaway: The protocol's speed comes from paying the expensive agreement step once per leader term, not once per write.

blocks.text: Basic Paxos decides one value and pays two round trips every time: prepare, then accept. Multi-Paxos observes that a single stable leader can hold the right to propose, so the prepare phase is done once and reused for a whole sequence of log entries. The result is a replicated log with half the message delays in steady state.

title: Quorums work because any two majorities must overlap
takeaway: Majority voting is not a compromise on safety; the overlap is what prevents two conflicting decisions.

blocks.text: In a five-node cluster a quorum is three, and any two groups of three share at least one node. That shared node cannot promise the same log slot to two different values, so two conflicting commits cannot both gather a majority. Requiring everyone instead would let a single failure stop the system, while a cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures.

title: A new proposer must adopt the highest value already accepted
takeaway: Safety comes from inheriting prior decisions instead of overwriting them.

blocks.text: During prepare, each acceptor promises to ignore lower-numbered proposals and reports any value it has already accepted. If the proposer sees an accepted value, it must propose the one with the highest accepted number rather than its own. That rule is what stops a late proposer from erasing a value that may already have been chosen.

title: The ballot belongs to the leader's term, not to each proposal
takeaway: Separating leadership epochs from proposal numbering is what makes the fast path possible.

blocks.text: In basic Paxos the proposal number rises with every attempt, forcing a prepare round each time. Multi-Paxos uses a ballot that changes only when leadership changes, so a stable leader can send accept messages under the same ballot for many entries. That removes one round trip from every subsequent write, cutting four message delays down to two.

title: Replicate the order of operations, not the state they produce
takeaway: A deterministic state machine plus an agreed log is enough to keep replicas identical.

blocks.text: Each log slot is its own Paxos instance, and the leader assigns incoming requests to monotonically increasing positions. Replicas apply committed entries in that same order to their local state. Because the starting state and the operation sequence match, every replica reaches the same final state without shipping state around the network.

title: Batching, pipelining and leader reads multiply the fast path
takeaway: Once agreement is one round trip, throughput comes from doing fewer of them and overlapping more.

blocks.text: A leader can pack several transactions into one log entry, so the consensus overhead is shared across them. Pipelining keeps multiple instances in flight so network latency overlaps with work instead of serializing it. Reads can skip consensus entirely when served by the leader, which already holds the newest committed state.

title: A crashed leader does not lose the transaction it was committing
takeaway: Recovery is built into the next election because promises carry the accepted history.

blocks.text: When followers time out on the leader, a candidate runs prepare with a higher ballot and collects promises. Those promises include previously accepted values, so the new leader can complete an entry the old one started. Leases reduce the chance of two leaders overlapping, which would cost efficiency rather than safety.

title: Routing every write through one leader makes hot keys the ceiling
takeaway: Strong ordering concentrates load, and the fix is to partition the hot range rather than add replicas.

blocks.text: Spanner replicates each tablet as its own Paxos group with a leader that handles all writes, so a key range receiving disproportionate traffic saturates one group. Splitting hot ranges into smaller groups spreads the write load. Read replicas and client-side caching of slowly changing data reduce pressure without touching the write path.

title: MySQL replication is a pull-based pipeline wrapped around an append-only log
takeaway: Once you see the dump thread, relay log and applier as separate stages, most replication failures have an obvious place to look.

blocks.text: The source records every change as an event in the binary log and keeps one dump thread per connected replica. The replica pulls those events with its I/O thread, parks them in a relay log, and applies them with a SQL thread. Splitting receipt from application is the design decision that lets a replica buffer, catch up, and resume after a disconnect.

title: Statement logging is compact until a non-deterministic function reaches the replica
takeaway: Row-based logging buys determinism with disk space, which is why it is the default.

blocks.text: Statement-based logging stores one SQL statement regardless of how many rows it touches, which is very compact. It breaks when the statement contains `NOW()`, `UUID()`, `RAND()`, or a `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`, because replay can produce a different result. Row-based logging ships the actual before and after images, so replicas get exactly the source's changes at the cost of one event per row.

title: The relay log keeps a slow applier from stalling the source
takeaway: Buffering received events locally is what makes asynchronous replication tolerant of slow consumers.

blocks.text: The receiver writes incoming events to relay files that use the same format as the binary log, and the applier reads from there. If applying is slow, the backlog grows on the replica's disk instead of applying backpressure to the source. The relay position also acts as a checkpoint for resuming after a disconnect.

title: A replica replays concurrency as a single line
takeaway: Single-threaded apply is the default reason a replica falls behind a busy source.

blocks.text: The source may commit many transactions in parallel, but a single-threaded applier executes them one after another in log order. Replica throughput is therefore capped by one thread's work, no matter how much parallelism the source had. That mismatch is why multi-threaded replication exists.

title: Transactions can replay in parallel only if they did not conflict on the source
takeaway: Parallel apply needs a safe independence signal, and MySQL offers two: commit groups and write sets.

blocks.text: Logical clock parallelism, added in 5.7, uses timestamps that mark which transactions committed together; those transactions did not conflict, so they can apply in parallel. MySQL 8's WRITESET approach goes further and tracks the actual rows each transaction touched, allowing parallelism across transactions that never shared a commit but wrote disjoint rows. WRITESET yields more parallelism and costs more memory.

title: Semi-synchronous replication buys durability with a wait, then gives up after a timeout
takeaway: The safety guarantee is only as strong as the timeout allows it to be.

blocks.text: In the default asynchronous mode the source commits without waiting, so a crash can lose transactions no replica received. Semi-synchronous mode holds the commit until at least one replica acknowledges receipt into its relay log. If no acknowledgement arrives within the timeout, ten seconds by default, the source reverts to asynchronous mode rather than block forever.

title: Give replicas equal resources and every table a primary key
takeaway: Most replication lag is configuration and schema, not bad luck.
section: Best Practices for Replication in Production

blocks.text: A replica with fewer cores, less memory or slower disks will lag no matter how well the network performs. Row-based logging avoids replay surprises, and crash-safe metadata prevents a restarted replica from losing its position. Primary keys on replicated tables are the single largest row-based performance lever.

items: Provision replicas at least as powerful as the source.
Use row-based logging for deterministic replay.
Store replication metadata in crash-safe tables.
Add a primary key to every replicated table.
Monitor lag continuously and test failover on a schedule.

title: A Bloom filter buys memory with the right to be occasionally wrong
takeaway: When a false positive costs a retry and a false negative costs correctness, a few bits per key can replace gigabytes.

blocks.text: A Bloom filter stores no keys, only a bit array and a set of hash functions, so it answers membership in constant time with a tiny footprint. It never reports absent for something present, but it can report present for something never added. The trade is deliberate: certainty in one direction, probability in the other, in exchange for roughly an order of magnitude less memory.

title: A zero bit is proof of absence; a one bit is only a hint
takeaway: The asymmetry of the bit array is the whole data structure.

blocks.text: Insertion hashes an element to k positions and sets those bits to one. A lookup that finds any zero knows the element was never inserted, because insertion would have set that bit. If all k positions are one, other elements may have set them, so the answer is only maybe.

title: Fifty billion seen-item IDs collapse to about a tenth of their size
takeaway: Storing membership as bits instead of keys is what makes per-user history affordable at scale.

blocks.text: Ten million users who have each seen 5,000 articles produce 50 billion 64-bit identifiers. Keeping them in hash sets costs hundreds of gigabytes before hash-table overhead, and a 1.5× factor on that set lands near 600 GB. A Bloom filter stores only bit positions and lands around 60 GB, roughly a tenth, while still answering the seen-before question.

title: One percent false positives costs about 9.6 bits per element
takeaway: The false-positive rate is a budget you can price in bits, and the price grows slowly.

blocks.text: Adding bits lowers the false-positive rate, while adding hash functions helps only up to an optimum for the given bits-per-element ratio. At 1% you need about 9.6 bits per element, and at 0.1% about 14.4. That is still roughly seven times smaller than storing 64-bit integers directly.

title: Two hash functions can generate all k bit positions
takeaway: Independent hashes are mathematically convenient but computationally wasteful.

blocks.text: The Kirsch–Mitzenmacher result shows that a linear combination of two hashes produces positions with the same asymptotic false-positive behavior as k independent hashes. This double hashing cuts the CPU cost of membership tests substantially, which is why most production filters use it. The subtlety is that a zero or non-coprime second hash can collapse several positions onto each other.

title: Deleting from a Bloom filter costs either four times the memory or some certainty
takeaway: A standard filter cannot forget, and every workaround pays for that.

blocks.text: Clearing a bit set by one element can erase another element that shares the position, creating a false negative. Counting filters replace bits with small counters, typically four bits, which quadruples memory and risks saturation when a counter tops out. Deletable Bloom filters instead track which regions have suffered collisions and only clear elements whose bits all sit in clean regions.

title: A filter per SSTable turns a multi-file lookup into a disk-read decision
takeaway: In an LSM store, the filter's job is to prove a key is absent before anyone touches the disk.

blocks.text: LSM writes land in a memtable and flush to immutable SSTables, so a read may have to check several files. A Bloom filter attached to each SSTable can rule out most of them without I/O. Cassandra exposes the trade directly: a lower `bloom_filter_fp_chance` uses more memory and avoids more pointless reads.

title: Broadcast the filter, not the table, when only a few rows match
takeaway: Filtering before the join can shrink the data that participates by an order of magnitude.

blocks.text: In a distributed join between a billion-row table and a small one, broadcasting the small table still makes every executor scan its full partition. A Bloom filter built from the small table's join keys is a few hundred kilobytes instead of megabytes, and it lets each executor drop rows that cannot match before joining. In one example, only about 5% of rows survive, cutting the join input from a billion rows to fifty million.

title: There is no global clock, only clocks with error bars
takeaway: Any design that treats timestamps as a total order assumes something the hardware cannot provide.

blocks.text: Every machine keeps time with its own oscillator, and no two oscillators run at exactly the same rate. Synchronization narrows the gap but never removes it, so a timestamp is really an estimate with a bounded uncertainty. Distributed systems either respect that bound or quietly rely on luck.

title: Two machines that never talk drift seconds apart within a month
takeaway: Quartz drift is large enough to break assumptions long before anyone notices.

blocks.text: Consumer clocks count a 32,768 Hz crystal, and temperature is the biggest source of error: a swing of about 10 °C can shift the rate enough to lose roughly 110 seconds a year. Manufacturing variation and aging add more. Two machines started together can differ by hundreds of milliseconds in a day and by seconds after a month.

title: Clock skew never raises an error; it silently reorders events
takeaway: Bad timestamps produce plausible but wrong history, which is harder to catch than a crash.

blocks.text: A build tool compares file timestamps, so a server clock running ahead makes a freshly edited source look older than the object file and the change is skipped. A database can timestamp a withdrawal before the deposit that funded it, so a snapshot shows money spent that was never added. Tracing systems draw effects before their causes.

title: Every physical sync algorithm is a bet on symmetric network delay
takeaway: NTP's accuracy is limited by the path as much as by the server's clock.

blocks.text: Cristian's algorithm estimates one-way delay as half the round trip, which is only right when the two directions take the same time. Real routes are asymmetric, so the estimate carries a bias that no amount of polling removes. The Berkeley algorithm avoids absolute times by sending each machine a relative adjustment, and it slows clocks rather than jumping them backward.

title: Lamport timestamps order causality but cannot detect concurrency
takeaway: If you need to know whether two events were independent, a single counter is not enough.

blocks.text: Lamport's rule increments a local counter per event and takes the maximum on receive, so A happening before B guarantees A's timestamp is lower. The converse fails: a lower timestamp may mean A preceded B, or that the two were concurrent. Vector clocks carry one entry per process, which distinguishes those cases at O(N) space per timestamp.

title: Spanner pays about 7 ms per commit to make time trustworthy
takeaway: Bounded uncertainty can be converted into strong ordering by waiting out the bound.

blocks.text: TrueTime returns an interval rather than a point, built from GPS receivers with atomic clocks as backup and cross-validation. A transaction gets a commit timestamp, and Spanner waits until the clock has provably passed it before reporting success. That commit wait is typically around 7 ms and is overlapped with other commit processing.

title: Hybrid logical clocks keep timestamps readable and causally correct
takeaway: You can get most of physical time's debuggability without atomic clocks.

blocks.text: An HLC keeps a physical component near wall-clock time and a logical component that advances when events share a tick or clocks skew. Timestamps stay close enough to real time to read during debugging, while causally related events still order correctly. CockroachDB uses a maximum offset around 500 ms and removes a node whose clock exceeds it. YugabyteDB reported up to 3× lower transaction latency after adopting a precision time source, because a smaller bound means less waiting.

title: Match the clock mechanism to the ordering guarantee you actually need
takeaway: Over-synchronizing wastes money; under-synchronizing silently corrupts order.
section: How do You Pick One Over the Other

blocks.text: Millisecond NTP is enough when transactions already take tens of milliseconds, because a sub-millisecond skew cannot reorder them. Logical clocks cover ordering without physical accuracy, and PTP with hardware timestamping reaches microseconds where regulation or physics demands it. The cost curve is steep, so state the requirement before buying the hardware.

items: State the maximum clock error your ordering can tolerate.
Start with NTP if transactions are slower than that error.
Use logical clocks where only causal order matters.
Adopt PTP only when microseconds are a real requirement.
Monitor clock rate and alert on backward jumps.

title: Adding Kafka partitions is cheap; the assumptions it breaks are not
takeaway: The command takes seconds, but key ordering and consumer state can change permanently.
