blocks.text: Kafka adds partitions by updating metadata and creating new directories; it never moves existing messages. The new partitions start empty and fill over time. What changes immediately is the mapping from key to partition and the assignment of partitions to consumers, which is where the damage happens.

title: A consumer group can never be more parallel than its partition count
takeaway: Partition count is the ceiling on both write throughput and read concurrency.

blocks.text: Producers write to partitions in parallel and each consumer in a group owns a disjoint set, so parallelism is bounded by how many partitions exist. A fifth consumer in a four-partition topic sits idle. Storage also spreads across brokers by partition, which is why expansion is used after adding nodes.

title: Changing the partition count remaps every key
takeaway: The default partitioner hashes the key and takes a modulus, so the modulus is part of your ordering contract.

blocks.text: Kafka picks a partition by hashing the message key with Murmur2 and reducing it modulo the partition count. Add partitions and the modulus changes, so the same key can land somewhere new. Old messages stay in the old partition while new ones go to the new one, which means two consumers can process the same entity concurrently.

title: Existing messages stay put because moving them would rewrite offsets
takeaway: Kafka's append-only log makes redistribution an application migration, not a broker operation.

blocks.text: Expansion leaves all historical messages in their original partitions; the new ones begin empty. Redistributing them would mean rewriting offsets and breaking every consumer's stored position. Kafka keeps the simpler invariant and pushes redistribution onto whoever needs it.

title: Migrate keyed topics by dual-writing to a new topic, not by expanding
takeaway: A new topic preserves key order and state placement; expansion does not.

blocks.text: The safe path is to create a topic with the target partition count and write to both old and new during the transition. Consumers keep reading the old topic until it drains, then switch over. For stateful stream processing the recommendation is stronger: create new topics, because changelog state is partitioned and does not follow redistributed keys.

title: Rebalancing used to stop the world; cooperative protocols move only what must move
takeaway: The cost of expansion depends as much on the rebalance protocol as on the partition count.

blocks.text: The original eager protocol revoked every partition from every consumer and reassigned from scratch, so a large group could spend 30 seconds or more processing nothing. Cooperative rebalancing, added in Kafka 2.4, releases only the partitions that need to move and lets the rest keep running. KIP-848 in Kafka 4.0 moves assignment to the broker and makes it asynchronous, so unaffected consumers never pause.

title: Idempotent producers survive expansion; assumptions about partition identity do not
takeaway: Sequence tracking is per partition and keeps working, but logic that hardcodes key-to-partition mappings can silently break.

blocks.text: Idempotent producers track a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers, and new partitions simply begin their own sequences, so deduplication stays correct. Transactions spanning partitions also remain atomic across the change. The risk is application logic that assumes a fixed partition count or a stable key mapping, including transactional IDs built from partition numbers.

title: Product quantization shrinks a vector by replacing each chunk with a centroid ID
takeaway: Compression without dimensionality reduction is what lets a billion-vector index stay in RAM.

blocks.text: PQ splits a high-dimensional vector into m subvectors and learns a small codebook of centroids for each subspace. A vector is then stored as m centroid indices instead of its original coordinates. Distances are computed against those codes, so the index gets much smaller while still approximating the original geometry.

title: A billion 128-dimensional vectors is 512 GB before any index overhead
takeaway: Raw float storage stops fitting on commodity hardware well before the dataset stops growing.

blocks.text: One million 128-dimensional vectors at 32 bits per dimension is 512 MB; a billion is 512 GB, before the graph structures of an HNSW index are counted. Modern embeddings make it worse: 3,072 dimensions at a billion vectors is roughly 12 TB of raw floats. Compression is the difference between an index that fits in RAM and one that does not.

title: PQ represents an exponential number of vectors with a linear codebook
takeaway: The Cartesian product is the trick: many small codebooks beat one impossible one.

blocks.text: Quantizing a 128-dimensional space directly would need an impractically large set of centroids, since the codebook grows exponentially with dimension. PQ instead keeps one codebook per subspace, each with k centroids, and any combination of choices is a valid reconstruction. With 8 subspaces and 256 centroids each, 2,048 stored centroids cover 256^8 possible vectors.

title: One byte per subspace turns a 512-byte vector into 8 bytes
takeaway: The compression ratio follows directly from m and the code width, which makes it easy to plan.

blocks.text: A 128-dimensional float vector occupies 512 bytes. With 8 subspaces and 256 centroids each, every index fits in a byte, so the code is 8 bytes — a 64× reduction. Training the codebooks needs only a representative sample, typically ten to a hundred thousand vectors, rather than the whole dataset.

title: Precompute the query's distances once, then score a vector with m lookups
takeaway: Asymmetric distance computation keeps the query exact and pays only on the database side.

blocks.text: SDC compares two codes, so both vectors carry quantization error. ADC leaves the query unquantized and compares it against quantized database vectors, so only the stored side is approximate. For a given query, it builds a table of distances from each query subvector to every centroid in the matching codebook, then scores any code with m lookups and additions.

title: PQ's compression is paid back in recall, so over-fetch and rescore
takeaway: Treat the compressed index as a candidate generator, not the final judge.

blocks.text: A compressed index returns approximate neighbors, so some true matches fall outside the candidate set. Systems recover recall by probing more lists, rescoring candidates with the original vectors, and combining keyword search with vector search. Over-retrieving before a reranker is the usual pattern: accept a wider candidate set, then pay for precision only on that set.

title: Attention works because Q, K and V are three different views of the same token
takeaway: Separating asking, being found, and carrying information is the mechanism, not an implementation detail.

blocks.text: Each input embedding is projected three ways: a query describing what the token needs, a key describing what it offers, and a value carrying what it passes on. Attention compares queries against keys to decide where to look, then mixes values accordingly. Using one projection for all three would collapse those roles into a single representation.

title: Read attention as a soft database lookup
takeaway: The database analogy makes the score-softmax-weight sequence predictable.

blocks.text: A query is the search term, keys are the indexed entries, and values are the records returned. Attention differs from a hard lookup in that it returns a weighted blend of every value rather than one exact match. The weights come from comparing the query with each key and normalizing the scores.

title: Three weight matrices, one input: the split is functional, not architectural
takeaway: Q, K and V are the same rows projected into different spaces, so their shapes follow from d_model and d_k.

blocks.text: With an input matrix of shape n × d_model, each weight matrix has shape d_model × d_k, so the projection produces n × d_k. The three matrices are learned independently because finding relevant keys, being findable, and carrying content are different jobs. The output dimension d_k is a capacity choice, not something fixed by the input.

title: Each attention head gets d_model divided by the head count
takeaway: The projection width is where capacity is traded against compute.

blocks.text: The per-head dimension is d_model divided by the number of heads, so a 768-dimensional model with 12 heads gives each head 64 dimensions. A smaller d_k is cheaper in memory and compute but captures less complex relationships. Larger projections model more but cost proportionally more, which is why production models balance heads against width.

title: Q, K and V are only the setup; the output is a weighted sum of values
takeaway: The matrices matter because of what happens after them: scores, softmax, and a value mix.

blocks.text: Attention multiplies Q by the transpose of K to score every token pair, scales by the square root of d_k, and applies softmax to turn scores into weights. Those weights then combine the rows of V into one output per position. The projection step is only the preparation for that sequence.

title: Inference is two workloads: a parallel prefill and a memory-bound decode
takeaway: Knowing which phase you are in tells you whether to tune compute, memory bandwidth, or cache size.

blocks.text: The prompt is processed all at once, then the answer is emitted one token at a time. Prefill does matrix-matrix math and saturates the GPU's compute; decode does one matrix-vector step per token and spends most of its time waiting on memory. Because the bottleneck changes mid-request, the optimizations that help each phase are different.

title: The KV cache trades quadratic recompute for linear memory
takeaway: Caching keys and values is the biggest single inference speedup, and the bill arrives as GPU memory.

blocks.text: Keys and values for tokens already processed never change, so only the newest token needs fresh projections. Caching the rest turns attention from repeated work over the whole history into a lookup. Generating 1,000 tokens takes about 10 seconds with the cache and about 50 without it, close to a 5x gap.
The cache grows with sequence length. For a 13B model each generated token costs roughly 1 MB, so a 4,000-token context needs about 4 GB — comparable to the weights themselves.

title: Latency that spikes on long prompts is usually the cache outgrowing GPU memory
takeaway: Check cache memory before blaming the GPU, because spilling is invisible in utilization charts.

blocks.text: Long inputs inflate the cache until it no longer fits, and the slowdown looks like a weak machine rather than a memory problem. In one case response times climbed with every long prompt until the cache was identified as the cause. Reducing cache precision from FP16 to INT8 cut response times by more than half.

title: Tokenizers decide your bill before the model runs
takeaway: Two prompts of equal length can cost very different amounts, because tokens are the unit of work, not characters.

blocks.text: Byte Pair Encoding starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token. Frequent words end up as one token; rare words split into familiar pieces, which keeps the vocabulary small without losing coverage.

Text is encoded to UTF-8 and then compressed by those merge rules into integer IDs. Languages that were underrepresented in tokenizer training need more tokens per word, so the same sentence costs more compute and more context.

title: Dropping precision takes a 7B model from 14 GB to 3.5 GB
takeaway: Precision is a dial that can fit a model onto hardware you already own.

blocks.text: Memory is roughly parameter count times bytes per parameter: 7B at two bytes each is about 14 GB, and at half a byte each it is 3.5 GB, small enough for consumer hardware. Training usually runs at FP32 or BF16, while inference tolerates FP16, INT8, and even INT4 with little quality loss.

Post-training quantization picks scaling factors by observing activation ranges on representative data. GPTQ and AWQ apply scales per channel or per group, and some methods keep activations at higher precision than weights.

title: Measure time-to-first-token and inter-token latency separately
takeaway: A single latency number hides which phase is failing and therefore which fix will work.

blocks.text: Time to First Token covers prefill, and it is the entire wait before a user sees anything. Inter-token latency covers decode, and it is what makes streaming feel smooth or stuttery. Throughput in tokens per second describes capacity, while low GPU utilization during decode points at memory traffic rather than arithmetic.

title: A serving framework is usually a cheaper throughput win than a bigger GPU
takeaway: Batching and cache management can multiply throughput on hardware you already have.

blocks.text: vLLM pairs PagedAttention for cache management with continuous batching and reports 2-4x the throughput of a naive implementation on identical hardware. TensorRT-LLM adds NVIDIA-specific kernels with in-flight batching and FP8 support. TGI trades some peak performance for broad model support and a streaming HTTP API.

title: A blocking queue replaces hand-written coordination with a wait
takeaway: Most synchronization code around a producer-consumer pipeline exists because the queue refuses to block.

blocks.text: A normal queue returns null or an error when it is empty, and rejects a write when it is full. A blocking queue suspends the caller instead, waking it when the condition it needs becomes true. That single change removes busy-wait loops and the explicit lock and condition-variable choreography around them.

title: A bounded queue gives you backpressure for free
takeaway: Choose a bound and you have chosen your failure mode: slower producers, not exhausted memory.

blocks.text: With a fixed capacity, producers park when the buffer fills and consumers park when it drains. The system slows down instead of growing without limit, and memory is committed up front so usage is predictable. An unbounded queue absorbs every burst silently and only reveals the problem when the process dies.

title: Capacity decides whether you pay in blocked producers or queued latency
takeaway: Queue depth is a latency budget, so size it from observed wait times rather than from a round number.

blocks.text: A tiny buffer makes producers spend their time blocked and holds throughput down. A huge one absorbs spikes but each task waits behind a long backlog before anyone touches it. An unbuffered channel is the extreme other end: sender and receiver must meet, which is good for synchronization and poor for throughput.

title: Every channel you leave open is a goroutine that cannot exit
takeaway: Design the shutdown path at the same time as the data path, or leaks accumulate quietly.

blocks.text: Consumers blocked on a channel that nobody closes will wait for the lifetime of the process. Poison pills work only if each consumer gets one, so the safer move is closing the channel and letting a range loop terminate. Sends on a channel with no ready receiver deadlock just as easily.

title: A worker pool is a blocking queue with a fixed number of consumers
takeaway: One queue plus a pool size is enough to turn overload into caller-visible backpressure.

blocks.text: Submitters push tasks onto a channel that a fixed set of workers reads. When the buffer is full, the submit call itself blocks, so the pressure reaches whoever is producing work. Pipelines extend the same idea by putting a queue between each stage, letting slow stages buffer independently instead of stalling the whole chain.

title: Audit every queue for a bound, a close path, and an exported depth
takeaway: Four checks catch most production concurrency bugs before they page you.

items: Replace every unbounded buffer with a capacity chosen from measured load.
Give each consumer an exit: close the channel from the producer side or cancel with a context.
Check the success flag whenever `select` has a `default` branch.
Export queue depth as a metric and alert when it grows without draining.
Keep heartbeat and handler paths free of blocking sends.

title: Failure detection is a timeout, and every timeout is a guess
takeaway: No threshold can tell a dead node from a slow one, so the design target is a tolerable rate of being wrong.

blocks.text: A node emits a small periodic signal, and a monitor records when it last arrived. Silence past a threshold is treated as failure, which is only ever an inference. Short thresholds catch real crashes quickly and misread congestion or a garbage-collection pause; long ones tolerate jitter and leave traffic pointed at a corpse.

title: Derive the timeout from measured round-trip time, not from a round number
takeaway: Two ratios keep a failure detector from firing on normal network variance.

blocks.text: The common rule is a timeout of at least two to three heartbeat intervals and at least ten times the observed round-trip time. Counting consecutive misses rather than a single gap absorbs isolated packet loss. At two-second intervals with three misses allowed, a node is declared failed after six seconds.
Those ratios have to be set per path: a cross-continent link that normally takes 80 ms can spike to 200 ms under congestion, so a locally tuned threshold would produce false alarms there.

title: At 1,000 nodes, a 500 ms heartbeat buys 2,000 messages a second of overhead
takeaway: Detection speed is a bandwidth line item, and it competes with the traffic you actually care about.

blocks.text: A thousand nodes reporting twice a second produce two thousand health messages per second before any application request is served. Very short intervals also turn brief pauses into apparent failures. The opposite mistake is worse for users: at a 30-second interval a crashed node keeps receiving requests for half a minute.

title: Phi accrual turns "dead" into a confidence level you can choose
takeaway: An adaptive detector removes the need to hand-tune one timeout for nodes on very different networks.

blocks.text: Instead of a binary verdict, the detector keeps a sliding window of recent inter-arrival times and estimates when the next heartbeat should have come. The phi value rises smoothly as lateness grows: roughly 1 means 90% confidence, 2 means 99%, and 3 means 99.9%. Cassandra marks a node down at phi 8, about 99.9999%.

title: Gossip scales failure detection by making every node a detector
takeaway: Constant per-node message cost and no central monitor, paid for with slower and less uniform agreement.

blocks.text: Each node keeps a membership list with heartbeat counters and periodically swaps the whole list with a few random peers, merging the newest entry per node. Messages per node stay flat as the cluster grows, and no single monitor can fail. The cost is convergence delay: nodes briefly disagree about who is alive, and the same state is copied many times over.
Cassandra gossips with up to three peers every second and tracks both a generation number, bumped on restart, and a version number, bumped each round.

title: A partition looks exactly like a crash from both sides
takeaway: Heartbeats tell you that someone went quiet; only a quorum tells you who is allowed to act.

blocks.text: When connectivity splits, each side stops hearing the other and can conclude the other side is gone. Two leaders then accept writes and diverge, which is far worse than a pause. Requiring a majority before electing or writing means only the larger side proceeds; in a five-node cluster, three nodes form a quorum and the remaining two stop accepting writes.

title: Push or pull is a question about who can reach whom
takeaway: Pick the direction the network and firewall already allow, then add the other as a backup.

blocks.text: A pushed heartbeat is only as reliable as the monitored node: a crash stops it, and outbound firewall rules can block it. A pulled probe works across asymmetric networks because the monitor opens the connection, but the monitor absorbs the load of polling everything. Many systems run both, using the active probe as a second opinion.

title: Cassandra writes are appends; consistency only decides when the client hears back
takeaway: Separate durability from acknowledgement, and the write path becomes a log append instead of a negotiation.

blocks.text: The coordinator sends a mutation to every replica as soon as it arrives and waits only for as many acknowledgements as the consistency level demands. Replication is part of the write, not a background catch-up job. Nothing is read, modified, and written back, which is why the path stays fast under load.

title: Any node can coordinate a write, but no node is the master
takeaway: Peer-to-peer coordination removes failover, at the cost of making the partition key decide everything.

blocks.text: A client may connect to any node, and that node becomes the coordinator for the request. It hashes the partition key, typically with Murmur3, into a 64-bit token that maps onto a range owned by specific nodes. SimpleStrategy walks clockwise from that token; NetworkTopologyStrategy sets replica counts per data center and spreads them across racks.

title: The write path is CommitLog, then MemTable, then SSTable
takeaway: Durability and speed come from never seeking: append, sort in memory, flush once.
section: The Write Path Within a Node

blocks.text: The mutation is appended to an on-disk CommitLog for crash recovery, then applied to a sorted in-memory MemTable; the ack goes out after both, in microseconds. When the MemTable hits its threshold it is frozen, written out as an immutable SSTable, and its log segments are released. An update is simply a newer timestamped entry, with reconciliation deferred to read time.

title: QUORUM works because the read and write majorities must overlap
takeaway: Pick the smallest acknowledgement set that still intersects whatever your reads will contact.

blocks.text: ONE acknowledges after a single replica and can leave a later read stale. QUORUM needs `floor(replication_factor / 2) + 1` acks — two of three — and survives one failure. ALL fails if any replica is down, while LOCAL_QUORUM keeps a multi-datacenter write from waiting on remote replicas.

items: ONE: 1-3 ms p99
QUORUM: 2-5 ms p99
ALL: 5-20 ms p99, bounded by the slowest replica

title: Hints are a best-effort patch that expires after three hours
takeaway: Hinted handoff covers a reboot, not an outage; without repair, replicas stay permanently divergent.

blocks.text: When one replica misses a write but quorum is still satisfied, the coordinator records a hint and replays it once that node returns. Hints are not guaranteed, they add load to the coordinator, and they stop being kept after `max_hint_window_in_ms`, three hours by default. Read repair only fixes divergence that a read actually touches, so long outages need an explicit repair run.

title: Last-write-wins is only as trustworthy as your clocks
takeaway: An unsynchronized clock silently inverts write order, and the data loss looks like an application bug.

blocks.text: Every mutation carries a microsecond timestamp and the highest one wins. If the client supplies none, the coordinator stamps it from its own clock, so a node running behind can let an older value beat a newer one. Keep NTP running with drift under 500 ms, and never mix `USING TIMESTAMP` with coordinator-assigned stamps.

title: Repeatedly writing one partition turns the cluster into a single node
takeaway: The partition key is the unit of both distribution and scaling, so hot keys cap throughput no matter how many nodes you add.

blocks.text: A table updated millions of times on the same key funnels every write to the replicas that own that token and creates a hot spot. Batches only help when all statements target one partition; logged batches pay for a batch log to get atomicity, while unlogged ones skip it. Use TTL for expiry instead of issuing deletes.

title: Redis pushes writes because waiting to be asked wastes its latency budget
takeaway: The replication model should follow from the latency the system promises, not from what other databases do.

blocks.text: A write is propagated to connected replicas the moment it executes, so the only delay is the network. Replication lag lands in single-digit milliseconds rather than in seconds. The price is that the master owns a connection, an output buffer, and a backlog slot for every replica.

title: A full resync is a snapshot plus the writes made while it was taken
takeaway: The backlog ring is what turns a brief disconnect into a resume instead of an expensive snapshot.

blocks.text: A replica sends `PSYNC`; the master forks an RDB snapshot, buffers writes that land during the fork, ships the snapshot, then replays the buffer. Afterwards every write streams over the same connection and replicas apply them in order. The 1 MB backlog keeps recent commands so a short outage can continue from an offset.

title: Push costs less than polling until the master runs out of buffers
takeaway: Push moves cost from idle polling to steady per-replica memory, which is the wrong trade at high replica counts.

blocks.text: A pull design spends a round trip per replica even when nothing changed, and adds a polling delay before any write is visible. Pushing spends bandwidth only when writes exist and removes the extra request layer. But a master with a hundred replicas holds a hundred connections and buffers, and every write pays replication bookkeeping.

title: A slow replica has no way to ask the master to slow down
takeaway: Cap per-replica output buffers so one sick consumer cannot consume the master.

blocks.text: Replicas consume at whatever rate the master sends, so a slow one accumulates data in its socket buffer with no back-channel to complain. The master watches those buffers and disconnects replicas that fall too far behind, governed by `client-output-buffer-limit` and `repl-timeout`. That protects the master, but the dropped replica then needs a full resync.

title: Refuse writes when too few replicas are keeping up
takeaway: A lag guard converts silent replication lag into an availability decision you made in advance.

blocks.text: `min-replicas-to-write` and `min-replicas-max-lag` make the master reject writes unless enough replicas are within a lag bound, so it cannot acknowledge data that exists only on one machine. `WAIT 1 1000` gives a single caller the same assurance on demand. Neither makes replication synchronous or consistent: replica reads can still return stale values.

title: Diskless replication removes the disk round-trip from a resync
takeaway: On snapshot-heavy workloads, the fastest disk operation is the one you skip.

blocks.text: A standard full resync has the master fork, write the RDB to disk, read it back, then send it. With `repl-diskless-sync yes`, the snapshot is written straight to the replica's socket. The master avoids both the write and the read, which matters when snapshots are large or frequent.

title: A CDN is an eventual-consistency system that chose speed over agreement
takeaway: Treat edge propagation as a window of mixed versions, because no CDN can update hundreds of locations atomically.

blocks.text: A request from Tokyo to Virginia costs 150-200 ms in round trips before TCP, TLS, and transfer are counted, so first delivery can pass half a second. Copies near the user remove that distance. But 200+ edges cannot switch versions together, so CDNs accept a propagation window and build around it rather than lock all edges during an update.

title: Push through a hierarchy, or every edge becomes a client of your origin
takeaway: Fan-out and request coalescing are what keep a popular object from becoming an origin outage.

blocks.text: A push job expands into a DAG: origin to a handful of tier-1 parents, parents to mid-tier caches, mid-tier to edges, with files chunked and moved in parallel. On the read side, coalescing lets one request go upstream while the other 9,999 wait for that same result. Without both, a viral object turns thousands of edges into simultaneous origin clients.

title: Push what is large and predictable, pull the long tail
takeaway: Replication policy per object class beats one global strategy for the whole site.

blocks.text: Push suits firmware, game patches, releases, and live events: big, stable, or needed everywhere at once, provided the origin can absorb the initial fan-out. Pull replicates only what someone requests, so content nobody asks for costs nothing, at the price of a slow first hit. Most CDNs combine them and let traffic prediction promote hot objects.

title: Put the hash in the URL so a deploy creates a new object
takeaway: Content-addressed URLs make deploys atomic at the edge without any purge at all.

blocks.text: When the content hash is part of the cache key, changed bytes produce a different object rather than a stale one under the same name. Old clients keep fetching the old version, new clients get the new one, and both can be cached safely at once. An ETag compared with `If-None-Match` also avoids resending bytes that did not change.

title: Purges are neither instant nor complete, and they trigger stampedes
takeaway: Plan for minutes of mixed versions and for every edge refetching at once.

blocks.text: Propagation is uneven: roughly 80% of edges within ten seconds, 99.9% within a couple of minutes, and stragglers for five to ten. A purge invalidates everywhere at once, so the next request at each edge goes back to the origin. Short TTLs with `stale-while-revalidate` serve the old copy immediately while a single fetch refreshes it.

title: Every extra edge location multiplies storage and origin egress
takeaway: Replication is a per-object decision, because the bill scales with copies and with misses.

blocks.text: Two hundred locations means two hundred copies of everything you place, plus origin bandwidth for each push and each cache miss that reaches back. Transfers between CDN nodes are usually free; the expensive boundary is origin egress. Content that few users request pays that cost without returning much.

title: gRPC needs HTTP/2 because streaming is a protocol property, not a library feature
takeaway: Four call shapes, including bidirectional streaming, only fit cleanly on a transport built for independent streams.

blocks.text: gRPC supports unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional calls. HTTP/1.1 allows one request per connection, and the streaming workarounds either restrict direction or leave HTTP behind with an upgrade. An HTTP/2 stream maps directly onto a call where both sides send frames whenever they have data.

title: Multiplexing over one connection removes cross-request head-of-line blocking
takeaway: A slow dependency stops holding up unrelated calls, which is the whole point in a service mesh.

blocks.text: HTTP/2 breaks messages into frames tagged with a stream ID, so frames from many calls interleave on a single TCP connection. A slow response on one stream no longer delays the others sharing that socket. HTTP/1.1 has to open more connections instead, and browsers cap those at six to eight per domain.

title: The connection count collapse from 540 to 180 is the real mesh win
takeaway: Fewer sockets means less handshake latency, fewer OS limits, and less per-connection state to exhaust.

blocks.text: In a ten-service mesh where each service calls the other nine, six pooled connections per peer works out to 540 TCP connections. One or two HTTP/2 connections per peer brings that to 180, a 67% reduction. Reported effects include 20-40% lower latency on concurrent work and two to three times the requests per second for small payloads.

title: HPACK makes repeated metadata nearly free per call
takeaway: In a mesh, the headers you forward on every hop are a bandwidth cost worth compressing.

blocks.text: HTTP/1.1 writes every header as text on every request. HTTP/2 keeps a dynamic table of headers already seen and sends an index for repeats, which cuts header overhead by roughly 85-90%. Auth tokens, trace IDs, and content types that propagate through many services become a few bytes instead of a block of text.

title: Use the flow-control window as streaming backpressure
takeaway: A window on unacknowledged bytes is the difference between a slow consumer and an out-of-memory error.

blocks.text: A stream starts with a 65 KB window of data the sender may have in flight. The receiver sends `WINDOW_UPDATE` as it consumes, and either side can adjust the window based on its own rates. The limit is unacknowledged bytes rather than message size, so a fast producer is throttled instead of buffering without bound.

title: HTTP/2 is the wrong default for one-off calls and constrained devices
takeaway: Choose the protocol from the workload shape, not from the fact that it is newer.

blocks.text: A single request can be faster on HTTP/1.1, which needs less negotiation and setup. HTTP/2 spends memory on HPACK tables, stream state, and flow-control windows, which hurts on small devices. Load balancers that downgrade to HTTP/1.1 or mishandle trailers, plus binary captures that need special tools, add operational friction.

title: Consensus exists because more than one node can be wrong at once
takeaway: If any node besides one can accept writes, agreement has to be an algorithm rather than a convention.

blocks.text: Replicated nodes that all accept writes must settle on the same order while facing partitions, crashes, delayed messages, and skewed clocks simultaneously. A single decision-maker or timestamp ordering looks sufficient until the network splits or two clocks disagree. Consensus algorithms exist to preserve agreement through exactly those conditions.

title: Two withdrawals and three servers can create money
takeaway: Per-node correctness does not compose; only a shared decision order does.

blocks.text: Three replicas hold a $1,000 balance. One node processes an $800 withdrawal and ends at $200, another processes $500 and ends at $500, and the third sees the pair in a different order. Each applied a valid local rule, yet the account as a whole is now wrong.

title: Safety and liveness are separate promises, and a system can fail either alone
takeaway: A perfectly consistent system that never decides is still broken, so both guarantees belong in the design review.

blocks.text: Safety means no two nodes decide differently and no conflicting decision is ever made. Liveness means a decision is eventually reached and the system does not stall forever. A protocol can hold safety trivially by refusing to decide, which is why progress is stated as a separate requirement.

title: A quorum is the smallest group allowed to act alone
takeaway: Quorum turns a partition into a slowdown on one side instead of divergence on both.

blocks.text: A majority is required to elect a leader or accept a write, so in a five-node cluster three nodes can proceed and two cannot. When a partition splits 3/2, the minority recognizes it has lost quorum and stops writing. Without that rule, both sides can believe they are in charge and elect separate leaders.

title: You already run consensus inside the systems you deploy
takeaway: The practical skill is knowing which state needs agreement and which can tolerate a stale read.
section: Real-World Scenarios: Where Consensus is Critical

blocks.text: Primary election in streaming replication, two-phase commit across shards, Kafka's controller, service discovery registries, fleet-wide configuration rollout, and Kubernetes' etcd all rest on agreeing to one value. The failure mode in each case is two components acting on different truths. You usually adopt consensus through one of these systems rather than implementing Raft yourself.

title: Deadlocks come from lock ordering, not from a bug you can test away
takeaway: Under enough concurrency, inconsistent acquisition order guarantees a cycle, so the fix is structural.

blocks.text: A deadlock is a circular wait: one transaction holds a lock the other needs, and each waits for what the other has. Any code path that takes the same resources in a different order will eventually close that circle. Testing harder does not remove the cycle; consistent ordering, detection, and retry do.

title: A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph, and one transaction gets cut
takeaway: The graph identifies which transactions to break apart, not which query is slow.

blocks.text: Transactions are nodes and wait relationships are edges; a loop means nobody can move. The database rebuilds this graph periodically — every second by default in PostgreSQL, every five seconds in SQL Server — because continuous checking costs CPU. Once a cycle is found it aborts a victim, often the transaction that triggered detection or the one that has done the least work.

title: Your lock order is not always the order the optimizer chose
takeaway: Two queries that look identical can deadlock each other through plan choice, escalation, or foreign keys.

blocks.text: The optimizer may pick different plans for similar statements, and different plans touch rows in different orders, especially with range scans and joins. Lock escalation converts many row locks into a table lock and pulls unrelated transactions into the cycle. Foreign-key checks add locks on child rows that the statement never mentions.

title: Postgres waits a second to check; MySQL checks immediately
takeaway: Detection policy is a latency-versus-CPU choice baked into your engine, so tune the timeout rather than fight it.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL waits `deadlock_timeout` (one second) before building the graph, betting that most waits clear by themselves; that keeps CPU low but adds a floor to resolution time. MySQL detects a simple two-transaction cycle immediately and falls back to timeout-based resolution for complex ones. The first trades a second of waiting for less overhead, the second does the reverse.

title: Order locks globally, keep transactions short, and retry the whole transaction
takeaway: Retrying a single statement after a deadlock replays work that the database already rolled back.

blocks.text: Enforce one acquisition order across every code path that touches the same rows. Keep transactions brief so each holds locks for less time, and make the queries themselves faster so the window for a cycle shrinks. When a deadlock error arrives, retry from the start of the transaction, since its earlier statements were already undone.

title: Instrument deadlocks before you try to prevent them
takeaway: Deadlock logs name the two statements and the order that clashed, which is the only reliable starting point.

items: Turn on deadlock logging and keep the statement pairs it reports.
Record which transaction was chosen as the victim and why.
Review slow query logs weekly, since deadlock-prone statements are the ones that wait.
Count deadlocks and retries per endpoint so regressions show up as a rate.
Add bounded retries with backoff around every transaction that writes multiple rows.

title: Cache locality can outweigh algorithmic complexity in real workloads
takeaway: The gap between L1 and main memory is 100-300x, so where your data sits can matter more than how many steps your algorithm takes.

blocks.text: A modern CPU does not read bytes from RAM one at a time; it moves 64-byte cache lines into a small hierarchy and hopes you touch the neighbours. When that bet fails, the cost is hundreds of cycles instead of a handful. The same loop over the same data can run 10x, 50x or 100x slower purely because of the order it visits memory.

title: The memory hierarchy is a latency cliff, not a smooth speedup
takeaway: Each cache level buys speed by shrinking capacity, which is why the CPU must guess what you will need next.

blocks.text: Fast memory is expensive and small, so the hardware stacks tiers that trade capacity for latency. L1 answers in a couple of cycles but holds tens of kilobytes; RAM holds gigabytes and costs roughly 200-300 cycles. Every optimisation is really a bet that the working set stays in the small, fast tiers.

items: L1: ~1-3 cycles, 32-64 KB per core
L2: ~10-20 cycles, 256 KB-1 MB per core
L3: ~40-75 cycles, 8-32 MB shared
RAM: ~200-300 cycles, 8-128 GB

title: Reusing an address and touching its neighbours are different bets
takeaway: Temporal and spatial locality fail for different reasons, so a fix for one often does nothing for the other.

blocks.text: Temporal locality is about seeing the same address again soon; the cache rewards it by keeping the line resident. Spatial locality is about touching nearby addresses; the hardware rewards it because one 64-byte fetch already brought them in. A tight loop over a huge array has spatial locality but no temporal reuse, while a small hot counter has the reverse.

title: Column-major traversal wastes 15 of every 16 integers it loads
takeaway: Loop order can change runtime by an order of magnitude even when the operation count is identical.

blocks.text: Setting every cell of an n-by-n matrix looks the same in either traversal order, but the memory traffic is not. Walking rows consumes all 16 integers in a 64-byte line; walking columns pulls a fresh line for each cell and discards the other 15. The benchmark gap widens sharply once the matrix stops fitting in cache.

title: Redis keeps eviction candidates in an array to avoid pointer chasing
takeaway: In a latency-critical path, a contiguous array beats a linked list because every node is already on the same few cache lines.

blocks.text: Redis samples random keys and keeps a small pool of around 16 eviction candidates ordered by idle time or access frequency. The pool is a static array rather than a linked list, so all candidates sit within a few cache lines and comparisons never stall on a dependent load. A list would turn each hop into a potential memory miss during the eviction decision.

title: A linear scan with good locality can beat a logarithmic search with bad locality
takeaway: Big O counts operations, not stalls, so a complexity win can still lose on real hardware.

blocks.text: Binary search touches scattered addresses and can miss on nearly every probe, while a sequential pass streams through prefetched lines. At realistic data sizes the stall cost can reverse the ranking that complexity analysis predicts. Use Big O to rule out bad algorithms, then measure locality before assuming the asymptotically better one wins.

title: Eventual consistency wins because partitions are not optional
takeaway: Once network partitions are treated as normal, consistency becomes a latency and availability budget rather than a correctness checkbox.
section: The CAP Theorem: The Fundamental Trade-off

blocks.text: Strong consistency sounds like the safe default: every replica agrees before a write is acknowledged. But a system spread across continents cannot wait for the farthest replica without paying in latency and uptime. Since partitions happen, the real decision is whether to refuse writes or accept them locally and reconcile later, and large systems mostly choose the second.

title: CAP collapses to a choice between consistency and availability
takeaway: Partition tolerance is the property you cannot decline, so the design question is which of the other two you sacrifice.
section: The CAP Theorem: The Fundamental Trade-off

blocks.text: Consistency, availability and partition tolerance cannot all hold at once. Networks drop packets, latency spikes and nodes vanish, so partition tolerance is effectively mandatory outside a single controlled data centre. That leaves a global profile update as a concrete fork: block for a cross-continental confirmation, or return immediately and let replicas converge.

items: Choose consistency: wait for every data centre, often 200-500 ms
Choose availability: acknowledge locally and propagate asynchronously

title: Eventual consistency promises convergence, not a deadline
takeaway: Staleness becomes a product decision, because the model tells you replicas will agree but not when.

blocks.text: Under strong consistency a completed write is immediately visible everywhere, with a linear order across replicas. Under eventual consistency different nodes may briefly return different values, and the only guarantee is that absent new writes they end in the same state. There is no bound on the disagreement window, so each read path has to decide how old data it can tolerate.

title: Coordination cost grows with every replica you add
takeaway: Strong consistency turns extra capacity into extra synchronisation, which is why it scales worse than the workload does.

blocks.text: A strongly consistent write waits for acknowledgements from all replicas, so its latency is set by the slowest network path and its throughput by the coordination overhead. Adding nodes adds participants to every write. Eventually consistent nodes accept work locally and sync in the background, so new capacity mostly adds throughput instead of contention.

title: Guarantee users their own writes while letting everyone else lag
takeaway: A hybrid model buys most of the UX benefit of strong consistency without paying global coordination on every write.

blocks.text: Many systems show an author their own change immediately while other readers see it seconds later. Vector clocks order concurrent updates, and CRDTs define merges that need no coordination at all. DynamoDB follows the same shape: eventual by default, with strong reads available on request for the paths that need them.

title: Money movement cannot absorb a stale read
takeaway: The exact anomalies eventual consistency permits are the ones that break payments and audit trails.
section: When Strong Consistency is Still Necessary

blocks.text: Double spending, negative balances and inconsistent audit records are not cosmetic delays; they are the failure modes an eventually consistent ledger allows. Bank transfers, payment processing and balance checks therefore need strong guarantees even when feeds and profiles do not. Consistency is chosen per operation, not per company.

title: Design the interface to absorb the delay instead of engineering it away
takeaway: A few seconds of perceived progress can be cheaper than enforcing global consistency for a UX problem.

blocks.text: If a short animation after publishing gives replication time to catch up, the system can skip coordination entirely and still feel instant. The delay is hidden inside an interaction the user already expects to take a moment. Treating the interface as part of the consistency strategy is often cheaper than strengthening the storage layer.

title: DNS is a two-protocol system, not a UDP system
takeaway: Assuming DNS is UDP-only leaves you blind to the failure mode where large answers quietly retry over TCP.

blocks.text: The common claim that DNS runs on UDP describes the routine case, not the protocol. Resolution uses UDP for ordinary lookups and switches to TCP when an answer will not fit or a transfer needs a stream. Both transports share port 53, and a resolver that cannot use both is only partially functional.

title: UDP wins because a lookup is two packets and no state
takeaway: Connection setup is pure overhead for a request that usually hits a cache and returns one small answer.

blocks.text: A UDP query and its response need no handshake and leave nothing behind, so a server handling 100,000 queries per second keeps no per-client connection state. TCP needs at least seven packets and a live socket per client. Because most lookups are served from browser, OS or resolver caches, paying connection setup on every miss is wasted work.

items: UDP: query plus response, two packets
TCP: handshake, query, response and teardown, seven or more
UDP: no server-side connection table at high query rates

title: The truncation bit is the handoff from UDP to TCP
takeaway: A truncated answer is a signal to retry, not an error, so resolvers must treat it as a normal branch.

blocks.text: When a response exceeds the UDP size the client advertised, the server sets the TC bit instead of sending a partial answer. The resolver then opens a TCP connection and repeats the same query. A timeout triggers the same path, because a dropped datagram and a slow server look identical from the client side.

title: DNSSEC, long TXT records and CNAME chains are what push DNS onto TCP
takeaway: The zones most likely to need TCP are exactly the ones where a UDP-only path fails hardest.

blocks.text: The original UDP limit was 512 bytes; EDNS0 raised the advertised ceiling to 4096, but middleboxes often fragment or drop packets that large anyway. Cryptographic signatures, SPF and DKIM text, many A/AAAA records and multi-step aliases all inflate the answer. Zone transfers are different again: AXFR and IXFR run only over TCP because they move thousands of records and need integrity.

title: Fallback doubles latency, so resolvers learn to skip UDP
takeaway: The mitigation for expensive retries is caching protocol knowledge, which turns a per-query cost into a one-time discovery.

blocks.text: A truncated answer costs the failed UDP attempt plus a full TCP retry, roughly twice the resolution time. Resolvers reduce that by recording which names or query types need TCP and going straight there next time, or by firing both queries in parallel for critical requests. The saving comes from remembering the outcome, not from making TCP faster.

title: Allow TCP on port 53 or DNS breaks only for the large answers
takeaway: A UDP-only firewall passes everyday traffic and fails exactly when DNSSEC or a zone transfer shows up.

blocks.text: Most production incidents here are configuration gaps rather than protocol bugs: the small queries work, so nobody notices that TCP 53 is blocked until a signed or oversized zone is queried. Monitor both transports and treat a rising fallback rate as a capacity and latency signal.

items: Open both UDP and TCP on port 53 in firewalls and security groups.
Confirm load balancers forward both protocols to resolvers.
Track the UDP success rate and how often TCP fallback fires.
Watch response size distribution to tune the EDNS0 buffer.
Alert on timeout patterns that suggest dropped UDP packets.

title: An OKR measures outcomes, so a task list is not an OKR
takeaway: If a key result can be completed without moving a number, it is a project plan wearing OKR labels.

blocks.text: Objectives describe where you are going; key results describe how you will know you arrived. A key result that reads like a ticket, such as shipping the batch API, can be finished while nothing about the business changes. The framework only works when every key result moves a metric that matters.

title: Two or three objectives, each with two to four key results
takeaway: The cap is the mechanism: more objectives make trade-offs invisible and split the effort that was supposed to concentrate.
section: Core Principles and the Sweet Spot

blocks.text: Focus is a design constraint, not a style preference. A quarter is long enough to finish a few things and too short to finish many, so the objective count is deliberately small and each one carries a handful of measurable results. When everything is an objective, prioritisation has effectively been skipped.

title: Rewrite an activity key result as the result the activity should produce
takeaway: The test is whether the KR can hit 100% while the objective still fails; if it can, you wrote a task.

blocks.text: "Test and deploy the Payments Batch API" describes effort, not progress. Restate it as the outcome the deployment is meant to create, and leave the testing detail to the description or a linked issue. A good key result names the change in the world; the work needed to produce it belongs elsewhere.

title: A vague metric invites you to pick the easiest number that satisfies it
takeaway: "Improve performance" is unfalsifiable, so any small change can be declared a win.

blocks.text: A key result phrased as "improve API performance and make it more efficient" has no target and no metric, so scoring it is a judgement call. The measurable version states the specific quantity to move and the value it must reach. The quieter version of the same mistake is choosing a metric that is easy to move but unrelated to the objective.

title: If your OKRs mirror the JIRA board, you are tracking output
takeaway: Copying tickets into the framework produces a status report with none of the accountability for impact.

blocks.text: The board records work in flight; OKRs record what success looks like at the end of the cycle. When the two lists are identical, the team is measuring busyness and nobody owns the outcome. A useful check is whether any key result would still make sense to an executive who has never seen the backlog.

title: Engineering and product OKRs should map one-to-one on business outcomes
takeaway: Overlap is the point; the legitimate differences are tech debt and product research, not the business results.

blocks.text: Engineering and product plans should share the same business-facing results, with engineering owning debt and excellence work and product owning discovery. Internal-only OKRs drift away from company goals and lose their claim on resources. When the mapping breaks, the two orgs can both hit their targets while the business does not.

title: Draft the objective first, then interrogate every key result
takeaway: A short review pass catches the vague metrics and disguised tasks before the team commits a quarter to them.

blocks.text: Crafting takes real time because the whole team will orient around the result for a quarter. Run the same checks on each draft rather than relying on taste.

items: Label objectives and results as O1, KR1, KR2 so they are easy to cite.
Phrase each objective as an inspiring destination, not a maintenance chore.
Give every key result a metric, a starting value and a target value.
Convert any key result that reads like a ticket into the outcome it should produce.
Cut down to two or three objectives with two to four results each.
Check that the survivors trace to a business outcome the company cares about.

title: Theta sketches exist because HyperLogLog cannot do set algebra
takeaway: If your questions involve overlap or exclusion between audiences, distinct-count sketches are the wrong tool no matter how small they are.
section: The problem that cardinality sketches solve

blocks.text: HLL answers how many distinct items a stream contains and merges by union, but it cannot express who saw campaign A and not campaign B. Theta sketches keep a sample of hashed values under a shared threshold, so union, intersection and difference each return another usable sketch. That composability is what justifies their larger memory footprint.

title: Theta is a sampling rate you divide by, not a count
takeaway: Separating the threshold from the retained-entry count is what makes set operations well defined.
section: The theta variable and what it buys you

blocks.text: A sketch is a pair: a threshold theta between 0 and 1, and the set of hashed values below it. Cardinality is the set size divided by theta. At theta equal to 1 the sketch holds everything and the count is exact; once it exceeds k entries, theta drops to the next smallest hash and the retained sample shrinks while the estimate stays unbiased.

title: Error is set by k: 4096 entries buys about 1.6%
takeaway: Sizing a sketch is arithmetic from your accuracy target, not a guess to be tuned in production.

blocks.text: Relative standard error is roughly 1 over the square root of k minus one, so k=4096 gives about 1.6% and k=16384 about 0.8%. Round up to the nearest power of two after solving for the target. Each retained entry is an 8-byte long, which makes the memory bill easy to predict.

items: 2% RSE: k=2501, so use 4096
5% RSE: k=401, so use 512
k=4096 compact: roughly 32 KB; k=16384: roughly 128 KB

title: Every set operation filters both sketches to the smaller theta
takeaway: A shared hash function and a common threshold are what let two independently built sketches be compared at all.
section: Set operations: the thing that makes Theta sketches irreplaceable

blocks.text: Union keeps entries from both sides below the minimum threshold. Intersection keeps entries present in both below that same threshold, and difference keeps A's entries that are missing from B. Since the hash function is shared, an element's sampling decision is comparable across sketches, and the output is itself a valid sketch that can feed the next operation.

title: Intersection error explodes when the overlap is tiny
takeaway: An intersection estimate can be off by more than 70% and still look like a legitimate number in a dashboard.

blocks.text: Intersection error scales with the square root of F, the ratio of union size to intersection size. With k=4096 and two million-element sets overlapping by 1,000, F is about 2000 and the error reaches roughly 71%, which is meaningless. Chaining intersections compounds the loss, and after a few steps on small overlaps the retained set can reach zero.

title: Sketches built with different hash seeds produce nonsense
takeaway: Seed choice is a system-wide contract, and a custom seed quietly breaks interoperability that used to work.
section: The seed problem and why you cannot ignore it

blocks.text: Set operations assume the same element hashes to the same value in every sketch. A custom seed, often added to prevent hash flooding, destroys that assumption unless every producer and consumer is updated together. There is no migration path for sketches already stored under the old seed, and DataSketches defaults to 9001.

title: Theta costs about 30x the memory of HLL, so only buy it for set operations
takeaway: If a column is only ever queried for distinct counts, paying for set algebra is pure waste.
section: Memory trade-offs vs. HLL and CPC

blocks.text: For pure cardinality, an HLL of matching accuracy occupies between one-half and one-sixteenth of the space a Theta sketch needs, and CPC trims a further 30-40% off HLL. A default 16384-entry Theta sketch is roughly 30x an HLL with lgK=12. The rule is blunt: intersection or difference means Theta; union and count alone means HLL or CPC.

title: A job is worth staying at only while it delivers two of three Ps
takeaway: Turning a vague urge to leave into a countable condition makes the decision reviewable instead of emotional.

blocks.text: Paisa is pay, Power is growth in core competency, and Position is upward movement on the ladder. The rule is a threshold rather than a score: two out of three is enough to stay, and fewer than two is the signal to start looking. The framework does not require a perfect job, only a defensible one.

title: Power is competency growth, not headcount or a bigger scope
takeaway: A title bump with no new skill is Position without Power, and the two are easy to confuse when a role looks impressive.

blocks.text: Power measures how much closer the role takes you to being a subject-matter expert: harder problems, unfamiliar methods, deeper domain work. Managing more people or owning more surface area is not the same thing if the underlying competence does not grow. Judging the two separately stops a prestigious but stagnant role from passing as progress.

title: One strong P can justify staying through a weak one
takeaway: The framework permits a deficit as long as it is being paid for deliberately by the other two dimensions.

blocks.text: Below-market pay can be rational when learning and promotion are strong; a flat title can be rational when pay and growth are good. What matters is that the missing dimension is a conscious trade rather than an unnoticed cost. Staying becomes a decision with a reason instead of inertia.

title: Re-score the three Ps every six months
takeaway: A regular review catches a slow decline in one dimension before it turns into years of stagnation.

blocks.text: A twice-yearly review names which two Ps you are optimising for at each company. In one career, the trade moved from Power and Paisa to Position and Paisa, then Position and Power, then Power and Paisa. Naming the pair makes the trade explicit.

items: Compare current pay with the market rate for your level.
List the competencies you actually gained in the last six months.
Check whether a concrete promotion path exists and how far away it is.
Name the two Ps you are currently optimising for and the one you are sacrificing.
If fewer than two are being served, start looking before the next review.

title: Start the function before the container image finishes loading
takeaway: Cold-start latency is governed by bytes moved on the critical path, not by image size.

blocks.text: Loading a multi-gigabyte container before execution makes startup time hostage to deployment size. Lambda instead begins running the function with the blocks it needs first and streams the remainder in the background. The design target is to keep the synchronous path short, even when the image behind it is huge.

title: Fetch container blocks on demand instead of the whole image
takeaway: Serving reads a page at a time lets a cold start complete in milliseconds while the rest of the image catches up.

blocks.text: Lambda flattens image layers into a single ext4 filesystem, so unchanged files occupy identical blocks across containers. A local agent answers reads from a worker-local cache, then a regional cache, then S3, pulling only the missing blocks. Writes use page-level copy-on-write, which keeps shared immutable data shared while the guest can still modify its view.

title: Convergent encryption makes encrypted layers deduplicable
takeaway: Deriving the key from the content lets identical chunks collapse into one stored copy without sharing a key store.

blocks.text: Each chunk is keyed by its own SHA-256 digest and encrypted with AES-CTR under a deterministic IV, so identical bytes produce identical ciphertext even across customers. Only the manifest's key table is encrypted with a per-customer KMS key. Deduplication therefore works on encrypted data without anyone inspecting plaintext or maintaining a central key directory.

title: 80% of new functions add no unique chunks at all
takeaway: The economics of on-demand loading depend on workload shape, and most serverless workloads are mostly shared base layers.

blocks.text: In production telemetry, about four in five newly uploaded functions produce zero unique chunks, and the remaining fifth average 4.3% unique content with a median of 2.5%. Base images dominate, so most of an image is already stored and cached somewhere. That is why fetching a few blocks beats transferring a whole container.

title: A rotating salt trades dedupe ratio for blast radius
takeaway: Widely shared chunks are both the source of the savings and the largest single point of exposure.

blocks.text: If one chunk is referenced by many tenants, compromising it affects every image that uses it. Lambda adds a salt to key derivation that can rotate by time, chunk popularity or infrastructure placement, which breaks some deduplication but bounds how many workloads one chunk can touch. The salt is a dial between storage efficiency and impact.

title: A 4-of-5 erasure code cuts redundancy to 25% overhead
takeaway: Coding redundancy costs far less storage than replication while still surviving a lost shard.

blocks.text: Instead of keeping full copies, Lambda encodes each chunk so that any four of five pieces reconstruct it. That costs 25% extra storage and a 25% higher request rate, but removes full replicas and improves tail latency because a slow or failed shard can be routed around. Redundancy is paid for in coding rather than duplication.

title: SQL's clause order fights the order the data actually flows
takeaway: Writing SELECT before FROM forces authors to describe a pipeline backwards and patch the gap with duplicated clauses.

blocks.text: A query begins with a table scan in FROM, but the syntax makes you start at SELECT near the top. The mismatch shows up as WHERE, HAVING and QUALIFY doing overlapping jobs, subqueries wrapping simple steps, and readers tracing logic in reverse. Pipe syntax rewrites the query in the order the engine executes it.

title: A pipe operator is a unary table-to-table function
takeaway: Isolation is what makes the stages reorderable, repeatable and safe to extend.

blocks.text: Each stage after `|>` takes one table and produces one table. Because it sees only its input and its arguments, it has no hidden dependency on earlier clauses, so stages compose in any order and any number of times. That contract is what allows new operators to be added without revisiting the grammar.

title: The prefix property lets you run half a query
takeaway: Debugging becomes truncating the pipeline at the suspect step instead of carving out a subquery.

blocks.text: Since every stage is a complete relational operation, cutting a query after any pipe still leaves valid SQL over an intermediate table. You can inspect the rows at that point, or attach `LOG` to see them and `DESCRIBE` to see their schema. `ASSERT` uses the same shape to fail a query when an intermediate condition is violated.

title: CALL and PIVOT show how new operators slot into the pipeline
takeaway: Once every stage is a table transform, awkward special cases become ordinary composable steps.

blocks.text: Table-valued functions are invoked with `CALL` as just another stage instead of a nested subquery, and `PIVOT` becomes a normal operator rather than a syntax exception. Existing joins, aggregations and subqueries still work and can be expressed in piped form. Extension stops requiring new reserved keywords or a new place in the clause order.

title: Ship the new syntax as an extension, not a replacement
takeaway: Adoption succeeds when old queries stay valid and migration can happen one query at a time.

blocks.text: Pipes are a suffix on existing queries, so a team can convert one stage without rewriting the statement and old SQL keeps parsing. The implementation produces the same algebra as standard SQL, so engines enable it without forking their planner. Migration cost is paid per query rather than per system.

title: NanoLog moves logging work out of the hot path and into compile time
takeaway: Logging is expensive because of when the work happens; shifting it earlier and later makes the call itself nearly free.

blocks.text: Conventional logging formats a string, takes a lock and writes to disk while the application waits. NanoLog generates specialised code at compile time, records only binary arguments at runtime, and formats later on a background thread. The result is roughly 8 nanoseconds per call and up to 80 million messages per second.

title: Generate a record and a compact function for every log statement
takeaway: Knowing the format at build time removes parsing and type inference from every call.

blocks.text: A preprocessor parses each `NANO_LOG` format string, infers the argument types and emits two functions: one that captures the dynamic values and one that compresses them. Static details such as file, line, severity and format go into a dictionary keyed by a compile-time identifier. At runtime the code just writes the id and the values, with no format string interpretation at all.

title: Give each thread its own single-producer ring buffer
takeaway: Removing the shared lock removes contention, context switches and allocation from the logging call.

blocks.text: A shared buffer protected by a mutex forces threads to serialise on every write. NanoLog instead allocates one fixed-size circular queue per logging thread, with a single producer and a single consumer, so appends are atomic and memory is reused rather than allocated. The emission thread drains queues while recording continues.

title: Pad producer and consumer state onto separate cache lines
takeaway: A lock-free design still loses to false sharing if unrelated fields share a cache line.

blocks.text: When the logging thread and the background thread keep their private variables on the same 64-byte line, each write invalidates the other core's copy. NanoLog aligns those fields to cache-line boundaries with `__attribute__((aligned(CACHE_LINE_SIZE)))`, paying a little padding to avoid coherence traffic on the hot path. The same padding trick applies to any frequently written shared structure.

title: Encode integers in the fewest bytes, with a nibble of length metadata
takeaway: General-purpose compression is the wrong cost profile for a path that must finish in nanoseconds.

blocks.text: Most logged integers are small and leave most of their bits unused, so NanoLog stores each one in the minimum number of bytes and prefixes a 4-bit header recording the length and sign. Small values fit in about 1.5 bytes including that header. LZ77 was rejected because its CPU cost defeats the purpose in a real-time log path.

title: Binary serialization beats text because rendering is the expensive part
takeaway: If you never need the string on the hot path, producing it at all is wasted work.

blocks.text: Converting values into readable characters costs far more than copying their bytes. NanoLog keeps parameters in binary, stamps them from the CPU time-stamp counter mapped to wall time, and lets a decompressor combine records with the static dictionary later. Text is produced once, offline, instead of on every call.

title: Keep the whole graph on one machine until it no longer fits
takeaway: A centralized design can beat a distributed one for years if the working set fits in memory.

blocks.text: Twitter's Who to Follow service initially kept the full follower graph in RAM on one host, using a purpose-built engine called Cassovary. That removed disk reads and network hops from every recommendation query and kept the architecture simple enough to change quickly. When the graph outgrew one machine's memory, the team partitioned it across servers in a second-generation system.

title: Microsecond graph access changes what a recommender can afford
takeaway: Latency class, not dataset size, often decides whether a graph algorithm is practical.

blocks.text: Holding edges in memory turns graph lookups from milliseconds into microseconds, which lets a service run many traversals inside one request. The same algorithm over disk or a remote partition would spend its budget on I/O and miss the interactive window. Twitter needed suggestions fast enough to appear while a user was still on the page.

title: Random walks find the neighbourhood a model would miss
takeaway: Repeated random traversals turn raw follow edges into a ranked list of nearby users.

blocks.text: A walk starts at the target user and repeatedly steps to a random follow neighbour, with many walks collecting visit counts. Nodes visited often are structurally close and become candidates. The randomness keeps the candidate set from collapsing onto the same few obvious accounts.

title: Random walks cover neighbours; SALSA covers influence
takeaway: Local exploration and global authority answer different recommendation questions, so combining them beats either alone.

blocks.text: Random walks are good at finding users near the query node, but they say little about whether a candidate is influential across the wider network. SALSA treats the graph as bipartite between users and content, then alternates scores between the two sides. Twitter used it to surface authoritative accounts that a purely local walk would not rank highly.

title: One server fails on memory, then on repair time
takeaway: Centralization buys simplicity now and charges you a migration later, so budget for that migration.

blocks.text: The single-server design eventually hit memory ceilings, and each capacity increase meant upgrading one very large machine. A single host also concentrates failure risk, so recovery depended on that machine returning. Twitter's rewrite spread the graph across servers and added replication and failover, trading operational simplicity for scale.

title: Store the graph as adjacency lists, not as generic records
takeaway: A compact, purpose-built representation is what makes an in-memory graph economical at Twitter's scale.

blocks.text: Cassovary represents users as nodes and follows as edges, packing adjacency lists and node data tightly to limit memory per user. That density is what let the whole graph fit on one machine. The engine was later reused for search, discovery and promoted products, so the storage work paid off beyond a single feature.

title: A design interview is a timed discussion, not a design test
takeaway: Splitting the slot into fixed phases keeps an open-ended prompt from consuming the whole hour.
section: Turn System Design Interviews into Discussions

blocks.text: System design prompts have no single correct answer, so the usual failure is drifting into one component and running out of time. The slot is divided across 40–45 minutes: understanding, a naive design, hardening, follow-up questions and implementation detail. The schedule turns the interview into a back-and-forth rather than a monologue.

title: Spend the first minutes buying constraints, not boxes
takeaway: Clarifying scope early prevents you from solving a different system than the interviewer asked about.
section: Turn System Design Interviews into Discussions

blocks.text: Before drawing components, ask about context, scale, constraints and what the interviewer expects to see. A few minutes of questions turns an intentionally vague prompt into a target. Designing immediately risks building the wrong system very well.

title: Draw the naive design early so it can be corrected
takeaway: A rough day-0 sketch gives the interviewer something concrete to redirect before you invest in details.
section: Turn System Design Interviews into Discussions

blocks.text: A simple unoptimized design is enough to show your mental model: clients, service, storage and the main data flow. It does not need scaling, replication or failure handling yet. The interviewer can then confirm the direction or point you at the component that deserves depth.

title: Run the 45 minutes on a fixed five-phase clock
takeaway: A repeatable schedule leaves room for hardening and discussion instead of spending everything on the first design.
section: Turn System Design Interviews into Discussions

blocks.text: A good routine assigns time to each phase and treats the later phases as part of the interview, not as extras. Hardening gets the largest block because that is where trade-offs surface.

items: 3-4 minutes: clarify context, constraints and expectations.
5-7 minutes: sketch a naive day-0 design end to end.
15 minutes: stress each component with load, crashes and network failures, then rearchitect.
8 minutes: take the interviewer's follow-up questions and justify your trade-offs.
8 minutes: go into concurrency, streaming, transient failures and other fine details.

title: Getting blocked is normal; staying blocked is the failure
takeaway: Treat unblocking as a repeatable skill rather than a personal deficiency.

blocks.text: Every engineer hits roadblocks, and a block often means the work is genuinely new. The cost comes from sitting in it: stalled delivery, mounting frustration and a standup update that repeats the same excuse. Unblocking is treated as a structured practice with several routes out.

title: Work the unblocking ladder from cheapest to most expensive
takeaway: A fixed escalation order stops you from burning a day before asking for help.

blocks.text: The available routes range from a quick question in the team channel to pulling in another team's manager. Going in order keeps the cost low and preserves relationships. The last rung exists because some blocks are organizational rather than technical.

items: Explain the problem to a teammate and ask what they would check first.
Post the question in the team or company channel with what you already tried.
Take a bounded detour into email or mundane work, then return with fresh eyes.
Cut the problem into one small piece you can test in a sitting.
Read source, docs and examples, try a small experiment, then ask an LLM for a hint.
For another team's dependency, build rapport, ask for prioritization, then escalate.

title: Saying the problem out loud often solves it mid-sentence
takeaway: A teammate is useful even when they know less about the code, because explaining forces structure.

blocks.text: Describing a block to another person makes you order the facts and notice the assumption that does not hold. The answer sometimes arrives while you are still explaining. Teams with existing rapport respond faster when you do need their input.

title: A deliberate detour lets the background mind work
takeaway: Switching to low-stakes tasks can break fixation better than staring harder.

blocks.text: When a problem refuses to move, switch to email, Slack replies or other mundane work. The break either lets the solution surface subconsciously or gives a fresh angle on return. The point is to leave the problem deliberately, not to abandon it.

title: Shrink the block until one piece is testable
takeaway: Decomposition turns an overwhelming problem into a sequence of answerable questions.

blocks.text: Large ambiguous problems create mental blocks because there is no obvious first move. Splitting them into smaller components gives each piece a concrete check and a visible result. Progress on one piece also restores the confidence to continue.

title: A cross-team block needs leverage, not patience
takeaway: When another team owns your dependency, waiting is a choice to stay blocked.

blocks.text: You cannot fix a dependency owned by another team by working harder on your side. Build rapport first, then ask for prioritization, persuade with business impact, and escalate through the proper channel if nothing moves. Escalation is a normal part of delivery, not an accusation.

title: Use an LLM for a nudge, then verify it yourself
takeaway: A plausible hint can break fixation as long as you treat it as a lead, not an answer.

blocks.text: A model can suggest an approach or point at a likely cause when you are stuck. Treat that output as a direction to investigate because it is not always correct. Confirming the cause is still your job.

title: Evolution buys polynomial time by giving up the optimum
takeaway: When exact dynamic programming is too slow, a genetic algorithm can return a good answer within a predictable budget.

blocks.text: 0/1 knapsack has an exact dynamic-programming solution whose runtime grows with the numeric capacity, not just the item count. A genetic algorithm instead evolves candidate packs and returns the best after a fixed number of generations. In one run it converged to value 12 while the optimum was 16.

title: O(n·W) is exponential in the bits that encode W
takeaway: A runtime that looks polynomial in a capacity is exponential in the input size, which is why large capacities hurt.

blocks.text: The memoized recurrence runs in O(n·W), which looks polynomial because W is a number. But W needs m bits to write down, so its value can be 2^m, making the real bound O(n·2^m). Pseudo-polynomial algorithms are fast for small numbers and collapse when the capacity is large.
