takeaway: A global canonical table is a lifetime decision, not just a speed switch.

blocks.text: The `interned` dictionary holds a reference to every interned string, so interning keeps objects alive past their last use. CPython's cleanup walks the table, marks entries `NOT_INTERNED`, and clears it so the objects can be collected. Interning arbitrary user input turns a bounded cache into an unbounded retention pool.

title: A decorator can reveal recursion's shape without touching the algorithm
takeaway: Wrapping entry and exit is enough to turn an invisible call stack into a readable trace.

blocks.text: The recursive function stays unchanged; a decorator wraps it and runs code before and after each call. Because the recursive body calls the decorated name, every nested invocation passes through the same wrapper. That gives one place to record the current depth, the arguments, and the returned value.

title: Track depth with a counter raised on entry and lowered on exit
takeaway: Indentation derived from live depth prints the call tree without building a tree object.

blocks.text: A `recursion_level` counter is increased before the wrapped function runs and reduced after it returns. Multiplying it by an indent width gives each printed line its offset, so siblings align and children sit one level deeper. The counter therefore mirrors the live stack rather than a precomputed layout.

title: Separate arrows for invocation and return make the log read as a tree
takeaway: A call log becomes a recursion tree only when entry and exit are distinguishable.

blocks.text: `->` marks a function being entered and `<-` marks its value coming back. Reading downward, the arrows show the descent into smaller subproblems; the returns show values being combined on the way up. A flat log without distinct markers would leave both directions ambiguous.

title: Use `recviz` instead of rebuilding the wrapper
takeaway: A published decorator gets you the trace with one import and one annotation.

blocks.text: The visualizer is packaged as `recviz` on PyPI. Install it, decorate the recursive function, and call it normally; the printed trace replaces the pen-and-paper diagram.

items: Run `pip install recviz`.
Import the decorator from the package.
Apply it above the recursive function definition.
Call the function with a small input such as `fib(3)`.
Read `->` as entry and `<-` as return.

title: Cardinality can be estimated from the longest run of trailing zeros
takeaway: A bit vector can replace a set of every distinct element when an approximation is acceptable.

blocks.text: Distinct-count normally needs a set holding every unique value. Flajolet-Martin instead hashes each element and records how many trailing zeros its bit pattern has, because deep patterns appear only when many distinct values are present. One pass and O(log m) bits produce an estimate of m.

title: Trailing-zero position is a logarithmic ruler for set size
takeaway: Probabilities that halve at each bit turn a maximum into an exponent.

blocks.text: In uniformly distributed bits, the rightmost set bit sits at position 0 half the time, at 1 a quarter of the time, and at k with probability 2^-(k+1). Across m distinct hashes, positions far beyond log2(m) are essentially never observed. The first position that never appears therefore estimates log2 of the cardinality.

title: Hash, record the bit position, then read the first empty slot
takeaway: The algorithm is one pass, one bit vector, and one scan for a zero.

blocks.text: Hash every element into a fixed range, compute the position of its rightmost set bit, and mark that position in a bit vector. After the stream ends, find the rightmost zero at position b; the estimate is 2^b. The vector needs only one bit per possible position.

title: One hash gives a noisy estimate; the fix is averaging, not more bits
takeaway: Probabilistic sketches need variance reduction before the number is usable.

blocks.text: A single bit vector can be thrown off by one unusually deep hash, producing an estimate with a wide error margin. The original method averages estimates from several independent hash functions. It also divides the averaged result by φ = 0.77351 to correct the estimator's bias.

title: Uniformity is an assumption, so raw values must be hashed first
takeaway: Sparse or clustered inputs break the trailing-zero argument unless a hash randomizes them.

blocks.text: The probability argument holds only if values are spread evenly across the bit space. Real streams arrive in runs, ranges, or repeated patterns, which would cluster the observed positions. A multiplicative hash with odd multipliers maps them into a uniform range before anything is recorded.

title: Duplicates cannot skew the estimate
takeaway: Because the sketch keeps an extreme rather than a sample, repeated elements carry no extra weight.

blocks.text: The algorithm never samples elements; it only records whether a trailing-zero position has ever occurred. An element seen a million times sets the same bit as an element seen once. Estimator error therefore grows with distinct cardinality, not with stream length or repetition.

title: On *The Jungle Book*, 7,150 distinct tokens were estimated at 7,606
takeaway: The approximation lands within a few percent while using a fixed, tiny amount of state.

blocks.text: The text was tokenized into a stream, and the exact distinct count was 7,150. Flajolet-Martin returned 7,606 from the same stream. A separate run over streams of 1,048 elements with varying distinct counts tracked the exact answer closely.

title: Recency alone cannot tell a scan from a working set
takeaway: A cache needs evidence of reuse before letting a new page displace a proven one.

blocks.text: LRU assumes the latest access predicts the next one, so a single touch is enough to enter the cache. A sequential scan then looks like a burst of extremely recent pages and evicts everything actually being reused. 2Q keeps recency for the main buffer but gates admission on a second reference.

title: A scan larger than the cache evicts the entire working set
takeaway: One unbounded scan can cost more than the memory it saves, especially when its pages are never revisited.

blocks.text: If a table is bigger than the buffer, reading it end to end fills the cache with pages from that single table. Every previously cached page is pushed out, and if the scanned pages are not read again, that work is wasted. Performance recovers only after those pages are themselves evicted.

title: A first access is probation, not a residency permit
takeaway: Admission should be earned by a second reference, the cheapest available signal of reuse.

blocks.text: 2Q's rule is that touching a page once does not justify keeping it; only a second access does. New pages wait in a secondary queue, and a repeat reference promotes them into the main LRU buffer. Pages never touched again age out without ever displacing hot data.

title: Two queues: FIFO probation in front, LRU residency behind
takeaway: Separating admission from eviction lets each policy do the job it is good at.

blocks.text: In simplified 2Q, `A1` is a FIFO queue of newly faulted pages and `Am` is the LRU buffer of admitted pages. A hit in `A1` moves the page to `Am`; a miss evicts from the tail of `A1`. The main buffer therefore contains only pages that have demonstrated reuse.

title: The probation queue's size is a knob with two failure modes
takeaway: Too small rejects genuinely hot pages; too large starves the cache meant to serve them.

blocks.text: If `A1` is tiny, a page must be re-referenced almost immediately to graduate, so legitimate warm pages are discarded. If `A1` is large, it consumes memory that `Am` needs, shrinking the effective cache. Simplified 2Q works, but these two errors have to be balanced by hand.

title: Split probation into in-memory and reference-only queues
takeaway: Keeping an evicted page's identity is enough to detect a second touch without keeping its data.

blocks.text: Full 2Q divides `A1` into `A1-In`, which holds the actual new pages, and `A1-Out`, which holds references to pages that have left memory. A page enters `A1-In` and stays while it is being accessed; once old, its data is dropped and its reference moves to `A1-Out`. A later access through `A1-Out` promotes the page directly to `Am`.

title: Postgres chose 2Q after ARC became patented
takeaway: A slightly less elegant policy with similar performance can be the pragmatic choice.

blocks.text: Postgres had used ARC for buffer management and moved to 2Q because of IBM's patent on ARC. Postgres reports that 2Q performs comparably to ARC. The replacement kept frequency-awareness while avoiding the licensing constraint.

title: Deriving priority from a friend reference lets a queue batch related work
takeaway: When setup dominates processing, grouping similar tasks is worth more than strict arrival order.

blocks.text: A normal priority queue takes priority as an input attached to each element. Israeli Queues infer it instead: an element names a friend already waiting and joins the tail of that friend's group. Similar tasks then sit together, so a worker can amortize one expensive setup across several items.

title: The friend reference is the priority
takeaway: Priority becomes a relationship between elements rather than an absolute rank.

blocks.text: `enqueue` takes an element plus a reference to a friend already in the queue, and inserts the new element at the back of that friend's group. An element with no friend goes to the rear and starts its own group. The resulting order is a set of small FIFO chains, not one global ordering.

title: A doubly linked list with per-group head and tail pointers
takeaway: Group insertion is O(1) when every group tracks both ends.

blocks.text: The queue is a doubly linked list, and the structure keeps pointers to the head and tail of each group. Joining an existing group appends at its tail; arriving without a friend appends at the list's tail and creates a singleton group. A common constraint is that the friend must be the group's leader, which keeps the reference unambiguous.

title: Batching buys reuse and risks starvation
takeaway: Every element without friends can be pushed back indefinitely by a stream of group-joining arrivals.

blocks.text: Grouping cuts redundant setup, but it suspends the fairness a FIFO queue provides. If friended elements keep arriving, items at the rear without friends may never reach the front. The structure trades latency guarantees for throughput on similar work.

title: Process a whole group per dequeue when setup dominates
takeaway: The batch, not the item, is the natural unit of work for this queue.

blocks.text: The original formulation processes an entire group in one service turn instead of one element at a time. That pays off when handling a single item is much cheaper than preparing to handle any item. The queue's shape and the worker's batch size have to be designed together.

title: Born in polling systems that drain a queue per visit
takeaway: The data structure's odd shape comes from a server that pays to visit a queue at all.
section: The original use case of Israeli Queues

blocks.text: A polling system has N queues visited in cyclic order by one server. Instead of taking a single element per visit, the server drains the queue's current batch, because the visit itself is the expensive part. Israeli Queues generalize that batching by letting related items cluster before the visit.

title: Convincing terrain comes from layering smoothed noise, not from one random pass
takeaway: A believable skyline needs structure at several scales, and that structure has to be built deliberately.

blocks.text: A natural 1D terrain has broad mountain shapes plus small irregularities, and a single random height per point supplies only the irregularities. The working recipe is to generate several random signals at different resolutions, smooth each one, and combine them with weights that favour the coarse layers. Randomness alone is never enough; the layering is what makes the result read as terrain.

title: Per-point randomness produces spikes because neighbouring heights share no information
takeaway: Independent samples give you static, not landscape.

blocks.text: Calling `random` once per x co-ordinate makes every height independent of the one before it. Plotted, that independence reads as high-frequency jitter: abrupt jumps and spikes that no real mountain range shows. The signal is random but has no spatial correlation, and spatial correlation is the property that makes terrain look natural.

title: Interpolation turns a few control points into a continuous slope
takeaway: Interpolation is the bridge between sparse random peaks and a dense, walkable profile.

blocks.text: Interpolation estimates the values between known points using a parameter `mu` that runs from 0 at the first point to 1 at the second. Linear interpolation walks a straight line between the endpoints. Cosine interpolation bends the path along a cosine curve instead, which removes the sharp seam that a straight line leaves at every control point.

title: Keep every k-th random height as a control point, then interpolate the gaps
takeaway: The sampling interval is the main dial between jagged noise and rolling hills.

blocks.text: Keeping only every `sample`-th point from the noisy terrain leaves a sparse set of peaks. Interpolating between consecutive controls fills the missing x positions with gradual transitions. A larger interval produces wider landforms and fewer spikes, while a smaller interval preserves more of the original jaggedness.

title: Sum octaves whose sample counts halve while their weights double
takeaway: Weighting coarse layers above fine ones preserves the mountain silhouette while keeping small detail.

blocks.text: Generate six terrains with sample counts 256, 128, 64, 32, 16 and 8. Give the densest terrain the smallest scale, 0.03125, and double the weight each time the sample count halves, ending at 1 for the eight-point terrain. The normalized weighted sum lets the coarse layers define the shape while the dense layers add only small aberrations.

title: Build the generator as noise, interpolation and octave combination
takeaway: A small pipeline with four exposed knobs covers most 1D terrain needs.

blocks.text: The generator is easiest to tune when uniform noise, gap filling and octave mixing stay separate. Sample interval, interpolator, octave count and weight schedule then become independent parameters instead of one hard-coded formula.

Write helper functions for mapping, linear interpolation and cosine interpolation.
Keep every k-th height and interpolate all skipped positions between controls.

title: MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity from shared minima, not from full intersections
takeaway: A fixed-size sketch can replace an expensive pairwise set operation at scale.

blocks.text: Exact Jaccard similarity requires intersecting and unioning entire sets, which becomes prohibitive across millions of document pairs. MinHash replaces that with a sketch: hash every element, keep the smallest hash under several permutations, and measure how often two sketches agree. The agreement rate estimates the Jaccard coefficient while comparison cost depends on sketch size rather than set size.

title: Jaccard similarity is also the chance a random element belongs to both sets
takeaway: The probabilistic reading is what makes a sampling-based estimator possible.

blocks.text: The coefficient is the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union, bounded between 0 for disjoint sets and 1 for identical ones. Read probabilistically, it is the chance that an element drawn from the universal set appears in both A and B. That equivalence turns a set-counting problem into a probability that can be estimated from samples.

title: The minimum element under a permutation is a fair sample of set overlap
takeaway: One shared minimum carries the same information as a full intersection, probabilistically.

blocks.text: For a set S, MinHash returns the position of the earliest element in a permuted universal set that also belongs to S. Materialising a permutation is expensive, so The replacement is a hash such as `(a*x + b) mod c`, where a and b are below the universe size and c is a prime just above it. Two sets share a minimum only when the winning element lies in their intersection, so the probability of agreement equals their Jaccard similarity.

title: A signature is k independent minima, and its match rate is the estimate
takeaway: Sketch size becomes a tunable accuracy budget instead of a property of the data.

blocks.text: Compute one minimum under each of k different hash functions and store the resulting vector as the set's signature. To compare two sets, count the positions where their signatures agree and divide by k. The signature has a fixed length regardless of how many elements the set contains, so both storage and comparison cost stop growing with the data.

title: More hash functions buy accuracy at a linear cost in space and time
takeaway: Choose k from the error you can tolerate, not from a default library value.

blocks.text: Every extra hash is another independent trial, so the estimate tightens as k grows. It also adds one more pass over the set and one more integer to every signature. Low k is cheap but noisy, while high k approaches exact Jaccard and erodes the speed advantage that motivated sketching.

title: The estimate tracks the true coefficient as two sets converge
takeaway: The approximation preserves the shape of the similarity curve while doing far less work.

blocks.text: The test began with two disjoint sets of equal cardinality and replaced one element of the first set with an element of the second at each step, moving similarity from 0 to 1. Exact Jaccard and the MinHash estimate were plotted together. The estimate followed the same curve with substantially fewer computations.

title: Choose the smoothing window that maximizes kurtosis, not the one that looks nice
takeaway: Smoothing can be tuned automatically for the thing you are actually trying to see.

blocks.text: Smoothing always trades noise removal against anomaly removal. Instead of eyeballing a window, score each candidate by the kurtosis of the smoothed series: anomalies occupy the tails, so preserving them raises tail weight. The window that maximizes kurtosis within a sensible range keeps the plot readable without erasing the spike.

title: Aggregation hides anomalies, while a moving average keeps the data density
takeaway: For anomaly review, preserve the original time resolution rather than binning it away.
section: Time Series and need of Smoothing

blocks.text: Binning a series into coarser buckets reduces the point count and can average a short spike into invisibility. A moving average instead replaces each point with the mean of its neighbours and keeps one output per timestamp. The trend becomes easier to read while the location and approximate height of a deviation remain on the chart.

title: A simple moving average is just the unweighted mean of the last n points
takeaway: The entire behaviour of SMA is controlled by one parameter, the window length.
section: Time Series Smoothing using Moving Average

blocks.text: SMA slides a window of length `n` across the series and writes the mean of the values inside it. A small window barely changes the shape, while a large window flattens everything, including the spikes. Because the output keeps one point per input timestamp, the only tuning decision is how wide that window should be.

title: A window that is too large erases the anomaly you are trying to see
takeaway: Over-smoothing is not a cosmetic problem; it destroys the signal the chart exists to show.

blocks.text: Short windows leave the short-term irregularity in place, so real deviations still compete with noise. Long windows remove the noise but also average a brief spike across many neighbours, lowering its peak until it disappears. No single window length works for every series; the value has to be derived from the data.

title: Kurtosis measures tail weight, and anomalies live in the tails
takeaway: A statistic that rewards extreme values is a natural objective for preserving anomalies.

blocks.text: Kurtosis is the fourth standardized moment of a distribution and describes how heavy its tails are. A rare extreme value far from the mean raises kurtosis sharply even when it is a tiny fraction of the points. Maximizing it therefore rewards a smoothed series that still contains its outliers.

title: Search window sizes inside a bounded range and keep the kurtosis peak
takeaway: A bounded search avoids the distortion that comes from chasing a global maximum.

blocks.text: A global maximum can push the window to a length that distorts the plot and loses information. Restrict candidates to a plausible interval, compute kurtosis for each smoothed result, and take the best value inside that interval.

items: Set a candidate window range from the sampling cadence, such as 10 to 40.
Smooth the series with SMA at every window length in the range.
Compute kurtosis on each smoothed series.
Select the window with the highest kurtosis inside the range.
Plot the result and confirm known anomalies are still visible.

title: LFU can run in constant time if you spend memory on pointers
takeaway: When an ordered data structure dominates latency, replace order with direct links.

blocks.text: The usual LFU cache keeps a min-heap keyed by access count, so every insert, hit and eviction pays O(log n) to restore heap order. A hash table plus two layers of doubly linked lists removes the ordered structure entirely: every operation becomes a fixed number of pointer updates. Time is traded for memory.

title: Heap-based LFU pays a rebalance on every single access
takeaway: The heap makes eviction selection cheap but makes every frequency change expensive.

blocks.text: A min-heap makes the least-frequently-used item easy to find, but only while its ordering invariant holds. Changing any item's frequency breaks that invariant, so a cache hit triggers sift operations just like an insert or an eviction. All three core operations therefore inherit O(log n), which is why many systems fall back to a simpler O(1) LRU.

title: The index is a hash table; frequencies and values form linked lists
takeaway: Two levels of lists let the cache find an eviction candidate and move any item without searching.

blocks.text: A hash table maps each cache key to a Value Node holding the cached value. A separate `freq_list` holds one Frequency Node per distinct access count, sorted ascending, and each Frequency Node owns a list of all values at that count. Value Nodes point back to their Frequency Node, so the structure can be navigated in both directions without a scan.

title: A cache hit moves the value to the next frequency node
takeaway: Promotion is a local pointer edit, not a global rebalance.

blocks.text: On access, look up the Value Node and read its Frequency Node. If the neighbouring node represents `freq + 1`, unlink the value from the current list and append it there; if not, create that frequency node and splice it in first. Both paths are pointer edits, so a hit stays O(1).

title: Insert at frequency one and evict from the lowest-frequency list
takeaway: The eviction candidate is always one pointer away, with no search or heap repair.

blocks.text: A new key is wrapped in a Value Node and placed in the list for frequency 1, creating that Frequency Node if it does not exist. Eviction takes the first Frequency Node in `freq_list` and removes one Value Node from its list. Neither path scans the cache or rebalances a tree.

title: Constant-time LFU trades RAM for latency, and every key stays resident
takeaway: The design fits latency-sensitive caches with bounded key spaces, not arbitrarily large ones.

blocks.text: The design follows the RUM conjecture: optimizing reads and updates forces a compromise on memory. Every cached key lives in the hash table, and every value and frequency carries several pointers, so overhead per entry is much larger than the payload. The scheme suits caches whose working set fits in memory, not enormous key spaces.

title: Count approximately in log-log space when exact totals do not matter
takeaway: For cardinalities at scale, a tiny probabilistic register can beat a wide exact counter.

blocks.text: Morris's counter stores a probabilistic estimate instead of the event count, using a register that grows like the logarithm of the count. That reduces the space needed to count to n from O(log n) bits to O(log log n) bits, with relative error that stays roughly constant as n grows. The trade is exactness, not asymptotic accuracy.

title: Counting every other event fixes absolute error but not relative error
takeaway: A constant error band is useless when the count itself is small.

blocks.text: Flipping a coin and incrementing only on heads makes the register hold about n/2, so doubling it recovers an estimate. The absolute error stays bounded, but at small n that error is a large fraction of the count. The trick also buys only one extra bit: an 8-bit register moves from 256 to roughly 512.

title: Store a logarithmic estimate so early increments buy more resolution
takeaway: Logarithmic growth is what makes the relative error independent of the final count.

blocks.text: Rather than holding a constant fraction of n, the register holds a value that grows logarithmically with the number of events. Because the inverse is exponential, the estimate moves quickly at small counts and more slowly later, keeping relative error nearly flat across magnitudes. The counter no longer tracks n directly; it tracks an encoded version of n.

title: Increment with probability proportional to the gap between estimates
takeaway: The update rule converts a deterministic counter into an unbiased estimator.

blocks.text: When an event arrives, estimate n from the current register and compute the jump to the estimate for `v + 1`. Set `d` to the reciprocal of that jump and draw `r` uniformly from [0,1). Increment only when `r < d`, so increments become rarer as the count grows and the expected estimate advances by one event.

title: A single byte can represent counts far beyond its exact range
takeaway: Log-log storage turns register width from a hard ceiling into a range parameter.

blocks.text: To count to n, the register only needs to reach about log n, and storing that value takes about log log n bits. A single byte can therefore represent counts far beyond the 256 it holds exactly, with relative error staying fairly flat as n increases. Twice the standard deviation on either side of the estimate gives the usual 95% confidence band.

title: Use Morris where a confidence interval beats an exact total
takeaway: Approximate counting belongs in telemetry, not in billing or quotas.

blocks.text: Absolute error still grows with n even though relative error stays stable, and any single run can sit well away from the true count. The method fits per-item cardinalities, traffic estimates and telemetry where an approximate magnitude is enough. It is a poor fit for billing, quotas or anything where the last unit matters.

title: Pessimal algorithms delay progress on purpose and never take a wrong step
takeaway: Deliberate inefficiency is a useful lens for seeing which parts of a fast algorithm do real work.

blocks.text: Slowsort belongs to a class of algorithms designed to be as inefficient as possible while still terminating with the right answer. Unlike a buggy sort, every comparison and swap moves toward a sorted array; the inefficiency comes from how much redundant work the recursion creates. Studying that shape shows which steps of a normal algorithm are actually necessary.

title: Multiply and Surrender multiplies subproblems instead of dividing them
takeaway: Recursion alone does not make an algorithm divide and conquer.

blocks.text: Divide and conquer splits a problem so the pieces are easier and then combines their answers. Multiply and Surrender also recurses, but it splits into barely simpler pieces and postpones the combination until no further delay is possible. The recursion still terminates, yet the number of overlapping subproblems explodes; naive recursive Fibonacci is the familiar example.

title: Slowsort replaces merge with one swap and a smaller recursive call
takeaway: Deleting the linear merge and paying with an extra recursive sort is the whole trick.

blocks.text: Sort the left half, sort the right half, then compare their last elements and swap so the larger sits at the end of the whole array. That element is now in its final position, so recurse on everything except it. Mergesort's linear merge is gone; the algorithm pays for the missing merge with an extra recursive sort of size n minus one.

title: The recurrence lands at O(n^log n), worse than bubble sort's worst case
takeaway: The slowest case of a pessimal sort can exceed the worst case of a genuinely bad one.

blocks.text: Two half-size recursive sorts plus a sort of size n minus one produce a recurrence whose lower bound is non-polynomial. For large n, `n^log n` exceeds `n^2`, so Slowsort's best case is worse than Bubble sort's worst case. The gap widens as inputs grow.

title: Slowsort is deterministic and monotone; Bogosort can undo its own progress
takeaway: A principled pessimal algorithm is still convergent, which Bogosort never guarantees.

blocks.text: Bogosort shuffles until the array happens to be sorted, so it may succeed on the first try and has no finite worst case. Slowsort always takes the same super-quadratic path and never swaps a pair out of order once placed, so its inversion count is non-increasing. That makes Slowsort the more principled pessimal algorithm even though Bogosort is the more famous joke.

title: Bitcask turns every write into an append and every read into one seek
takeaway: Separating the write path from the read path lets each one be optimal.

blocks.text: Bitcask stores each key-value record in an append-only datafile and keeps an in-memory hash table pointing at the record's file and offset. Writes never seek because they only extend the active file; reads need a single lookup plus one positional disk read. The design trades RAM for predictable, low-latency I/O.

title: The write path appends a record, then updates the index atomically
takeaway: A put is complete once the append and the index insert both succeed.

blocks.text: A record carries `crc`, `timestamp`, `key_size`, `value_size`, the key and the value. The engine appends it to the active datafile, then inserts the key's `file_id` and offset into KeyDir in the same atomic step. If either half fails, neither becomes visible.

title: A read is one KeyDir lookup followed by one positional read
takeaway: The in-memory index eliminates every read-time search except the final fetch.

blocks.text: KeyDir resolves the key to a datafile and byte offset without touching disk. The engine reads that one record, verifies the stored CRC, and returns the value; the filesystem read-ahead cache can absorb repeated reads. There is no scan, no tree descent and no second seek.

title: Updates and deletes are appends; old versions become garbage
takeaway: Never mutating a record in place is what keeps every write sequential.

blocks.text: Bitcask has no in-place update, so writing an existing key appends a full new value and repoints KeyDir at it. A delete appends a record carrying a unique tombstone value and removes the key from the index. Both leave the previous record on disk until compaction reclaims it.

title: Compaction rewrites only the live value of each key
takeaway: Disk usage tracks the live key space instead of the entire write history.

blocks.text: Updates and deletes leave dead records behind, so Bitcask periodically merges immutable datafiles. The merge keeps only the newest live version of each key, writes fresh files in the same record format, and updates the affected KeyDir offsets atomically. Superseded files are then discarded.

title: Hint files rebuild the index without reading a single value
takeaway: Fast recovery comes from separating key metadata from the payload on disk.

blocks.text: A hint file mirrors each datafile's keys and metadata but omits the values. On boot, the engine rebuilds KeyDir from these small files instead of scanning every record in the log. Compaction reduces the number of files; hints reduce how much must be read from each.

title: The entire key space must fit in RAM, so scale by sharding
takeaway: Bitcask's memory ceiling is the price of its one-seek reads and simple writes.

blocks.text: KeyDir holds every key and its metadata in memory, which caps a single instance at the machine's available RAM after filesystem buffers. The rest of the profile is strong: high write throughput, one seek per read, fast bounded recovery and a directory copy for backup. Sharding keys across instances is the straightforward way past the memory ceiling.

title: Report suspicion as a continuous score, and let the application choose the threshold
takeaway: Separating detection evidence from the decision makes one detector usable by many services.

blocks.text: A fixed-timeout detector has to decide up front whether a missed heartbeat means dead or merely slow. Phi accrual instead computes how unlikely the current silence is given past heartbeat intervals, and outputs that as a value that rises with the delay. Applications then pick the threshold that matches their tolerance for false positives.

title: A fixed heartbeat timeout cannot distinguish a crash from a slow node
takeaway: The timeout encodes a guess about latency that the network is free to invalidate.

blocks.text: Heartbeat detectors emit a boolean: alive if a message arrived inside the timeout, dead otherwise. A short timeout catches real failures quickly but also flags ordinary network stalls; a long timeout reduces false alarms but delays every real detection. The threshold is a fixed guess about a system whose latency keeps changing.

title: Phi is minus log10 of the probability that the heartbeat is merely late
takeaway: The logarithmic scale turns a probability into a usable, open-ended suspicion score.

blocks.text: The detector estimates the chance that the next heartbeat would arrive later than the current silence, then applies `-log10` to that probability. As the chance falls toward zero, phi climbs toward infinity; as a heartbeat becomes likely, phi approaches zero. The result is not a probability but a scale on which thresholds have a clear interpretation.

title: Fit recent heartbeat intervals to a normal distribution and integrate the tail
takeaway: The detector is only as good as its model of recent inter-arrival times.

blocks.text: Keep a sliding window of arrival timestamps, derive the inter-arrival intervals, and compute their mean and variance. Treating the intervals as normal, integrate the probability density from the current elapsed time to infinity to get the probability of a later heartbeat. That probability feeds the phi calculation.

title: A phi threshold is a false-suspicion budget, not a liveness fact
takeaway: Each extra unit of phi divides the chance of being wrong by ten, which makes thresholds easy to reason about.

blocks.text: Because phi is built from `-log10`, each extra unit divides the chance that the suspicion is wrong by ten: threshold 1 corresponds to roughly 10%, 2 to 1%, and 3 to 0.1%. Thresholds can be layered so mild suspicion triggers probing while severe suspicion triggers failover. The detector supplies evidence; the service owns the consequence.

title: Repeating-key XOR leaks its key length through ciphertext self-similarity
takeaway: A stream cipher's weakness is not the XOR; it is reusing the same key material at a predictable period.

blocks.text: XOR is self-inverse, so reusing a short key across a long message creates a detectable pattern. When two ciphertext bytes were produced by the same key byte, XORing them cancels the key and leaves the XOR of two plaintext bytes. English-like plaintext is measurably closer than random bytes, and the signal is strongest at offsets aligned with the key.

title: Encryption and decryption are the same XOR operation
takeaway: XOR's self-inverse property is both what makes the cipher convenient and what makes it breakable.

blocks.text: The key is repeated to the plaintext length, then each plaintext byte is XORed with the corresponding key byte. Because `a = b ^ c` implies `b = a ^ c`, running the same routine on the ciphertext with the same key returns the plaintext. The output is a raw byte stream, not text, so it must be handled as bytes.

title: Hamming distance counts bit flips; normalize it to compare different lengths
takeaway: The normalized score exposes whether two byte streams came from the same narrow alphabet.

blocks.text: XOR two byte streams and count the set bits to get their Hamming distance, the number of positions where they differ. Divide by the number of bit pairs to get a Hamming score that is comparable across stream lengths. Random byte pairs score about 3.9999 bits, while lowercase English pairs score about 2.45, so plaintext-versus-plaintext comparisons look unusually close.

title: The key length is the chunk size with the lowest average Hamming score
takeaway: Key-length detection is a search for alignment, and misalignment shows up as noise.

blocks.text: Split the ciphertext into chunks of a candidate length, XOR corresponding chunks, and average their Hamming scores. At the true key length, bytes in corresponding chunk positions were XORed with the same key byte, so comparing them reduces to plaintext XOR plaintext and the score dips. Multiples of the key length produce the same dip, which helps confirm the period.

title: Once the period is known, solve each column as single-byte XOR
takeaway: Breaking one repeating key reduces to several independent single-byte problems.

blocks.text: Reshape the ciphertext into `key_length` columns; every byte in a column was XORed with the same key byte. Each column is therefore a single-byte XOR problem, solved by trying all 256 candidates and scoring the plaintext with letter frequencies and a fitting quotient. The winning bytes concatenate into the full key.

title: The method recovered 99 of 100 random English messages
takeaway: The attack is reliable on natural-language plaintext but not guaranteed on every input.

blocks.text: The test encrypted 100 random English sentences with random keys of varying length, then ran key-length detection and frequency scoring. The pipeline recovered 99 of the 100 plaintexts. The miss rate is low but non-zero, so the output still needs a plausibility check.

title: The detector assumes natural-language plaintext and can lock onto a multiple
takeaway: Treat the detected period as a hypothesis and verify it by decrypting the text.

blocks.text: The Hamming dip exists only because English characters occupy a narrow numeric range; compressed, already-encrypted or binary plaintext destroys the signal. A multiple of the true key length can score just as low as the key itself, so one minimum is not proof of the period. Decrypt with each candidate and score the resulting text before trusting it.

title: A 256-value key space turns decryption into scoring, not key recovery
takeaway: When the key is one byte, exhaustive search is cheap enough that the hard part becomes recognizing English.

blocks.text: A single-byte XOR cipher has only 256 possible keys. Rather than attacking the cipher, try every key in `[0, 256)`, decrypt with each, and keep the candidate that most resembles the original language. The search is trivial; the real work is a scoring function that can rank one real plaintext above 255 pieces of garbage.

title: XOR is its own inverse, so encryption and decryption are one function
takeaway: The same routine both hides and reveals a message, which is why brute force only needs a decrypt path.

blocks.text: Because `a = b ^ c` implies `b = a ^ c`, XORing a byte with a key twice restores it. Encryption and decryption therefore share one implementation: apply the key to every byte of the input. Keying `abcd` with `69` produces `$'&!`, and running the same function on `$'&!` returns `abcd`.

title: Brute-force all 256 keys, then keep the best-looking plaintext
takeaway: Exhaustive search is only usable when you can automatically tell a correct answer from 255 wrong ones.

blocks.text: The decipher loop decrypts the ciphertext once per candidate key and scores each result. It returns the candidate with the best score instead of asking a human to inspect 256 outputs. At this key size the cost of trying everything is negligible, so search replaces cryptanalysis.

title: English letter frequencies act as a fingerprint for plaintext
takeaway: A language has a stable distribution of letters, so a wrong key leaves a statistical signature you can detect.

blocks.text: Letters are not equally common: `a` appears about 8.239% of the time and `b` about 1.505%. The rough ordering of the twelve most frequent letters is captured by ETAOIN SHRDLU. Decrypting with the wrong key smears this distribution, while the right key restores it.

title: The fitting quotient turns 'looks like English' into a single number
takeaway: Averaging per-letter frequency error gives brute force an objective ranking function.

blocks.text: For a candidate plaintext, compute each letter's relative frequency and compare it with the expected English percentage. The fitting quotient averages the absolute differences across the alphabet. Lower is better, so the key that minimizes it is reported as the decryption.

title: Frequency scoring collapses on short or symbol-heavy text
takeaway: The method is statistical, so it needs enough letters before its verdict means anything.

blocks.text: The approach was tested on 100 random English sentences with random keys and recovered all of them. It fails when the message is very short or contains many symbols, because too few letters accumulate to approximate the language's distribution. The scoring function, not the cipher, is the limiting factor.

title: An integer's iterability is one C slot, and filling it breaks unpacking
takeaway: Iterability is a property of a type's C struct, which is why a one-line patch can change language semantics.

blocks.text: CPython decides whether an object can be looped over by looking at the `tp_iter` slot of its type. For integers that slot is `NULL`, so `for x in 7` raises a `TypeError`. Filling the slot makes `7` iterate as `range(0, 7)`, which works but breaks a different part of the language.

title: An iterable only has to return an object that implements `__next__`
takeaway: The protocol is two methods, so any type that can supply them becomes loopable without a base class.

blocks.text: `__iter__` must return an iterator, and that iterator's `__next__` yields items until it raises `StopIteration`. `__iter__` is the method that makes an object iterable in the first place. Custom types join the club by implementing these two methods, not by inheriting from a common ancestor.

title: Every Python type is a C struct whose behavior lives in optional slots
takeaway: A type's capabilities are a set of function pointers, and an empty pointer is a deliberate absence.

blocks.text: Each Python type is an instance of `PyTypeObject`, which holds metadata plus C function pointers for individual operations. Most of those slots are optional: fill one and the corresponding behavior appears. `PyLong_Type` leaves `tp_iter` at `0`, which is the mechanical reason integers cannot be iterated.

title: Implement `long_iter` as a thin wrapper over a range iterator
takeaway: Reuse the range machinery instead of writing a new iterator, so the semantics match `range(0, n, 1)`.

blocks.text: The slot function receives the integer object and must return an iterator instance. A helper `PyLongRangeIter_ZeroToN` builds a `longrangeiterobject` with start `0`, end `n` and step `1`. Assigning `long_iter` to `tp_iter` on `PyLong_Type` is all that is needed to change the behavior.

title: Iterable integers make unpacking depend on the number's value
takeaway: Two nearly identical assignments diverge, so a global convenience silently breaks a core language feature.
section: Why it is not a good idea

blocks.text: Unpacking iterates the right-hand side. With iterable integers, `a, b = 7` yields seven values for two targets and raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)`. Meanwhile `a, b = 2` succeeds because the iteration stops at two, so the outcome depends on the magnitude of the number.

title: Treating numbers as single values is an invariant other features depend on
takeaway: Making an object iterable is not a local change when other syntax already assumes it is not.
section: Why it is not a good idea

blocks.text: Unpacking treats any iterable on the right-hand side as a sequence of values. Integers are exempt because they are singular, so a single scalar on the right is an error today. Removing that exemption changes what every assignment of the form `a, b = 7` means.

title: Embedding a parent struct first is enough to emulate inheritance in C
takeaway: C lacks inheritance but guarantees a layout that lets a child pointer stand in for a parent pointer.

blocks.text: If a struct places another struct as its first member, the child's memory begins with a complete parent. A pointer cast then reinterprets those same bytes as the parent type. That single property supports shared operations across node types and underpins structures from the Linux kernel to CPython's object model.

title: Structure composition stores the parent by value, not by pointer
takeaway: Value embedding is what makes the layout contiguous and the later cast possible.

blocks.text: Composition means one struct contains another as a native member, so the inner struct's bytes live inside the outer allocation. A list node can embed a `list_head` holding `next` and `prev` alongside any payload. A `list_int` reaches the links as `list.next` and `list.prev` rather than through a separate object.

title: Casting a child to its parent just re-reads the first bytes
takeaway: When the parent sits at offset zero, an upcast changes the type without moving or copying data.

blocks.text: Casting `list_int *` to `list_head *` maps the parent's field layout onto the start of the child's memory. Because `list_int` begins with `list_head`, those bytes already are the parent. No pointer arithmetic or copy is involved; only the interpretation changes.

title: The cast is safe because C lays members out in declaration order
takeaway: The technique rests on a layout rule, not on the compiler knowing that the two types are related.

blocks.text: C structs carry no metadata and are allocated just enough space for their fields, laid out contiguously in the order declared. A `list_int` holding two pointers and an integer therefore takes 12 bytes. That ordering is what guarantees the embedded parent occupies the prefix.

title: Write list operations against `list_head *` and every node type inherits them
takeaway: One implementation serves int nodes, string nodes and future payloads, which is the practical payoff.

blocks.text: Insertion, deletion, splicing, rotation and swapping only manipulate `next` and `prev`. Defining them to accept `list_head *` lets any embedded node pass through. The caller keeps a typed pointer and the callee ignores the payload entirely, so new node types need no new list code.

title: A shared root header lets one refcount routine serve every object type
takeaway: The same trick scales from a list node to a language runtime's entire object model.

blocks.text: CPython defines `PyObject` with a reference count and a type pointer, and every object struct places it first. Incrementing and decrementing references can then be written once against `PyObject *`. The Linux kernel applies the same pattern to linked lists through `list_head`.

title: Every storage engine pays for fast reads with write cost or space
takeaway: RUM names the bill, so engine choice becomes an explicit trade instead of a feature checklist.

blocks.text: The RUM conjecture says no access method can be simultaneously optimal for reads, updates and memory. Improving two forces a sacrifice in the third, making the three a competing triangle much like CAP. The conjecture is widely observed rather than proven, yet it predicts why storage systems cluster into recognizable families.

title: Overheads are ratios of total work to useful work, not absolute times
takeaway: Amplification separates the cost a system imposes from the speed of the hardware underneath it.

blocks.text: Read amplification is total bytes read, main plus auxiliary, divided by the main data requested. Write amplification is total bytes written divided by the main data actually updated. Space amplification is total space used divided by the space the main data alone needs. Each ratio rises when an auxiliary structure must be consulted or maintained.

title: Read-optimized engines buy lookup speed with index maintenance
takeaway: Hash and tree indexes make reads cheap but turn every write into at least two writes.

blocks.text: Point indexes, B-trees and skiplists keep auxiliary structures that narrow a lookup to a constant or logarithmic number of probes. Every update to main data must also update that structure, adding write amplification. When updates become frequent, the read advantage erodes because maintenance dominates.

title: Update-optimized engines batch writes and make reads reconcile tiers
takeaway: Deferring work to bulk flushes moves cost from the write path to the read path and to disk.

blocks.text: LSM trees and partitioned B-trees absorb changes into a delta area and merge them in bulk later. Writes stay cheap, but a read must consult multiple tiers and resolve which version wins. Keeping those tiers around is itself the space overhead.

title: Memory-optimized structures trade exactness for a smaller footprint
takeaway: Bloom filters and sketches save space by accepting error, and that error is paid at read time.

blocks.text: Lossy indexes, sparse indexes and lossy encodings compress what they store or deliberately allow false positives. Compression shrinks the auxiliary footprint but adds encode and decode work to both reads and writes. Sparse structures skip detail, so a lookup may have to scan further before it finds the record.

title: Clustering the data into the index removes a second read
takeaway: When the index holds the rows, read amplification drops without a separate fetch.

blocks.text: Block-based clustered indexing keeps a shallow tree of page pointers and stores the main data inside the index structure. A lookup that lands on the right page already has the row, so there is no follow-up read against main storage. This places it between the three pure optimizations rather than at one corner of the triangle.

title: Modulo hashing ties every key to the node count, so one resize reshuffles the cluster
takeaway: Consistent hashing exists to make scaling move a slice of data instead of most of it.

blocks.text: Hashing a key modulo the number of nodes spreads keys evenly while the cluster is fixed. Add or remove a node and the modulus changes, so nearly every key gets a new home. Consistent hashing keeps the hash space constant and makes placement relative to node positions instead.

title: Going from five nodes to seven moved every file in the example
takeaway: The remap is proportional to the number of keys, not to the number of nodes added.

blocks.text: With `mod 5` the sample files landed on nodes E, A, B, C and D. With `mod 7` the same files landed on D, E, F, G and A. Every association changed. At real scale the same effect would require migrating most of the dataset to add a little capacity.

title: A fixed hash space makes placement independent of cluster size
takeaway: Hashing into a constant space decouples where a key lives from how many machines exist.

blocks.text: Both keys and nodes hash into one large, fixed space. A key belongs to the first node encountered clockwise from its own position, wrapping at the end. Adding capacity only inserts a node into that space, so the mapping rule itself never changes.

title: Keep nodes and positions in parallel sorted arrays and binary search them
takeaway: Successor lookup in a sorted array gives ring semantics in logarithmic time without materializing the space.

blocks.text: One array holds node identities, the other their hashed positions, and both stay sorted by position. To find a key's owner, binary search for the first position greater than the key's hash. If none exists, wrap to index zero.

title: Adding a node only moves the arc immediately before it
takeaway: The migration set is bounded by one node's share of the ring, which is the entire point of the technique.

blocks.text: When node K is inserted between B and E, only keys hashing in the segment from B to K change owners, moving from E to K. Everything else keeps its existing node. The new node can be populated from its successor before it joins the ring.

title: Removing a node hands its keys to its clockwise successor
takeaway: Departures are as cheap as arrivals: one node's worth of data moves, not a full remap.

blocks.text: Locate the departing node's position in the sorted keys array, move its data to the next node to the right, then delete the entry. Only that node's keys are affected. Scale-down therefore touches a single arc of the ring, just as scale-up does.

title: One array slot per hash value is too large to store and too slow to scan
takeaway: The obvious ring implementation fails on both memory and lookup cost.

blocks.text: Placing keys and nodes at their literal hashed index needs memory proportional to the hash space. Finding the next node then means walking right until one appears, which is `O(hash_space)` per lookup. The sorted-array representation replaces both problems with an `O(log n)` search over a small structure.

title: Python trades fixed-width speed for unbounded size, then buys speed back for small values
takeaway: The integer cache is a narrow optimization aimed at where most values actually come from.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: Python integers are not 2-, 4- or 8-byte values; they are digit arrays in base 2^30, which removes overflow but makes allocation and arithmetic expensive. To soften that cost, CPython preallocates the integers from -5 to 256 as singletons at startup. Referencing one of those values returns a shared object instead of allocating.

title: An integer is a base-2^30 digit array, so its size follows its value
takeaway: Unlimited range is convenient, but it means even addition pays allocation and carry costs.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: Because there is no fixed width, the number of digits grows with the value being stored. Operations on very long numbers work without overflow checks, but the convenience is paid for in allocation and in slower arithmetic. The small-integer cache only partially offsets that fundamental trade.

title: The range -5 to 256 is preallocated once and shared thereafter
takeaway: Small integers are the common case, so caching them avoids a large number of allocations.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: CPython creates these values during initialization and hands out references to the existing objects. The optimization is visible in the source as the `IS_SMALL_INT` macro and the `get_small_int` function in `longobject.c`. Values outside the range are allocated normally.

title: `id()` exposes the cache: equal small values share an address
takeaway: Identity is a direct test for whether a value came from the singleton table.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: `id` returns the object's memory address in CPython. Two references to the same small value report the same address, while two equal large values report different ones. The check also holds for computed results, so `2 + 4` and `10 - 4` can return the very same integer object.

title: Outside the cached range, equal values stop being the same object
takeaway: Small-int identity works by accident of caching and silently stops being true at 257.
section: Verifying smaller integers are indeed a singleton

blocks.text: The cache ends at 256, so larger values are freshly allocated whenever they are produced. Two variables holding the same large number can therefore have different addresses even though their values match. Any code that tests identity rather than equality for numbers breaks exactly at that boundary.

title: Startup reference counts peak at 0 and spike at powers of two
takeaway: The cache saves roughly two thousand allocations before the interpreter runs a single line of user code.
section: Verifying if these integers are indeed referenced often

blocks.text: Measuring `getrefcount` across -5 to 300 shows counts falling as values rise, with 0 at the top at 359 references. Spikes appear at 32, 64, 128 and 256. Preallocating the range avoided about 1993 allocations during interpreter startup alone.

title: Cascading replaces repeated searches with one search and a bridge per list
takeaway: Preprocessing that links sorted lists can turn a multiplicative cost into an additive one.

blocks.text: Searching k sorted lists for the same value costs `O(k log n)` when each search is independent. Fractional cascading precomputes where an element's neighbourhood lives in the next list, so later levels need only a constant comparison. The result is one binary search followed by k cheap steps.

title: The naive baseline is k independent binary searches
takeaway: Knowing the exact baseline is what makes the later space-for-time trade legible.
section: The naive approach - k binary searches

blocks.text: For each of the k lists, find the first element greater than or equal to the target. Python's `bisect_left` does exactly this, giving `O(k log n)` time and no extra space. This is the version to beat on time without blowing up memory.

title: A single merged list removes the k-factor but multiplies storage
takeaway: One search over everything is fast, but storing a k-tuple per element is a steep space price.

blocks.text: Precompute, for every element, a tuple giving its position in each of the k lists, then merge all elements into one sorted auxiliary list. One binary search finds the right element and its tuple answers the query. Time drops to `O(log(kn))`, but space becomes `O(k*kn)`.

title: Build auxiliary lists bottom-up by promoting every other element
takeaway: Halving the promoted set keeps total auxiliary storage under twice the input.

blocks.text: `M(i)` contains all elements of `L(i)` plus every second element of `M(i+1)`, kept sorted. Lists are built from the deepest level upward so each level can draw on the one below. Because the promoted share halves at each step, total auxiliary size stays below twice the original data.

title: A two-item tuple is the bridge: local position plus where to land below
takeaway: The tuple carries both the answer and the next hop, so traversal needs no further searching.

blocks.text: For each auxiliary element, the first tuple entry gives its position in that level's original list, which is part of the answer. The second gives its position in the auxiliary list one level down. Following the second entry lands in the right neighbourhood for the next comparison.

title: After crossing a bridge, only two candidates can be correct
takeaway: The halving rule is what bounds the local check, so promotion is doing real correctness work.

blocks.text: Suppose the bridge lands at index `b` in the next list. Because every other element was promoted from below, the target must be at `b` or `b - 1`. A lower value would have been promoted and bridged elsewhere, so comparing those two gives the position without another search.

title: Fractional cascading lands at `O(k + log n)` time and `O(kn)` space
takeaway: It captures most of the merged-list approach's speed without its quadratic storage.

blocks.text: One binary search on the top auxiliary list is followed by constant work per remaining level. Auxiliary storage stays linear because promoted elements halve at each level and every tuple is a fixed two items. That combination makes the technique practical in range-search structures and FD-trees.

title: Copy-on-write bets that most copies are never modified
takeaway: Deferring the copy converts an upfront cost into a conditional one that often never arrives.

blocks.text: Instead of duplicating a resource when a second reference appears, both references share it and cloning happens at the first write. When a copy exists only to be read, or is immediately replaced, the expensive duplication never occurs. The technique wins precisely when reads vastly outnumber mutations.

title: A deep copy duplicates the whole graph; copy-on-write shares it until forced
takeaway: The cost difference is structural, since deep copying a linked list clones every node.

blocks.text: Deep copying allocates new storage for the object and for everything it references, so duplicating a list means cloning each node. Copy-on-write instead copies a reference and marks the resource shared. Mutating either side at that point requires cloning just enough to restore independence.

title: `fork` followed by `exec` is the ideal copy-on-write workload
takeaway: When the child will discard the inherited address space, pre-copying it is pure waste.

blocks.text: `fork` produces a child that starts as an exact copy of the parent's program space. Deep copying a large process would make process creation slow and memory-hungry. In the fork-exec pattern the child immediately replaces that space with another program, so copy-on-write avoids a copy that would have been thrown away.

title: Clone-then-swap removes the need for write locks
takeaway: Never mutating in place means readers always see a complete version, so there is no critical section to guard.

blocks.text: In-place updates force locking so writers do not observe each other's partial changes. Copy-on-write instead builds a new version and publishes it with one atomic compare-and-swap. Old versions are reclaimed later, and readers never block or see a torn state.

title: Keeping the old versions turns copy-on-write into time travel
takeaway: Snapshots and rollback fall out for free if you simply do not collect the previous copies.

blocks.text: Each write creates a new version, so retaining the discarded ones yields a history of the resource. That is how collaborative editors offer document history and how databases take point-in-time backups. Garbage collection decides how much of that history stays available.

title: Copy only the path from the changed node to the root
takeaway: Partial sharing keeps persistent updates proportional to depth instead of to structure size.

blocks.text: After sharing a tree by reference, modifying one node does not require duplicating the whole tree. Clone the nodes on the path from that node up to the root and let every untouched subtree stay shared. The new root defines the new version while the old root still defines the previous one.

title: A write-heavy workload turns copy-on-write into allocation churn
takeaway: If most copies get modified, the deferred cost arrives every time plus garbage collection on top.

blocks.text: Aggressive copy-on-write allocates a fresh version for every write. In a write-heavy system that means constant allocation and constant collection of the previous versions, consuming CPU and stalling other work. The technique belongs where reads dominate and mutations are occasional.

title: Strict LRU lets a one-off scan masquerade as hot data
takeaway: A cache policy that trusts first access will hand the working set to whatever touched it last.

blocks.text: Under LRU, every page read becomes the most recently used page. A full table scan therefore promotes page after page, evicting the pages real queries depend on. InnoDB changes where new pages enter the list so that a first read cannot claim the top spot.

title: Caching works because access is spatially and temporally clustered
takeaway: Prefetching and caching are both bets on locality, and each targets a different kind.

blocks.text: Spatial locality says rows near an accessed row will be needed soon, which justifies large pages and read-ahead. Temporal locality says an accessed page will be needed again soon, which justifies keeping recent pages in memory. Together they explain why a memory tier far smaller than the disk can serve most requests.

title: A scan larger than the cache evicts the entire working set
takeaway: The damage is not the scan's own cost but the misses it causes afterwards.

blocks.text: Scanning a table touches every page in order, and strict LRU inserts each at the head while evicting from the tail. If the table exceeds cache capacity, the cache ends up holding the tail of the scan and little else. Performance recovers only as those pages age out and useful pages return.

title: Split the buffer pool into a young and an old sublist
takeaway: Separating admission from promotion lets the cache distinguish a first touch from a repeated one.

blocks.text: InnoDB divides the pool into a young region of about 5/8 and an old region of about 3/8, joined into one recency order. Eviction still happens at the old tail. New pages enter at the boundary between the regions, the midpoint, rather than at the young head.

title: A page earns its way into the young region on a second access
takeaway: First-touch pages age out quickly unless something actually asks for them again.

blocks.text: A page read for the first time lands in the old sublist. If it is referenced again, it moves to the head of the young sublist and stays much longer. Pages touched once by a scan remain near the eviction end and leave without displacing the working set.

title: Tune the midpoint and watch the buffer pool's own counters
takeaway: The split is configurable, and the server reports whether the policy is actually protecting the cache.

blocks.text: `innodb_old_blocks_pct` sets the old sublist's share of the buffer pool; the default 37 corresponds to roughly 3/8. `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` exposes pages made young, evictions without access, hit ratio and read-ahead rate. Those counters show whether scans are still pushing useful pages out.

items: Record the buffer pool hit ratio before changing anything.
Set `innodb_old_blocks_pct` to match how much scan traffic the workload carries.
Run a known full-scan job and watch pages made young and evictions without access.
Compare the read-ahead rate against actual disk latency during that scan.
Re-check the hit ratio after the scan to confirm the working set survived.

title: A state machine is easiest to read when each state is a paused function
takeaway: Mapping one state to one resumable function keeps the code shaped like the state diagram.

blocks.text: A finite state machine is always in exactly one of a finite set of states and moves to another when it receives input. Implement each state as a coroutine that waits for a token, decides the next state, and pauses again. The transition logic then lives inside the state it belongs to instead of in a central switch.

title: Coroutines consume values where generators produce them
takeaway: Pausing preserves local state without concurrency, which is exactly what a state machine needs.

blocks.text: Both generators and coroutines pause at `yield` and keep their local state across the pause. A generator hands values out through `next`, while a coroutine receives values through `send`, which become the result of the paused `yield` expression. No background thread runs; control simply returns to the caller between inputs.

title: Give each state a loop that waits at `yield` and rewires the machine
takeaway: A state's transition table is just the body of its loop.

blocks.text: The coroutine for state `q2` loops forever, receives the next token, and assigns `fsm.current_state` based on that token. Receiving `b` selects `q2` and receiving `c` selects `q3`, mirroring the diagram's edges. The loop never exits; the machine moves by changing which coroutine receives the next token.

title: Funnel every input through one `send` method on the FSM object
takeaway: One dispatch point keeps state ownership in a single object.

blocks.text: The `FSM` class owns every state coroutine and a `current_state` pointer. Its `send` method forwards the incoming token to the current state, which decides where to go next. Callers never choose a state themselves, so legal transitions stay encapsulated.

title: Test acceptance on the final state, separately from the transitions
takeaway: Separating transition from acceptance makes the same machine reusable for different questions.

blocks.text: Running the input only moves the machine; it does not decide the answer. After the stream is exhausted, a predicate such as `does_match` checks whether the current state is an accepting one. Regex matching, divisibility, and SQL validation all reuse this split.

title: Coroutine FSMs favor a direct mapping over raw speed
takeaway: When the diagram is the specification, readability can be worth more than efficiency.

blocks.text: This approach is intuitive rather than the most efficient implementation. Transitions read like `if` and `elif` branches, and execution passes from one coroutine to the next like a baton in a relay. That clarity is the point; throughput is not.

title: A fair rating needs a prior, not just the average of its own reviews
takeaway: Blending in a population-level prior prevents small samples from dominating a leaderboard.

blocks.text: An item's own mean says little when it has one or two ratings. Bayesian averaging pulls sparse items toward the system-wide mean and lets well-reviewed items settle near their own mean. The prior supplies the confidence that the raw average lacks.

title: Arithmetic mean lets a single five-star review top the chart
takeaway: An average without a sample-size penalty rewards flukes.

blocks.text: The MovieLens top ten by plain average were all rated 5 out of 5 by exactly one user. Those scores are not wrong so much as unsupported: one rating cannot distinguish a masterpiece from a lucky pick. Low cardinality makes both the score and the rank unstable.

title: Cumulative ratings reward popularity and produce unbounded scores
takeaway: Replacing an average with a sum trades small-sample noise for a popularity bias.

blocks.text: Summing ratings pushes well-known items upward, which is why the top ten starts to look plausible. But an item with 10,000 one-star ratings scores 10,000 and beats a superb item with 1,000 five-star ratings at 5,000. The score also grows without bound, so it is hard to compare across systems.

title: Bayesian average is a weighted blend of item mean and system mean
takeaway: The prior acts as borrowed evidence until the item has enough of its own.

blocks.text: The score combines the item's mean `A` with the system mean `S` through a weight `w`. With few ratings the result stays near `S`; with many it approaches `A`. Because both inputs are bounded, the blended score is bounded too.

title: Shape the weight so it crosses 0.5 at the average rating count
takeaway: Encoding sample-size confidence as a monotonic weight makes the blend predictable.

blocks.text: The weight must stay in `[0, 1]`, rise monotonically with the rating count `m`, start near 0, equal 0.5 when `m` reaches the corpus average `m_avg`, and approach 1 thereafter. Those constraints make the switch from system mean to item mean gradual. The weight is the knob that decides how much evidence counts as enough.

title: Ranks smooth out instead of swinging as reviews accumulate
takeaway: Stability under accumulating evidence is the property that makes a ranking usable over time.

blocks.text: Tracking Kingsman, Logan, and The Scorpion King shows wider percentile swings under the arithmetic mean, sometimes after a good number of reviews. Bayesian ranks wobble early and then converge. The score behaves like a filtered estimate rather than a fresh average at every count.

title: A sliding window limiter is a per-key sum over recent time buckets
takeaway: Start from the counting semantics; the storage and scaling choices follow from them.

blocks.text: The decision is whether a key's requests in the last `time_window_sec` exceed its limit. Because that range is recomputed on every request, the window moves forward continuously instead of resetting on a schedule. The rest of the design exists to make this sum cheap and correct.

title: The window ends at the current request, so there is no reset boundary
takeaway: Anchoring the window to the request makes every decision a fresh range query.

blocks.text: A fixed window counts inside a recurring bucket, so its allowance resets at bucket boundaries. This design instead looks back a full `time_window_sec` from the moment each request arrives. That makes the counting range move with every call.

title: Store counts as key, then epoch second, then a counter
takeaway: Bucketing by second turns a time-range count into a short loop over integers.

blocks.text: The request store is a nested dictionary: the outer key identifies the user, token, or IP, and the inner key is an epoch second with its request count. Summing the inner entries newer than `start_time` yields the window total. Entries older than the window can be deleted because they can never matter again.

title: Concurrent increments lose counts unless the update is atomic
takeaway: A rate limiter's correctness depends on atomic counting, not just on the algorithm.

blocks.text: Several threads handling the same key can read the same old counter and each write back the same incremented value. Requests then disappear from the window and the limiter over-admits. The available fixes are compare-and-swap, a pessimistic lock, or a hardware fetch-and-add.

title: Cleaning old buckets can race with an in-flight request
takeaway: Garbage collection in a shared time-indexed store is part of the concurrency design.

blocks.text: One request may compute an older `start_time` while a newer request deletes buckets that older window still needs. The total then comes out too low. Deleting with a safety buffer, such as ten seconds before `start_time`, or locking reads during deletion avoids the race.

title: Per-second buckets cost O(window) work; coarser buckets trade precision for speed
takeaway: Bucket size is a direct dial between decision cost and timing precision.

blocks.text: An hour-long window at second granularity means up to 3,600 counters to sum on every request. Aggregating at the minute level cuts that to about 60, at the cost of a window that slides in minute steps. The granularity can be stored alongside the limit configuration.

title: Scale configuration and request data on separate paths
takeaway: Different read and write profiles deserve different stores, even inside one service.

blocks.text: Configurations are small, rarely change, and need durability, so they live in a key-value store and are cached in memory. Request counts are hot and large, so they live in memory and are sharded by key with consistent hashing behind a proxy. The decision engine sits behind a load balancer and calls both.

title: IDF measures rarity, and rarity is what makes a term worth matching
takeaway: Ranking signals come from contrast, so corpus-wide frequency matters as much as local frequency.

blocks.text: A term that appears in almost every document cannot distinguish one document from another. A term that appears in few documents carries more information when it does appear. IDF turns that intuition into a weight that falls as document frequency rises.

title: Any decreasing function of document frequency can act as an IDF
takeaway: Knowing the invariant lets you substitute a curve that fits your scoring range.

blocks.text: The only hard requirement is that the weight falls as more documents contain the term. Different decreasing curves satisfy it and produce different weight scales. The commonly used logarithmic form is a choice that works well, not the definition of the measure.

title: IDF is the negative log probability that a random document contains the term
takeaway: A probabilistic interpretation makes the statistic estimable and connects it to information content.

blocks.text: The fraction `df(t) / N` is the chance that one randomly chosen document mentions `t`. The usual IDF fraction is its inverse, so IDF equals the negative log of that probability. This reading also means IDF can be estimated from a random sample instead of the full corpus.

title: Assume independence and a multi-term query's IDF becomes a sum
takeaway: Independence turns a combinatorial conjunction into simple addition.

blocks.text: If term occurrences are treated as independent, the probability that a document contains all query terms is the product of the individual probabilities. The negative log of a product is the sum of the negative logs. A document's query score can therefore be computed by adding its per-term IDF scores.

title: Choose the IDF variant by its behavior at the edges
takeaway: The right variant depends on whether you need penalties, boundedness, or safe multiplication.

blocks.text: Probabilistic IDF assigns a negative weight to terms present in more than half the documents. Smooth IDF avoids the undefined value at zero document frequency and the hard zero at `df = N`. Those edge behaviors matter when IDF is multiplied by term frequency, because a zero or undefined factor destroys the product.

title: A document ranks high only when a rare term also appears often in it
takeaway: Relevance is a joint property of the document and the corpus, not of either alone.

blocks.text: TF-IDF multiplies a term's count within the document by its IDF. High IDF alone is not enough, since a single mention of an obscure word proves little. The product rewards terms that are both frequent locally and rare across the collection.

title: Programming skill compounds through scheduled practice, not occasional bursts
takeaway: A cadence you can sustain beats an ambitious plan you abandon.

blocks.text: The habits share a structure: a repeated activity, a cadence, and a concrete deliverable. Writing code, reading code, building systems, and collaborating are each put on a calendar. Improvement is treated as maintenance rather than a project with an end date.

title: Put each kind of practice on its own horizon
takeaway: Separating daily, monthly, and seasonal practice keeps one cadence from crowding out the others.

blocks.text: Different skills need different repetition rates. Small contributions keep the habit alive, larger contributions build depth, and periodic systems stretch architecture skills.

items: Make one small contribution to any project every three days.
Ship one substantial change to a project on a fortnightly cadence.
Work through two practice problems weekly until you hit 300.
Build one complex system every four months.
Model a real-world phenomenon every six months.
