title: Reading expert code builds vocabulary that writing alone cannot
takeaway: Code reading is a separate skill with its own practice loop.

blocks.text: Skimming an open-source project is hard at first and becomes clearer over repeated passes. The payoff is exposure to practices, paradigms, and structuring choices you would not invent in isolation. A useful practice is returning to the same codebase rather than reading it once.

title: Language constructs transfer even when syntax does not
takeaway: Learn the paradigm, then expect to re-express it in whatever language the job uses.

blocks.text: A language is a tool for expressing business logic, so the durable knowledge is the construct: functional programming, polymorphism, event-driven design, the actor model. A construct learned in one language can be rebuilt in another. One example is carrying callbacks from JavaScript into Python.

title: Write the scope and execution plan before the code
takeaway: A short planning pass is cheaper than retrofitting structure into rushed code.

blocks.text: Code written before any thought tends to lose simplicity, reuse, and extensibility. The remedy is to define the scope and sketch a rough execution plan first. That plan is what keeps the implementation from sprawling.

title: The prompt is an object Python stringifies, so it can be dynamic
takeaway: Treating the prompt as a value rather than a setting enables live, computed status displays.

blocks.text: `sys.ps1` and `sys.ps2` are ordinary attributes that the shell reads when it renders a prompt. Assign a string and the prompt changes immediately. Assign something else and Python calls `str()` on it every time, which opens the door to stateful prompts.

title: `sys.ps1` and `sys.ps2` are live attributes, not startup configuration
takeaway: Because the values are read continuously, experimentation costs nothing.

blocks.text: The primary prompt is `ps1` and the continuation prompt is `ps2`, both exposed through the `sys` module. Assignment takes effect at the next prompt with no restart. Colors work because the terminal interprets bash escape sequences embedded in the string.

title: Assign a non-string object and Python calls `__str__` on every render
takeaway: A one-method object turns a static prompt into a tiny live dashboard.

blocks.text: The documentation guarantees that a non-string prompt is converted with `str()` each time it is shown. A class can therefore keep mutable state and return a different string per render. This builds an IPython-style counter that increments a line number on each primary prompt.

title: Load prompt code automatically through `PYTHONSTARTUP`
takeaway: One environment variable makes a shell customization permanent without touching site packages.
section: Setting new prompt strings every time the shell starts

blocks.text: The `PYTHONSTARTUP` environment variable names a readable file that interactive Python executes before showing the first prompt.

items: Put the prompt code in a file such as `ipython.py`.
Export `PYTHONSTARTUP` with the absolute path to that file.
Start a new interactive shell and confirm the prompt changed.
Keep the file import-safe so a bad edit cannot block startup.

title: Deterministic chaos is enough for pseudorandomness when the seed stays secret
takeaway: Pseudorandomness is a property of the observer's knowledge, not of the generator's physics.

blocks.text: A pseudorandom generator is a deterministic function of a seed that produces a sequence with no visible pattern. Rule 30 supplies the aperiodic behavior; the seed supplies the unpredictability. Anyone who knows the seed can reproduce the entire stream.

title: Rule 30 reduces to `left XOR (central OR right)` on three cells
takeaway: A single compact rule is enough to generate unbounded structural complexity.

blocks.text: Each cell has two states and looks at itself plus its immediate neighbors. The eight possible neighborhoods map to next states through one Boolean expression. Rows are generations, and the row wraps at its ends.

title: Harvest random bits in batches from the center column
takeaway: Serial output is not inherent to the generator; separate columns can be harvested concurrently.

blocks.text: The center column is read downward and cut into `n`-bit chunks, each becoming one random number; the next chunk supplies the next number. Reading multiple columns in parallel yields multiple streams at once. The grid is evolved only as far as the harvest requires.

title: Skip a seed-derived number of bits before harvesting
takeaway: A deterministic generator becomes pseudorandom by randomizing where you start reading.

blocks.text: Starting at row 0 makes the output identical every run, which is predictable. Using a seed value such as the current timestamp as the number of bits to skip moves the harvest to a different offset. The same rule then yields a different-looking sequence per seed.

title: Using the seed as the first row is faster but concentrates risk
takeaway: Skipping work shifts the burden from computation to seed entropy.

blocks.text: Rule 30 can start directly from a seed-shaped initial row and read batches from row 0. That avoids evolving and discarding skipped generations. The catch is that a poor seed produces a correspondingly predictable stream, so the shortcut leans entirely on seed quality.

title: Overloading is dispatch, and Python makes you build the dispatch table
takeaway: Once overload resolution is framed as key lookup, the missing feature becomes a small library.

blocks.text: Python binds one object per name in a namespace, so defining `area` twice leaves only the second definition. Overloading therefore needs two things Python does not provide: a registry that keeps both implementations and a rule that selects one at call time. Both can be assembled from decorators and a dictionary.

title: Python's namespace keeps one entry per name, so the last definition wins
takeaway: The absence of overloading follows directly from the namespace's one-key-one-value model.

blocks.text: `locals()` and `globals()` expose namespaces as dictionaries mapping names to objects. A second `def` with the same name overwrites the first entry rather than adding a variant. This is why the language cannot distinguish two functions that share a name.

title: Key each implementation by module, class, name, and argument count
takeaway: A composite key turns an overload set into an ordinary dictionary.

blocks.text: The `Function` wrapper exposes a `key` method returning a tuple of module, class, function name, and parameter count. That tuple is unique per implementation even when names collide. Registering under the tuple is what lets two `area` definitions coexist.

title: Use a decorator as the hook that registers each definition
takeaway: Definition time is the only moment when every overload is still visible to be captured.

blocks.text: A decorator runs when the interpreter executes the `def`, which is exactly when the implementation becomes available. The `overload` decorator registers the wrapped function and returns a callable `Function` instance. Calling the decorated name then enters the wrapper rather than the original function.

title: Rebuild the key at call time and look up the implementation
takeaway: One key function used on both sides keeps registration and lookup consistent.

blocks.text: `Function.__call__` asks the namespace's `get` for the implementation matching the current arguments. `get` constructs the same tuple key and reads the registry, raising if nothing matches. Registration and dispatch share one key function, so they cannot drift apart.

title: Argument count is the simplest discriminator; types are the next step
takeaway: Decide the discrimination rule first; it determines both the key and the lookup cost.

blocks.text: In practice, overloading is limited to differing numbers of parameters, which is enough to separate one-argument circle area from two-argument rectangle area. Type-based dispatch is possible by recording argument types in the decorator, but it requires inspecting the signature. `getfullargspec` sets the practical limit on how fine-grained the discrimination can get.

title: Anomalies are easier to isolate than normal behavior is to model
takeaway: Inverting the modeling target can make the rare class the easy one to find.

blocks.text: Most detectors learn what normal looks like and flag deviations, which spends effort on the majority class. Isolation Forest instead repeatedly splits the data at random and measures how quickly a point becomes alone. Anomalies, being few and different, tend to need fewer splits.

title: Random splits isolate anomalies faster for two reasons
takeaway: Path length captures both rarity and distinctiveness without a distance metric.

blocks.text: Anomalies are a minority, so a random partition is more likely to separate one into a small region. Their attribute values also differ sharply from normal ones, so an early random split can cut them off. A short average path across many trees is therefore evidence of abnormality.

title: Models optimized for normal instances are tuned for the wrong class
takeaway: A detector's objective should match the class you actually care about.
section: The usual approach for detecting anomalies

blocks.text: The standard approach defines normality through statistics, classification, or clustering, then labels everything else anomalous. Its objective rewards describing the majority, not isolating the minority. The practical result is either many false positives or too few detections, often at high computational cost.

title: Subsample before building each tree to sharpen the separation
takeaway: Less data per tree can produce a clearer signal when the rare class is being crowded out.

blocks.text: Normal points that sit near anomalies can mask them in a full dataset. Building each tree from a random subsample removes much of that interference and makes the two groups easier to separate. It also keeps each tree small.

title: Stop growing trees at `log2(n)` because anomalies isolate near the root
takeaway: Knowing where the signal lives lets you truncate the model without losing it.

blocks.text: A proper binary tree over `n` points has an average height near `log2(n)`. Anomalies, which isolate early, are unlikely to need more splits than that. Capping height saves construction time and memory, and the leaf records how many points remain unbuilt for scoring.

title: The anomaly score is normalized path length, centered at 0.5
takeaway: A bounded, comparable score turns path lengths into a usable ranking.

blocks.text: Scores average the isolation depth across trees and normalize it by the expected path length for the sample size. Values near 1 indicate anomalies, values well below 0.5 indicate normal points, and a cluster around 0.5 means the sample has no clear anomaly. Sorting by score and taking the top `m` produces the final labels.

title: Steganography hides that a message exists; encryption only hides what it says
takeaway: Layering concealment over encryption means an intercepted file never even looks like a payload.

blocks.text: Cryptography makes a message unreadable to whoever intercepts it, but the intercept itself is visible and suspicious. Steganography instead hides the fact that anything was sent, using a carrier such as an image, an audio file or a network packet. Neither technique is sufficient alone, so the strongest setups encrypt the payload and then conceal it.

title: A 24-bit image stores far more colour precision than the eye can resolve
takeaway: Redundancy, not secrecy, is what turns an ordinary photo into a usable hiding place.

blocks.text: An image is a grid of numbers describing colour intensity, and in a 24-bit RGB file each pixel spends 8 bits on each of red, green and blue. Human vision cannot resolve a one-step change in any of those channels, so the low bits are spare capacity. Every image technique in the field is a way of spending that spare precision on data.

title: Replace the low bit of every colour channel with one payload bit
takeaway: The cheapest place to hide data is in the bits the display already ignores.

blocks.text: LSB substitution turns the payload into a bitstream and overwrites the least significant bit of some or all bytes in the image. In 24-bit colour that is three bits per pixel, and each channel shifts by at most one step in intensity. An 800 × 600 image therefore holds 1,440,000 bits, roughly 175 KB, with no difference a person can see.

title: Sequential LSB is trivial to recover, so a key should choose the pixels
takeaway: Embedding in a fixed order gives the payload away to anyone who knows the technique.

blocks.text: Conventional LSB substitution starts at pixel 0 and runs forward until the payload ends. Anyone who suspects a payload can read those low bits in order and reconstruct it without breaking any encryption. Sender and receiver can share a secret key that decides which pixels get modified, making the embedding pattern itself part of the secret.

title: Adaptive LSB spends more bits where the image can hide them
takeaway: Matching embedding depth to local image content buys capacity without raising visible distortion.

blocks.text: Flat, textured and edge regions tolerate different amounts of change before an edit shows. Adaptive LSB analyses brightness, edges and texture, assigns a `k` to each region and then performs k-bit substitution there, keeping `k` high in busy areas and low in sensitive ones. Pixel-value differencing is a concrete version: it derives `k` from the difference between two neighbouring pixels in a block.

title: Palette images break LSB because the pixel value is a table index
takeaway: A one-bit edit is only invisible when neighbouring values are also visually similar.

blocks.text: In GIF and other palette formats a pixel byte indexes a colour lookup table instead of naming a colour directly, and the bit depth is capped at 8, so at most 256 colours exist. Changing the low bit moves that index to a neighbouring entry, which may be an unrelated colour, making the edit obvious. Sorting the palette by colour, or padding it with near-duplicate colours when the image uses fewer than 256, keeps adjacent indices close in appearance.

title: Spatial embedding is simple and fragile; frequency embedding is robust and complex
takeaway: Pick the embedding domain from what will happen to the file after you embed.

blocks.text: Editing pixel values directly is easy and works best on lossless formats, because a later re-compression can overwrite the payload. Frequency techniques transform the image first and hide data in coefficients that compression, cropping and other processing disturb less, at the cost of transform mathematics. The carrier decides the domain: PNG, GIF and BMP suit direct edits, while JPEG calls for transform-domain work.

title: Sandwich the payload between JPEG's lossy and lossless stages
takeaway: In a lossy pipeline, hide data after the loss and before the encoding that preserves it.

blocks.text: JPEG converts RGB to YCbCr, downsamples chroma, then quantises 8 × 8 DCT blocks, and that quantisation is where irreversible loss happens. The resulting coefficients are then Huffman-coded, a step that reproduces bits exactly. Embedding after quantisation but before Huffman means the substituted bits are never rounded away, which is how a format assumed unusable for steganography still carries a payload.

title: Python integers have no fixed width because they are variable-length arrays
takeaway: Arbitrary precision is a data-structure choice, not a language magic trick.

blocks.text: A CPython integer is a C struct whose digits live in a heap-allocated array, so its storage grows with the value instead of stopping at 64 bits. Since Python 3 every integer uses this bignum representation, and the only ceiling is the memory of the machine. That is why 2^20000 evaluates to a number while a C `powl` call returns `inf`.

title: `ob_size` and `ob_digit` make an int as stretchy as a list
takeaway: The same variable-length header that lets a list grow is what lets an integer grow.

blocks.text: CPython's integer struct embeds `PyObject_VAR_HEAD`, the header shared with bytes, tuples and lists. It expands into `ob_size`, the count of digits in use, and `ob_digit`, an array of `uint32_t` declared with length one that is really a pointer and can be reallocated. Allocation is deliberately over-provisioned, and `ob_size` alone decides how many of those slots carry meaning.

title: CPython packs 30 bits into each digit instead of one decimal place
takeaway: Base choice is where a bignum implementation wins or loses its memory efficiency.

blocks.text: Putting a single decimal digit in each 32-bit slot would waste most of every word. CPython instead stores the value in base 2^30, so a digit runs from 0 to 1,073,741,823 and nearly fills its 32 bits while keeping grade-school arithmetic intact. Digits are ordered least significant first, which makes 2^60 an `ob_size` of 3 with `ob_digit` equal to `[0, 0, 1]`.

title: Addition walks the digits with a carry, exactly like grade school
takeaway: Arbitrary precision reduces to looping over digits with a carry, which is why it is cheap to implement.

blocks.text: Because a number is stored as a sequence of base-2^30 digits, `x_add` in `longobject.c` adds corresponding positions and propagates a carry into the next one. `x_sub` mirrors it with a borrow. No special big-number hardware is involved; the loops implement the same procedure taught on paper, just in a much wider base.

title: Multiplication switches to Karatsuba rather than n² schoolbook passes
takeaway: Past a certain operand size, the multiplication algorithm matters more than the machine.

blocks.text: Naive digit-by-digit multiplication costs quadratic time in the number of digits. CPython implements Karatsuba in `k_mul` and `k_lopsided_mul`, splitting operands and combining three smaller products to achieve O(n^log₂3) growth. Addition and subtraction stay linear, so multiplication is where bignum cost actually becomes visible.

title: Small integers from -5 to 256 are shared singletons
takeaway: The most common values never pay allocation cost, and the exact range is worth knowing.

blocks.text: CPython preallocates every integer in the range -5 to 256 during initialisation. Since integers are immutable, the runtime can return a reference to an existing object instead of building a new one. `IS_SMALL_INT` and `get_small_int` implement the shortcut, which covers most counters and list indices in ordinary code.

title: Breaking the interpreter on purpose is the fastest way to learn how it runs
takeaway: A deliberately wrong build teaches internals that a correct one hides.

blocks.text: Reading CPython's C source only goes so far; changing one behaviour forces you to follow the path from source text to opcode to C function. Rewriting addition to pick a random operator makes that path impossible to skip. The change is small, but it touches the evaluation loop, the numeric API and every caller that assumes addition adds.

title: The patched build returns 0, 10 or 24 for `4 + 6`
takeaway: A visibly wrong answer proves the change reached the part of the pipeline that matters.

blocks.text: In the modified interpreter, `4 + 6` is routed through a randomly chosen operation. Depending on the pick it yields 10 for addition, 0 for subtraction, 24 for multiplication, and other values for division and exponentiation. Correctness disappears, but each output maps to one identifiable operation.

title: `BINARY_ADD` is opcode 23, and arithmetic is a stack operation
takeaway: Operators are dispatch entries in a stack machine, which is why one opcode edit changes every addition.

blocks.text: CPython compiles `a + b` into a `BINARY_ADD` instruction, opcode value 23. When the evaluation loop reaches it, the instruction pops two operands off the stack, performs the addition and pushes the result back. The patch guards the operands with `PyNumber_Check` so it only fires on numeric objects.

title: Randomise by dispatching across the existing `PyNumber_*` functions
takeaway: Reusing the runtime's own operator table keeps the experiment to a few lines.

blocks.text: CPython already exposes one C function per arithmetic operation: `PyNumber_Add`, `PyNumber_Subtract`, `PyNumber_Multiply`, `PyNumber_FloorDivide` and `PyNumber_Power`. The patch takes the current epoch second modulo the number of choices to select one, then calls a helper that applies that function to both operands. Randomness comes from the clock, so no extra state is needed.

title: Instrumenting a function used during startup segfaults the build
takeaway: Any hook on a core operation fires during boot, not only when a user asks for it.

blocks.text: The first rebuild crashed during `make`, because the modified addition path also runs while the interpreter bootstraps itself. Random subtraction and multiplication broke invariants that initialisation code depends on, producing segmentation faults before a prompt ever appeared. A patch written with interactive use in mind still executes for every non-interactive caller.

title: Thread a source flag from `PyRun_InteractiveLoopFlags` down to the opcode
takeaway: Scope a risky experiment by where the call came from, not by guessing which callers exist.

blocks.text: The fix records the origin of the request: `PyRun_InteractiveLoopFlags` supplies a `source` value of 1 for the REPL, while every other entry point defaults to 0. That flag is passed down the call chain to the opcode evaluation site, where the random operator is used only for interactive input. Scripts and interpreter startup keep real addition.

title: MongoDB paginates either by skipping rows or by seeking past the last id
takeaway: Two pagination primitives look equivalent at small scale and diverge as the collection grows.

blocks.text: Offset pagination tells the cursor to discard `n` documents and return the next page. Keyset pagination remembers the last document's `_id` and asks for everything greater than it. Both return correct pages; they differ in how their cost responds to a larger result set.

title: `skip(n)` plus `limit(n)` is the whole offset recipe
takeaway: Offset pagination is two cursor calls and no stored state.

blocks.text: A MongoDB `find()` returns a cursor over the collection, and page `p` is simply `skip(p × size)` followed by `limit(size)`. The database does the slicing, which avoids shipping documents to the client that the client will throw away. Nothing about the previous page needs to be remembered for the next request.

title: ObjectIds sort naturally because their leading bytes are a timestamp
takeaway: The document id doubles as an insertion-ordered cursor key.

blocks.text: A MongoDB `ObjectId` is 12 bytes: four bytes of epoch seconds, a three-byte machine identifier, a two-byte process id and a three-byte counter starting from a random value. That layout gives ids a natural order, so the usual less-than and greater-than comparisons behave as expected. `_id` is indexed by default, which makes a range filter on it cheap.

title: Keyset pagination is a range query from the last id you saw
takeaway: Remembering the boundary instead of the offset removes the work that grows with page number.

blocks.text: Fetch one page, keep the `_id` of its final document, and request the next page with a filter for `_id` greater than that value plus the same limit. Each query enters the index at a known position rather than counting forward from the start of the collection. The client carries exactly one id between requests.

title: `skip` is slow because MongoDB walks every document it discards
takeaway: A skip is a read you pay for and then throw away.

blocks.text: MongoDB's own documentation warns that `cursor.skip` must iterate over the documents it skips rather than jumping to a stored offset. Reading the implementation confirms the skip path does no index lookup to find its starting point. Cost therefore scales with how far into the result set a page begins, which is exactly what late pages ask for.

title: Indexing the collection does not speed up `skip`
takeaway: Some costs are not index problems, and treating them as such wastes tuning effort.

blocks.text: An index helps a query find matching documents, but skipping happens after matching and does not consult that index. So the intuition that a better index will fix slow deep pages is wrong. The work stays proportional to the distance from the start of the result set, no matter how the collection is indexed.

title: `skip` is efficient for small result sets, which is why it survives
takeaway: Judge `skip` by the depth you actually page to, not by its worst case.

blocks.text: With a small result set, walking a few hundred documents costs almost nothing, and offset pagination stays the simpler option. That is why MongoDB kept the method and why the community never abandoned it. The deciding variable is page depth, not a blanket rule against skipping.

title: Keyset pagination stays flat while offset pagination degrades past a few hundred documents
takeaway: The choice between pagination styles is a question about collection size, not correctness.

blocks.text: The benchmark paged through an unindexed collection with both strategies and timed every page. Below roughly 500-600 documents the two were comparable. Beyond that point the `skip` and `limit` curve rose sharply, while `_id` and `limit` remained close to constant as the collection grew.

title: The crossover sits near 500-600 documents, and the keyset curve stays level after it
takeaway: A crossover point is more useful to a team than a claim that one method is faster.

blocks.text: Both approaches fetched a fixed page size, with each page timed three times and the results averaged. The curves overlapped until the collection reached roughly 500-600 documents, then offset pagination climbed while keyset pagination held steady. Repeating the run on different machines and disks produced the same shape.

items: Collection was not indexed.
Page size was held fixed.
Each page was fetched 3 times and averaged.
Comparable below ~500-600 documents; keyset near-constant beyond.

title: Below the crossover, prefer `skip` and `limit` for its simplicity
takeaway: Adopt the more complex pagination only where the measurements show it paying off.

blocks.text: For smaller result sets the benchmark found no meaningful difference, so the simpler offset approach is the reasonable default. Keyset pagination earns its extra moving part only when pages go deep. Page size also changes the picture: once a page exceeds about 100 documents, the gap narrows, though that region was not benchmarked in detail.

title: Isolated latency spikes are disk contention, not a pagination result
takeaway: Separate storage noise from query cost before drawing a performance curve.

blocks.text: Some page timings jumped above the trend line for both strategies. Those spikes come from disk contention rather than from either query shape. A single slow sample can look like a performance cliff, so repeated runs and different disks are needed to confirm that the curve is real.

title: An HTTP request is text you can type into a TCP socket
takeaway: Seeing the wire format once makes every HTTP client and framework less mysterious.

blocks.text: Clients such as curl, requests and Postman assemble the request message for you, which hides the fact that HTTP is a line-oriented text protocol running over TCP. Connecting to a server with netcat and typing the request yourself uses the same connection those tools use. The reply comes back as raw bytes with headers and body intact.

title: `nc` supplies the socket; standard input supplies the request
takeaway: A TCP connection plus a keyboard is a complete HTTP client.

blocks.text: Running netcat against the server's host and port opens a TCP connection and attaches standard input to it. Anything typed afterwards travels over that connection, and whatever the server writes back appears in the terminal. There is no request builder, no URL parsing and no header defaults between you and the protocol.

title: Bytes that are not a valid request line earn a 400
takeaway: HTTP servers do not guess intent; malformed input fails at the first line.

blocks.text: Typing a plain sentence into the socket produced `400 Bad Request` and a matching entry in the Flask log. The server tried to parse the input as an HTTP message, failed at the request line and rejected it. Any text sent to an HTTP port is treated as protocol, never as a free-form message.

title: The method and headers decide how the server reads the rest
takeaway: Changing what you send changes where the server looks for your data.
section: Complex Requests and HTTP Request Messages

blocks.text: A request opens with a method, a path and the protocol version, then headers, then a blank line before any body. A `GET` puts its parameters in the path, a form `POST` sends key-value pairs in the body, and a JSON `POST` sends an object there instead. The method and headers tell the server which endpoint logic and which parser to apply.

title: Send one real request by hand before reaching for a client library
takeaway: One manual request turns the protocol from an abstraction into something you have watched happen.

blocks.text: A local server on a non-public port makes this safe: nothing leaves the machine and malformed requests only hurt a throwaway process.

items: Start a minimal HTTP server and confirm one endpoint answers in a browser.
Open a TCP connection with `nc` to that host and port.
Type a `GET` request line, a `Host` header and a blank line, then read the raw response.
Repeat with a query parameter, a form-encoded `POST` and a JSON `POST`.
Compare the bytes on screen with what curl prints for the same call.
